\newpage

# HOW TO USE THIS PACK

1. **The pack is in two parts.** Part A holds the twenty question papers. Part B holds the answer key, marking scheme, curriculum blueprint, cognitive-level distribution, quality-control summary and examiner notes for each paper. **Photocopy Part A for the candidates only.**
2. **Each paper stands alone.** A paper may be used as an end-of-topic test as soon as its sub-strand has been taught, or several papers may be combined into a terminal mock.
3. **Edit page one of a paper before printing.** The school name, the academic year and the examination title are meant to be changed to suit your school.
4. **Timing.** Each paper is set for 2 hours: about 40 minutes for Section A and 80 minutes for Section B. Candidates who are new to the format should be given the full time.
5. **Figures.** Every figure is drawn in pencil style and prints clearly in black and white. Check the photocopies before the examination; a figure that has printed faintly should be redrawn on the chalkboard.
6. **Marking.** Section B answers are marked against the points listed in the marking scheme. The italic *Marking note* under each part states what is compulsory for the mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors. Accept any other correct and relevant answer.
7. **Recording.** Use the mark-sheet grids in this pack to record the papers written by each candidate, and the Section A answer sheet for the objective test.
8. **Difficulty.** Every paper is built to approximately 30% easy, 50% moderate and 20% challenging items, weighted by marks. A class average of 50-60% on a paper is normal at the first attempt.

\newpage

# INSTRUCTIONS TO THE INVIGILATOR

1. Seat the candidates so that no candidate can see another's work. Collect all notes, textbooks and mobile telephones before the papers are given out.
2. Give out the question paper and the answer booklet together. Candidates may use a pencil, a ruler and an eraser; calculators are not required for any paper in this pack.
3. Read out the instructions on page one of the paper and announce the starting time and the finishing time on the chalkboard.
4. Remind the candidates that **Section A carries 40 marks and Section B carries 60 marks**, and that all questions in both sections must be answered.
5. Allow no talking, no lending of instruments and no leaving of the room in the first and the last fifteen minutes.
6. Announce the time remaining thirty minutes and ten minutes before the end.
7. At the end, collect the answer sheets first and then the answer booklets, counting them against the number of candidates before anyone leaves.
8. Report any irregularity in writing to the head teacher on the same day.

## 2. The curriculum areas in full

*The wording of every content standard and indicator below is taken from the NaCCA Common Core Programme Science Curriculum (B7/JHS1 - B7/JHS1), 2021 edition. The curriculum areas (topics) are the teaching headings used in the blueprint of each paper to group the items under an indicator.*

### STRAND 1: Diversity of Matter

#### Sub-Strand 1: Materials — Paper 1

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.1.1.1** — Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.1* — Classify materials into liquids, solids and gases.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.2* — Discuss the importance of liquids in the life of humans.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.3* — Discuss the importance of specific solids to life.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.1.1.2** — Understand the periodic table as different elements made up of metals and non-metals and noble gases arranged in an order.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.2.1* — Demonstrate the knowledge of the orderly arrangement of metals, non-metals and noble gases in the periodic table.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 1.1 Materials and Their Properties; 1.2 Solids, Liquids and Gases Compared; 1.3 The Importance of Liquids to Life; 1.4 The Importance of Solids to Life; 1.5 The First Twenty Elements and Their Symbols; 1.6 Metals, Non-Metals and Noble Gases in the Periodic Table.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells — Paper 2

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.1.2.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the structure of organisms and functions of cells in living systems.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.2.1.1* — Describe the structure and function of living cells of an animal.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.1.2.1.2* — State the functions of each organelle in a plant cell.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 2.1 Cells as the Units of Living Things; 2.2 The Structure of the Animal Cell; 2.3 Functions of the Organelles of the Animal Cell; 2.4 The Structure of the Plant Cell; 2.5 Functions of the Organelles of the Plant Cell; 2.6 Comparing Plant and Animal Cells.

### STRAND 2: Cycles

#### Sub-Strand 1: Earth Science — Paper 3

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.2.1.1** — Recognise that the water cycle is an example of repeated patterns of change in nature and understand how it occurs.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.1.1.1* — Explain how the water cycle occurs as a repeated pattern of change in nature.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.1.1.2* — Describe the importance of the water cycle.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 3.1 Natural Sources of Water; 3.2 Evaporation and Transpiration; 3.3 Condensation and Cloud Formation; 3.4 Precipitation, Run-off and Collection; 3.5 The Water Cycle as a Repeated Pattern; 3.6 The Importance of the Water Cycle.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms — Paper 4

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.2.2.1** — Show skills in showing the stages of the life cycle of the housefly, the effects of its activities on humans and how to reduce them.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.2.1.1* — Describe the life cycle of the housefly.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.2.1.2* — Discuss the housefly as a menace to humans and how to reduce it.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 4.1 Life Cycles and Metamorphosis; 4.2 The Stages of the Life Cycle of the Housefly; 4.3 Features of Each Stage of the Housefly; 4.4 Feeding Habits and Breeding Places of the Housefly; 4.5 The Housefly as a Menace to Humans; 4.6 Reducing the Housefly Menace in the Community.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production — Paper 5

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.2.3.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the different plant nutrients (organic and inorganic fertilizers) and their application in school farming or gardening.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.3.1.1* — Observe and list all the sources of plant nutrients in the community and categorise them as organic or inorganic.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.3.1.2* — Describe the physical characteristics of the different plant nutrients and how each of them is applied in the field.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 5.1 Plant Nutrients and the Needs of Crops; 5.2 Organic Sources of Plant Nutrients; 5.3 Inorganic Sources of Plant Nutrients; 5.4 Comparing Organic and Inorganic Sources; 5.5 Physical Characteristics of the Nutrient Sources; 5.6 Applying Plant Nutrients in the Field and School Garden.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production — Paper 6

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.2.4.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the differences among domestic animals (ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, which are monogastric herbivores).
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.1.1* — Examine and list the domestic animals found in the community.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.1.2* — Show the differences and similarities among ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.2.4.2** — Demonstrate understanding of the usefulness of the different types of animals for domestic and commercial purposes.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.2.1* — Discuss and write the domestic and commercial uses of the different types of animals.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.2.2* — Observe and compare the uses of the different types of animals, including their by-products.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 6.1 Domestic Animals and their Breeds; 6.2 Ruminants; 6.3 Monogastric Animals and Poultry; 6.4 Comparing Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry; 6.5 Domestic Uses of Animals; 6.6 Commercial Uses and By-Products.

### STRAND 3: Systems

#### Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System — Paper 7

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.3.1.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the concept of food, the process of digestion and its importance in humans.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.1* — Explain the concept of food and the need to eat.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.2* — Examine what happens to food at the various stages of digestion.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.3* — Identify the end products of digestion of starchy, protein and oily foods and explain how they are absorbed.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 7.1 The Concept of Food and the Need to Eat; 7.2 The Parts of the Alimentary Canal; 7.3 What Happens to Food at Each Stage of Digestion; 7.4 End Products of Digestion; 7.5 Absorption and the Use of Digested Food; 7.6 Food Tests.

#### Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System — Paper 8

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.3.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of the inner planets of the solar system and understand their movement in the system.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.2.1.1* — Identify the inner planets of the solar system and describe their properties.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.2.1.2* — Discuss the properties and the relative motions of the planets Mercury and Venus.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 8.1 The Solar System and the Sun; 8.2 The Inner Planets and Their Properties; 8.3 The Galaxy and the Milky Way; 8.4 The Paths and Movements of the Planets; 8.5 The Planets Mercury and Venus; 8.6 Making a Model of the Solar System.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem — Paper 9

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.3.3.1** — Recognise the components of and interdependences in an ecosystem, and appreciate their interactions.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.3.1.1* — Analyse the components of ecosystems and identify the interactions within.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 9.1 The Concept of an Ecosystem; 9.2 Terrestrial, Aquatic and Arboreal Ecosystems; 9.3 Biotic Components of an Ecosystem; 9.4 Abiotic Components of an Ecosystem; 9.5 Organisms of Different Ecosystems; 9.6 Interactions and Interdependence in an Ecosystem.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems — Paper 10

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.3.4.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the differences among the various farming systems: Land Rotation, Crop Rotation, Mixed Cropping, Mixed Farming, and Organic Farming.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.1* — Examine and discuss the differences among the various farming systems.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.2* — Categorise different farming systems.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.3* — Discuss the usefulness of different farming systems.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 10.1 Meaning and Types of Farming Systems; 10.2 Land Rotation; 10.3 Crop Rotation; 10.4 Mixed Cropping; 10.5 Mixed Farming; 10.6 Organic Farming and the Choice of a System.

### STRAND 4: Forces and Energy

#### Sub-Strand 1: Energy — Paper 11

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of forms of energy and their daily applications.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.1.1* — Identify the various forms of energy and show how they are related.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.1.2* — Explain daily applications of forms of energy.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.2** — Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of heat transfer and its applications in life.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.2.1* — Explain and demonstrate how heat is transferred in various media.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.3** — Demonstrate understanding of characteristics of light, such as travelling in a straight line, reflection, refraction and dispersion.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.3.1* — Demonstrate how light travels in a straight line.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 11.1 Forms of Energy; 11.2 Potential, Kinetic and Mechanical Energy; 11.3 Daily Applications of Energy; 11.4 Calculating Potential and Kinetic Energy; 11.5 Transfer of Heat; 11.6 Characteristics of Light.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics — Paper 12

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.2.1** — Demonstrate understanding of forms of electricity, its generation and effects on the environment.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.1.1* — Describe the various forms of electricity generation.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.1.2* — Explain the impact of electricity generation on the environment.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.2.2** — Demonstrate knowledge of how to assemble and explain the functions of basic electronic components and their interdependence in an electronic circuit.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.1* — Demonstrate how to assemble basic electronic components in an electronic circuit.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.2* — Discuss the function of each electronic component and their interdependence with each other.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.3* — Discuss the function of each electronic component such as resistor, diode, and inductor, and their interdependence for the functioning of an electronic gadget.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 12.1 Generation of Thermal and Nuclear Electricity; 12.2 Effects of Electricity Generation on the Environment; 12.3 Basic Electronic Components and Their Functions; 12.4 The P-N Junction Diode; 12.5 Assembling a Simple Electronic Circuit; 12.6 How the Components Affect One Another.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy — Paper 13

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.3.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the principle of conservation and conversion of energy and their application in real life situations.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.1* — Explain the principle underlying conservation and conversion of energy.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.2* — Demonstrate the conversion of energy into useable forms.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.3* — Know how energy could be conserved for future use in life.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 13.1 The Law of Conservation of Energy; 13.2 Energy Conversions in Everyday Devices; 13.3 Energy Chains and Simple Calculations; 13.4 Useful Energy and Wasted Energy; 13.5 Conserving Energy for the Future.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion — Paper 14

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.4.1** — Examine the concept of motion, Newton's first law of motion, magnetic force in relation to motion and understand their applications to life.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.1* — Understand that unbalanced forces acting on an object cause it to move.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.2* — State and explain Newton's First Law of motion.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.3* — Examine the application of Newton's First Law of motion in life.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.4* — Demonstrate the behaviour of magnet and its use to life.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.4.2** — Recognise some simple machines, and show understanding of their efficiency in doing work.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.2.2* — Describe the types and functions of levers.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.2.3* — Know work input, and output and efficiency as they apply to machines.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 14.1 Forces, Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Inertia; 14.2 Newton's First Law of Motion; 14.3 Applications of Newton's First Law in Everyday Life; 14.4 Magnets: Their Behaviour and Uses; 14.5 Simple Machines and the Classes of Levers; 14.6 Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools — Paper 15

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.4.5.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in handling and maintenance of basic and simple agricultural tools.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.5.1.1* — Explain the basic rules in handling and maintaining simple agricultural tools.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.4.5.1.2* — Apply the handling and maintenance of basic and simple agricultural tools in their community.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 15.1 Simple Agricultural Tools and Their Uses; 15.2 The Meaning and Importance of Handling and Maintenance; 15.3 Basic Rules for Handling Tools Safely; 15.4 Maintenance Practices for Particular Tools; 15.5 Applying Tool Handling and Maintenance in the Community.

### STRAND 5: Humans and the Environment

#### Sub-Strand 1: Waste Management — Paper 16

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.1.1** — Exhibit knowledge and skill of scientific basis for management practices of types of waste in the environment.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.1.1.1* — Apply information from research on good management practices of waste to make the environment clean.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 16.1 Types and Sources of Waste; 16.2 Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Waste; 16.3 Good Waste Management Practices; 16.4 Composting and the Science Behind It; 16.5 Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Human Health — Paper 17

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of common deficiency diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.2.1.1* — Explain the relationship between food nutrients and common deficiency diseases and how they affect humans.
- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.2.2** — Demonstrate knowledge of the nature of selected viral diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and management.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.2.2.1* — Explain the nature of viral diseases with special emphasis on corona virus (COVID-19), Ebola and H1N1 disease, its causes, symptoms, effects on humans and its prevention.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 17.1 Food Nutrients and Their Uses in the Body; 17.2 Deficiency Diseases and the Nutrients Concerned; 17.3 Symptoms, Effects and Prevention of Deficiency Diseases; 17.4 The Nature and Transmission of Viral Diseases; 17.5 Symptoms, Effects and Prevention of COVID-19, Ebola and H1N1; 17.6 Roles of the Individual, the Community and Government.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry — Paper 18

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.3.1** — Realise how careers in science can improve human life, and research about Ghanaian and internationally recognised scientists and science educators and model after them.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.3.1.1* — Discover and explain how careers in science can improve human conditions and relate these careers to the work of great national and international scientists and science educators.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 18.1 Careers in Science and What Each Worker Does; 18.2 Ghanaian Scientists and Science Educators; 18.3 Internationally Recognised Scientists and Their Work; 18.4 The Impact of Science, Technology and Innovation; 18.5 Science and Technology Careers Ghana Must Focus On.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Climate Change and Green Economy — Paper 19

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.4.1** — Demonstrate understanding of sustainable energy choices and their impact on the environment.
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.4.1.1* — Search for information on ways sustainable energy choices and scientific ideas are used to protect the environment.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 19.1 Sustainable and Non-Sustainable Energy Choices; 19.2 Scientific Ideas Used to Protect the Environment; 19.3 The Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming; 19.4 Minimising Greenhouse Effects and Coping with Climate Change; 19.5 Local Projects that Sustain Energy, and Green Jobs.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Understanding the Environment — Paper 20

- **Content standard B7/JHS1.5.5.1** — Demonstrate understanding of different plants and animals found in different land forms and how they survive (with emphasis on land forms in Ghana).
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.5.1.1* — List and describe the different types of plants and animals that live in different land forms such as plateau, plain, mountain and valley (with emphasis on land forms in Ghana).
  - *Indicator B7/JHS1.5.5.1.2* — Explain the nature of associations that exist among plants and animals in different land forms and their mechanisms for survival.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 20.1 Land Forms in Ghana and the Living Things Found in Them; 20.2 Characteristics that Enable Animals to Live in a Land Form; 20.3 Characteristics that Enable Plants to Survive in a Land Form; 20.4 Associations among Plants and Animals; 20.5 Mechanisms for Survival, Field Study and the Album.

**Strand 1: Diversity of Matter | Sub-Strand 1: Materials | B7/JHS1.1.1.1 and B7/JHS1.1.1.2**

# BEACON EDUCATIONAL CONSULT

## INTEGRATED SCIENCE (SCIENCE)

### BECE-STYLE MOCK EXAMINATION (PAPER 1)

**Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)  
**Time:** 2 hours (Suggested: Section A - 40 min; Section B - 80 min)  
**Total Marks:** 100  
**Academic Year:** 2026/2027 Academic Year

---

### INSTRUCTIONS

1. Write your name and class clearly in the spaces provided on your answer sheet.
2. This paper has TWO sections: Section A and Section B.
3. Answer ALL the questions in both sections.
4. Section A has 40 multiple-choice questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) and record it on the answer sheet provided.
5. Section B has 6 theory questions totalling 60 marks. Write your answers clearly and neatly in your answer booklet. Study the figures carefully before you answer the questions on them.
6. Use a pencil and a ruler where a diagram, a labelled sketch or a table is required. Do not use correction fluid.
7. Hand in your answer sheet and your answer booklet at the end of the examination.

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Anything that has mass and occupies space is called

A. a force
B. a shadow
C. matter
D. energy

**2.** The three states in which materials are commonly found are

A. wood, metal and glass
B. hard, soft and rough
C. natural, artificial and waste
D. solid, liquid and gas

**3.** A pupil described a material as hard, rough and grey, and said that it kept its own shape. The material is MOST likely

A. palm oil
B. a stone
C. cooking gas
D. kerosene

**4.** Which of the following properties would a pupil record by LOOKING at a material only?

A. Its smell
B. Its colour
C. Its temperature
D. Its mass

**5.** Which group contains only solids?

A. Chalk, sand, iron nail
B. Sand, petrol, oxygen
C. Chalk, water, iron nail
D. Iron nail, air, palm oil

**6.** Which of the following is a liquid at room temperature?

A. Oxygen
B. Charcoal
C. Groundnut oil
D. Common salt

**7.** A material that has no colour, cannot be held in the hand and spreads to fill the whole room is

A. a liquid
B. a gas
C. a solid
D. a mixture of solids

**8.** A material that has a fixed shape and a fixed volume is

A. a solid
B. a gas
C. a vapour
D. a liquid

**9.** A liquid has

A. both a fixed shape and a fixed volume
B. a fixed shape but no fixed volume
C. neither a fixed volume nor a fixed mass
D. a fixed volume but no fixed shape

**10.** Water poured from a bucket into a bottle takes the shape of the bottle. This shows that a liquid

A. has no mass of its own
B. has no shape of its own
C. has no volume of its own
D. changes into a gas in the bottle

**11.** In which state of matter are the particles packed closely together in a regular pattern?

A. Vapour
B. Gas
C. Liquid
D. Solid

**12.** The particles of a gas are

A. far apart and move about freely
B. joined in long chains that cannot move
C. close together but able to slide over one another
D. close together and fixed in position

**13.** A cylinder of cooking gas feels heavy because

A. a gas has no mass but the air presses on it
B. a gas has mass even though it cannot be seen
C. the gas has a fixed shape inside the cylinder
D. the gas has turned into a solid inside

**14.** Which property is shared by solids, liquids and gases?

A. They can all be compressed easily
B. They all have mass and occupy space
C. They all have a fixed shape
D. They can all be poured from one container into another

**15.** The liquid that is most important for the survival of humans is

A. kerosene
B. petrol
C. water
D. palm oil

**16.** Which of the following is a use of water in the human body?

A. It hardens the bones of the body
B. It changes food into oxygen
C. It helps in the digestion and transport of food
D. It makes the body produce light

**17.** Blood is an important liquid in the body because it

A. carries food and oxygen to all parts of the body
B. stores all the fat of the body
C. removes bones that are damaged
D. keeps the bones stiff and strong

**18.** A farmer at Techiman uses a liquid obtained from the oil palm fruit for cooking. The liquid is

A. palm oil
B. vinegar
C. kerosene
D. petrol

**19.** Which of the following shows the need to preserve liquids in a community?

A. Pouring left-over drinking water on the ground
B. Leaving the tap running while brushing the teeth
C. Covering the water in a storage drum and using it carefully
D. Washing the compound with pipe-borne water every morning

**20.** A tanker of petrol is important to a town MAINLY because petrol is used

A. for drinking during the dry season
B. as a fuel in vehicles and machines
C. for watering crops on a farm
D. for washing cooking utensils

**21.** Which practice would BEST protect the liquid stored in a water tank at a school?

A. Keeping the tank covered and cleaning it regularly
B. Siting the tank beside the refuse dump
C. Allowing pupils to dip their cups into the tank
D. Leaving the lid open so that air can enter

**22.** Which solid material is used MAINLY for roofing buildings in many Ghanaian towns?

A. Glass
B. Cotton wool
C. Rubber
D. Aluminium sheet

**23.** A solid obtained from plants and used for making tables and chairs is

A. clay
B. cement
C. iron
D. wood

**24.** Common salt is an important solid in the home because it

A. adds taste to food and supplies minerals the body needs
B. makes food cook without fire
C. keeps the kitchen cool
D. turns food into a liquid

**25.** Which of the following solids is used by a mason to build a wall?

A. Palm fronds
B. Rubber tyres
C. Cement blocks
D. Cotton cloth

**26.** Iron is widely used for making farm tools such as cutlasses MAINLY because it is

A. shiny and colourful
B. cheap and smooth
C. hard and strong
D. light and soft

**27.** A Basic 7 class was asked to explain why useful solids in the environment should be preserved. The BEST reason is that

A. they are found only in the forest zone
B. they are limited in supply and are needed by humans and other living things
C. they are too heavy to be carried away
D. they lose their colour when they are used

**28.** A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical method is

A. an element
B. a mixture
C. an alloy
D. a solution

**29.** The chemical symbol of sodium is

A. So
B. Sn
C. S
D. Na

**30.** The element whose chemical symbol is K is

A. potassium
B. carbon
C. calcium
D. krypton

**31.** Which of the following gives the correct symbol of calcium?

A. Cl
B. C
C. Cm
D. Ca

**32.** The first element in the periodic table is

A. oxygen
B. helium
C. hydrogen
D. lithium

**33.** The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of increasing

A. atomic number
B. the date on which the element was discovered
C. mass of one litre of the element
D. the first letter of the name of the element

**34.** An element has atomic number 8. The element is

A. sulphur
B. carbon
C. oxygen
D. neon

**35.** Which of the following is a property of MOST metals?

A. They break easily into powder
B. They are poor conductors of heat
C. They are always liquids at room temperature
D. They conduct heat and electricity

**36.** Which of the following elements is a non-metal?

A. Aluminium
B. Sulphur
C. Potassium
D. Magnesium

**37.** Helium, neon and argon are grouped together in the periodic table because they

A. burn easily in air
B. are all liquids at room temperature
C. are all metals
D. are unreactive gases

**38.** Elements that are found in the same group of the periodic table

A. have exactly the same mass
B. have similar chemical properties
C. are all metals
D. have the same atomic number

**39.** Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are all found in Period 3 of the periodic table. This means that they

A. belong to the same group
B. have the same number of protons
C. are in the same horizontal row of the table
D. are all noble gases

**40.** A pupil found that a shiny element conducted electricity, could be beaten into sheets and did not break when it was bent. The element is BEST described as

A. a mixture
B. a non-metal
C. a noble gas
D. a metal

## SECTION B: THEORY (60 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Write your answers in your answer booklet. The marks for each question are shown in brackets.*

### Question 1  [10 marks]

Fig. 1 shows three sealed jars, **P**, **Q** and **R**. Each jar holds a different material, and the small circles stand for the particles of the material.

![Fig. 1: Three sealed jars holding different materials.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig86.png)

*Fig. 1: Three sealed jars holding different materials.*

**(a)** State the state of matter of the material in EACH of the jars **P**, **Q** and **R**.  **[3 marks]**

**(b)** Give ONE reason, taken from Fig. 1, for EACH of your answers in (a).  **[3 marks]**

**(c)** The lid of jar **R** is taken off.

(i) State what happens to the material in the jar.  **[1 mark]**

(ii) Give a reason for your answer.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** Give ONE example, found in a Ghanaian home, of the material in jar **P** and ONE example of the material in jar **Q**.

---

### Question 2  [12 marks]

A Basic 7 class at Winneba collected the following materials from the school compound and the kitchen: a piece of chalk, borehole water, cooking gas in a cylinder, groundnut oil, river sand and the air inside a blown-up balloon.

**(a)** Copy and complete the table below in your answer booklet, writing each material under the correct heading.  **[6 marks]**

| Solids | Liquids | Gases |
|---|---|---|
| ......... | ......... | ......... |
| ......... | ......... | ......... |

**(b)** State whether EACH of the following has a fixed shape and whether it has a fixed volume:

(i) a solid;  **[1 mark]**

(ii) a liquid;  **[1 mark]**

(iii) a gas.  **[1 mark]**

**(c)** Describe a simple activity the class could carry out to show that a gas occupies space.

---

### Question 3  [10 marks]

The people of a village near Dormaa fetch water from a borehole and store it in covered drums at home. Other liquids used in the village are palm oil, kerosene and petrol.

**(a)** State FOUR uses of water in the home.  **[4 marks]**

**(b)** State TWO uses of water inside the human body.

**(c)** Give TWO reasons why the people of the village should preserve the water they fetch.

**(d)** Name ONE liquid used in the village other than water and state ONE use of it.

---

### Question 4  [10 marks]

A carpenter, a mason and a blacksmith work side by side in a small workshop at Suame. Between them they use wood, cement blocks, iron and glass.

**(a)** Copy and complete the table below in your answer booklet.  **[4 marks]**

| Solid material | ONE use of the material |
|---|---|
| Wood | ......... |
| Cement blocks | ......... |
| Iron | ......... |
| Glass | ......... |

**(b)** Give the property of the material that makes it suitable for the work named:

(i) iron for the blade of a cutlass;  **[2 marks]**

(ii) wood for a stool.  **[2 marks]**

**(c)** Suggest TWO ways in which the workers could help to preserve the solid materials they use.

---

### Question 5  [10 marks]

Fig. 2 shows part of the periodic table containing the first twenty elements. Four of the elements have been replaced by the letters **W**, **X**, **Y** and **Z**.

![Fig. 2: Part of the periodic table showing the first twenty elements.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig87.png)

*Fig. 2: Part of the periodic table showing the first twenty elements.*

**(a)** Name the elements represented by **W**, **X**, **Y** and **Z**.  **[4 marks]**

**(b)** (i) Which letter represents a noble gas?  **[1 mark]**

(ii) Which letter represents a non-metal that is not a noble gas?  **[1 mark]**

**(c)** (i) Name the element in Fig. 2 that is in the same group as **W**.  **[1 mark]**

(ii) State what elements in the same group of the periodic table have in common.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** State the rule by which the elements in Fig. 2 have been arranged from left to right, and give ONE piece of evidence from the figure that supports your answer.

---

### Question 6  [8 marks]

A Basic 7 pupil was given four labelled samples in the science room: carbon, sodium, aluminium and helium.

**(a)** Write the chemical symbol of EACH of the four elements.  **[4 marks]**

**(b)** Describe a simple test the pupil could carry out to find out whether the sample of aluminium is a metal.

**(c)** State TWO differences between metals and non-metals.

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** The smallest unit of a living organism that can carry out all the activities of life is

A. the system
B. the cell
C. the organ
D. the tissue

**2.** The instrument used in the laboratory to see cells clearly is

A. the microscope
B. the barometer
C. the stethoscope
D. the thermometer

**3.** A thin piece of onion was placed on a glass slide and viewed with a microscope. The many small boxes seen were

A. drops of water
B. crystals of salt
C. grains of sugar
D. cells

**4.** Which of the following statements about living things is correct?

A. Only animals are made up of cells
B. Both plants and animals are made up of cells
C. Only plants are made up of cells
D. Neither plants nor animals are made up of cells

**5.** A group of similar cells working together to perform the same work forms

A. an organism
B. a tissue
C. an organelle
D. an organ

**6.** The small structures found inside a cell, each doing a special work, are called

A. systems
B. tissues
C. organs
D. organelles

**7.** Which of the following parts is found in an animal cell?

A. Cell membrane
B. Cell wall
C. Chloroplast
D. Large central vacuole

**8.** The part of an animal cell that forms its outer boundary is the

A. cell wall
B. nucleus
C. cell membrane
D. cytoplasm

**9.** The jelly-like material in which the organelles of a cell float is the

A. nucleus
B. cell sap
C. chloroplast
D. cytoplasm

**10.** The largest organelle in a typical animal cell is usually the

A. ribosome
B. mitochondrion
C. nucleus
D. vacuole

**11.** Which of the following is NOT found in an animal cell?

A. Mitochondrion
B. Cell wall
C. Cytoplasm
D. Nucleus

**12.** The sausage-shaped organelles found in the cytoplasm of an animal cell are the

A. nuclei
B. chloroplasts
C. mitochondria
D. cell walls

**13.** An animal cell has an irregular shape MAINLY because

A. it has no cell wall to hold it in a fixed shape
B. it has no cell membrane
C. it has no nucleus
D. its cytoplasm is too thick to move

**14.** A cell was taken from the cheek lining of a goat. The cell would contain

A. chloroplasts, a cell wall and a nucleus
B. a cell wall, cytoplasm and a large vacuole
C. a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane
D. a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole

**15.** The part of the cell that controls all the activities of the cell is the

A. decreases each time the sun shines

D. The adult

**1.** Substances that plants take in from the soil for healthy growth are called

A. lacks enough plant nutrients

A. green manure

D. inorganic

A. are always applied in larger quantities

B. acts within one or two days

A. the soil becomes richer in humus each year

A. clear, colourless and watery

A. a dark crumbly heap
B. a wet, smelly paste
C. small hard granules in a sealed sack

**29.** Which of the following nutrient sources is a liquid?

A. Farmyard manure

A. dry, light and odourless

A. turns into compost when it is left open

**32.** Why is a bulky organic manure usually worked into the soil rather than left on the surface?

A. dissolves in the air

A. broadcasting

**13.** The four chambers of the stomach of a ruminant include the

A. gizzard
B. crop
C. rumen
D. caecum only

**14.** An animal with a simple stomach of one chamber is described as

B. a monogastric animal
C. a ruminant
D. a herbivore

**15.** Which of the following is a monogastric animal?

B. The cow
C. The pig
D. The goat

**16.** Birds kept on a farm for their meat and eggs are known as

A. draught animals
B. livestock feed
C. ruminants
D. poultry

**17.** Which of the following is NOT poultry?

B. The turkey

D. The duck

**18.** The part of the digestive system of a fowl that grinds its food is the

B. rumen
C. crop only
D. udder

**19.** A pig is usually fed on kitchen waste, maize bran and other concentrates rather than on grass alone because the pig

B. has a simple stomach and cannot digest much fibre

**20.** A rabbit is a monogastric animal, yet it feeds mainly on leaves and grass. This shows that

A. leaves contain no fibre

**21.** Ruminants, monogastric animals and poultry are alike in that all of them

A. have four stomach chambers
B. lay eggs

**22.** Which of the following is a difference between a fowl and a goat?

C. The fowl is a ruminant while the goat is not
D. The goat has a gizzard while the fowl has a rumen

**23.** A pupil wrote: 'Cattle and pigs are both ruminants because both are kept on farms.' The statement is wrong because

A. only wild animals are ruminants
B. pigs have four stomach chambers
C. being kept on a farm does not determine the type of stomach an animal has
D. cattle are not kept on farms

**24.** A farmer who has very little money for feed but plenty of grass on his land should best keep

A. broiler fowls only
B. rabbits only
C. pigs only
D. sheep and goats

A. Watching whether the animal brings food back to its mouth to chew again while resting
B. Noting the colour of its hair
C. Measuring the length of its tail
D. Counting the number of its legs

**26.** Poultry are kept in large numbers on a small piece of land more easily than cattle mainly because poultry

A. produce no waste at all
B. are small, grow quickly and need less space
C. cannot move about
D. do not need any feed

**27.** The use of an animal to meet the needs of the family at home is called

A. industrial use
B. wild use
C. commercial use
D. domestic use

**28.** Which of the following is a domestic use of a fowl?

A. Providing eggs and meat for the family
B. Exporting frozen chicken
C. Supplying a hotel with eggs every week
D. Selling day-old chicks in the market

**29.** A farmer uses his bull to pull a plough on his farm. This use of the animal is called

A. draught (work) use
B. commercial sale
C. a breed
D. a by-product

**30.** Cattle dung spread on a food crop farm is useful because it

A. kills all insects on the farm
B. prevents rain from falling

**31.** A family keeps goats and sells two of them to pay school fees. The goats have been used

A. as draught animals
B. commercially
C. domestically only

**32.** Which of the following best shows the domestic use of a cow in a home?

A. Renting the cow to another farmer
B. Supplying milk to a factory

**33.** Animals are also kept for social and cultural purposes in Ghana, such as

A. providing sheep and fowls for naming ceremonies and festivals
B. guarding the national borders
C. producing electricity for the home
D. pulling vehicles in the city

**34.** Keeping animals mainly in order to sell them or their products for money is called

A. cultural use
B. domestic use
C. subsistence use
D. commercial use

**35.** A useful material obtained from an animal apart from its meat is called

A. a by-product
B. a carcass only
C. a ration
D. a breed

**36.** Which of the following is an animal by-product?

A. Maize bran fed to the animal
B. Water given to the animal

D. Hide used for making leather

**37.** The skin of a goat is used in many Ghanaian communities to

A. feed other animals
B. replace roofing sheets

A. a by-product that can be used as manure

A. cultural

C. commercial
D. domestic

A. protein

C. starch
D. vitamin

A. physical (mechanical) digestion
B. absorption
C. assimilation

A. rectum

D. stomach

A. absorbing the oil into the blood

A. glucose
B. amino acids

D. vitamins

A. sweet in taste

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** An ecosystem is best described as

A. a place where only animals are found
B. a group of animals of the same kind
C. a unit in which living things and their non-living surroundings interact
D. the soil in which plants grow

**2.** An ecosystem is said to be self-sustaining because

A. no living thing ever dies in it
B. it never changes from year to year
C. its parts supply one another with what they need to continue
D. it is kept going by human beings

**3.** Which of the following is an example of an ecosystem?

A. A piece of iron sheet
B. A pond
C. A bucket of sand
D. A single mango fruit

**4.** The place where a plant or an animal lives in an ecosystem is called its

A. nutrient
B. community
C. population
D. habitat

**5.** All the living things of different kinds living together in one place form

A. a community
B. a habitat
C. an organ
D. a population

**6.** Which of the following best explains why the Owabi forest can be called an ecosystem?

A. It is found in the Ashanti Region
B. It contains very many trees
C. Its plants, animals, soil, water and air act on one another as one unit
D. It is protected by the government

**7.** The study of ecosystems is important mainly because it

A. helps us to use and protect our surroundings wisely
B. shows us how to build better houses
C. helps us to kill dangerous animals
D. teaches us the names of all plants

**8.** An ecosystem found on land is described as

A. artificial
B. terrestrial
C. aquatic
D. arboreal

**9.** An ecosystem found in water is described as

A. arid
B. terrestrial
C. arboreal
D. aquatic

**10.** An ecosystem made up of the life found on trees is described as

A. terrestrial
B. arboreal
C. marine
D. aquatic

**11.** Which of the following is an aquatic ecosystem?

A. The Kakum forest
B. The Volta Lake
C. The Accra plains
D. A baobab tree

**12.** A grassland in the Northern Region of Ghana is an example of

A. a terrestrial ecosystem
B. a man-made lake
C. an arboreal ecosystem
D. an aquatic ecosystem

**13.** Monkeys, birds, orchids and insects living in the branches of a tall forest tree make up

A. a desert ecosystem
B. an arboreal ecosystem
C. an aquatic ecosystem
D. a soil ecosystem

**14.** Which of the following pairs are BOTH aquatic ecosystems?

A. The sea and a grassland
B. A mangrove tree and a rock
C. A pond and a forest
D. A river and the sea

**15.** The living parts of an ecosystem are called

A. mineral components
B. physical components
C. abiotic components
D. biotic components

**16.** Which of the following is a biotic component of a pond?

A. Sunlight
B. Tilapia
C. Mud
D. Water

**17.** Green plants in an ecosystem are called producers because they

A. produce the water of the ecosystem
B. break down dead bodies
C. are eaten by all other organisms
D. make their own food using sunlight

**18.** Animals in an ecosystem are called consumers because they

A. produce oxygen for other organisms
B. use sunlight to make food
C. depend on other organisms for their food
D. live only in water

**19.** Bacteria and fungi in an ecosystem are important as

A. decomposers that break down dead plants and animals
B. producers that make food from sunlight
C. abiotic components of the ecosystem
D. animals that feed on living plants

**20.** If all the decomposers in a forest were removed, the MOST likely result would be that

A. more rain would fall in the forest
B. all the animals would become plants
C. the forest would grow faster
D. dead plants and animals would pile up and nutrients would not return to the soil

**21.** The non-living parts of an ecosystem are called

A. biotic components
B. decomposers
C. abiotic components
D. consumers

**22.** Which of the following is an abiotic component of a forest ecosystem?

A. Earthworm
B. Climbing plant
C. Sunlight
D. Mushroom

**23.** Which group contains ONLY abiotic components?

A. Water, fish, soil, air
B. Water, air, soil, temperature
C. Air, water, bacteria, rock
D. Soil, grass, light, air

**24.** Sunlight is an important abiotic component of an ecosystem chiefly because

A. it keeps animals awake
B. it makes water salty
C. it helps the wind to blow
D. green plants need it to make food

**25.** Water is important in an ecosystem because

A. it prevents plants from growing too tall
B. it supplies the soil with sunlight
C. it is a living part of the ecosystem
D. all living things need it for their life processes

**26.** A pond dries up completely during a long dry season. The fish die mainly because an abiotic component

A. needed by the fish has been removed
B. has turned into a biotic component
C. has eaten the fish
D. has multiplied too fast

**27.** Fish are suited to life in water because they

A. have lungs and legs
B. have roots that take in water
C. have gills for breathing in water and fins for swimming
D. have wings and feathers

**28.** Which structure helps a monkey to live in the branches of trees?

A. A hard shell for protection
B. Long limbs and a gripping tail for holding on to branches
C. Gills for taking in air
D. Fins for moving about

**29.** Water lilies are suited to life in a pond because they have

A. deep woody roots
B. leaves reduced to spines
C. broad floating leaves that stay on the surface
D. thick bark on the stem

**30.** Grasses of the northern savanna survive the long dry season mainly because they

A. take in food from the air
B. can swim to wetter places
C. grow best without any water
D. have underground parts that sprout again when the rains come

**31.** Which of the following animals is found in a terrestrial ecosystem?

A. Grasscutter
B. Crab in a rock pool
C. Tilapia
D. Shrimp

**32.** An earthworm taken from the soil and placed in a bucket of water soon dies. This shows that

A. an organism survives best in the ecosystem to which it is suited
B. earthworms are not living things
C. every animal can live anywhere
D. water is harmful to all animals

**33.** The MAIN difference between the organisms of a pond and those of a grassland is that

A. pond organisms are all larger
B. each group has features suited to the conditions of its own surroundings
C. grassland organisms do not need water
D. pond organisms do not need food

**34.** The feeding relationship in which a hawk feeds on a chick is an example of

A. predation
B. competition
C. decomposition
D. pollination

**35.** Two mango trees growing very close together struggle for light, water and soil nutrients. This is an example of

A. competition
B. predation
C. decomposition
D. pollination

**36.** Which of the following shows a dependence of a plant on an animal?

A. A plant taking in water through its roots
B. A plant using sunlight to make food
C. A plant losing water from its leaves
D. A bee carrying pollen from one flower to another

**37.** Green plants in an ecosystem supply animals with

A. wind and rain
B. soil and rock
C. food and oxygen
D. light and heat

**38.** Which of the following best shows how a biotic component depends on an abiotic component?

A. A tree takes up water from the soil
B. A bird builds a nest with twigs
C. A fungus grows on a dead log
D. A goat feeds on grass

**39.** A factory pours waste into a river and most of the fish die. The farmers who catch the fish also suffer. This shows that

A. fish are not part of the ecosystem
B. rivers can clean themselves at once
C. the parts of an ecosystem are linked, so a change in one affects the others
D. only the fish are affected by pollution

**40.** Which of the following human activities would MOST help to protect a wetland ecosystem near a town?

A. Catching all the fish before the rains
B. Stopping the dumping of refuse in the wetland and replanting the plants around it
C. Filling the wetland with sand for building
D. Burning the plants at the edge of the water

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** A farming system is best described as

A. the way a farmer arranges and manages the growing of crops and the keeping of animals
B. the tools used to clear a piece of land
C. the number of workers on a farm
D. the type of soil found on a farm

**2.** Which of the following is NOT one of the farming systems studied at this level?

A. Cold storage farming
B. Organic farming
C. Crop rotation
D. Mixed farming

**3.** A farmer chooses a farming system mainly according to

A. the day of the week on which he starts
B. the number of children in his house
C. the colour of his farm tools
D. the land, the crops, the animals and the money available to him

**4.** Growing crops and keeping animals on the same farm at the same time is called

A. land rotation
B. mixed farming
C. mixed cropping
D. crop rotation

**5.** Growing two or more crops together on the same piece of land at the same time is called

A. mixed cropping
B. mixed farming
C. crop rotation
D. monocropping

**6.** Growing only one type of crop on a piece of land season after season is called

A. mixed farming
B. organic farming
C. mixed cropping
D. monocropping (sole cropping)

**7.** In land rotation, the farmer

A. uses only manure and no chemicals
B. keeps animals and crops on the same land
C. grows different crops on the same land each year
D. cultivates one piece of land for a few years, then leaves it and moves to another piece

**8.** Land rotation is also known as

A. crop rotation
B. shifting cultivation
C. plantation farming
D. mixed farming

**9.** Land that has been left uncultivated so that it can regain its fertility is said to be under

A. rotation of crops
B. fallow
C. mulch
D. irrigation

**10.** During the fallow period the fertility of the land is restored mainly by

A. the fertilizer spread before the land is left
B. the heat of the Sun on the bare soil
C. the ploughing done by the farmer
D. the natural vegetation that grows and decays on it

**11.** Land rotation is practised mostly in areas where

A. land is scarce and the population is large
B. the soil is already very rich
C. there are many tractors and fertilizers
D. land is plentiful and the population is small

**12.** Which of the following is a disadvantage of land rotation?

A. It gives the land no time to rest
B. It needs a large area of land and the burning of bush destroys soil organisms
C. It cannot be practised without a tractor
D. It makes the farmer grow only one crop

**13.** Land rotation is becoming less common in many parts of Ghana today mainly because

A. the government has banned all farming
B. the soil has become too rich for it
C. the growing population has reduced the amount of land available
D. farmers no longer know how to practise it

**14.** In crop rotation, the farmer

A. grows different crops on the same piece of land in a planned order, season after season
B. keeps animals instead of growing crops
C. moves to a new piece of land each year
D. grows the same crop on the land every year

**15.** The MAIN reason for including a legume such as groundnut in a crop rotation is that the legume

A. takes all the pests away
B. adds nitrogen to the soil
C. dries the soil quickly
D. gives the largest harvest

**16.** The nitrogen added to the soil by a groundnut crop comes from

A. the leaves falling on the soil
B. bacteria living in nodules on its roots
C. the water the plant takes in
D. the sunlight trapped by the plant

**17.** Crop rotation helps to control pests and diseases because

A. the pests of one crop do not find their food plant in the following season
B. the crops are sprayed with more chemicals
C. the pests are frightened by the new crops
D. the land is burnt before every planting

**18.** In a good crop rotation plan, a deep-rooted crop is followed by a shallow-rooted one so that

A. the soil becomes harder
B. only one type of nutrient is used up
C. the plants draw nutrients from different depths of the soil
D. the farmer can harvest at the same time

**19.** Which of the following is the MAIN difference between crop rotation and land rotation?

A. In land rotation the crops are changed each season
B. In crop rotation the same land is used and the crops are changed; in land rotation the land itself is changed
C. In crop rotation only one crop is grown
D. Crop rotation can be practised only with animals

**20.** A farmer at Wenchi grows maize, then beans, then cassava and then rests the land on the same plot year after year. This farmer is practising

A. crop rotation
B. monocropping
C. mixed cropping
D. land rotation

**21.** Which of the following is an example of mixed cropping?

A. Maize, cassava and cowpea growing together in the same field
B. Maize this year and cassava on the same field next year
C. Maize grown alone on a large field
D. Maize grown on one field and goats kept on another

**22.** One advantage of mixed cropping is that

B. the crops never compete for anything

A. the different crops cover the soil and reduce erosion

C. the farmer ploughs the soil more often
D. the crops are burnt after harvesting

**24.** A disadvantage of mixed cropping is that

A. the soil cannot hold water at all
B. no crop can be grown with another

**25.** Mixed cropping is difficult to carry out with machines mainly because

A. the crops are planted too deep
B. the farmer plants only in the dry season

A. covering the ground and adding nitrogen to the soil

**27.** Which of the following describes a farm practising mixed farming?

**28.** In mixed farming, the animals are useful to the crops mainly because they

A. shade the young crops from the Sun

**29.** In mixed farming, the crops are useful to the animals mainly because they

A. provide medicine for the animals
B. supply water to the animals
C. keep the animals warm at night
D. supply feed such as crop residues and grain

**30.** One financial advantage of mixed farming is that the farmer

A. is paid by the government each month

D. pays no money for labour

**31.** A disadvantage of mixed farming is that it

A. gives the farmer only one source of income
B. needs more capital, more labour and more skill than a single enterprise
C. cannot be practised in Ghana
D. always destroys the soil

**32.** Mixed farming is said to make good use of a farm's resources because

A. the farmer buys everything from the market
B. nothing is ever harvested from the farm
C. the waste of one enterprise is used by the other
D. the animals are kept far away from the crops

**33.** Organic farming is a system in which the farmer

A. keeps animals in cages all year round
B. grows only one crop on a large farm

**34.** Which of the following would an organic farmer use to feed his crops?

D. Compost and animal manure

**35.** An organic farmer controls insect pests mainly by

A. leaving the pests to multiply freely
B. burning the whole farm every month

**36.** One advantage of organic farming is that

A. it works only on very poor soils
B. it needs very little labour
C. the yields are always the highest possible

**37.** A disadvantage of organic farming is that

A. yields are often lower and more labour is needed
B. the food produced cannot be eaten
C. it cannot be practised without machines
D. it destroys the structure of the soil

**38.** Organic produce often sells at a higher price than other produce because

A. the government fixes a higher price for it
B. it can be stored for ten years
C. many buyers are willing to pay more for food grown without chemicals
D. it is always larger in size

**39.** A farmer with a small piece of land near Kumasi, little money and a family to feed all year would be BEST advised to practise

A. leaving the land to fallow for five years
B. land rotation on several large plots

D. monocropping of one crop on the whole land

**40.** Which statement about the farming systems is correct?

A. Organic farming cannot be combined with crop rotation
B. Only one system may be used on a farm

A. prevent too large a current from spoiling the LED

A. brighter, because the resistance is reduced

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** The law of conservation of energy states that energy can be

A. created whenever it is needed
B. destroyed after it has been used
C. stored only in dry cells
D. changed from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed

**2.** The unit in which energy is measured is the

A. joule
B. newton
C. ampere
D. volt

**3.** A system into which no energy enters and from which no energy escapes is described as a

A. moving system
B. closed system
C. heated system
D. wasted system

**4.** In a closed system, the total amount of energy at the end of a change is

A. always less than at the beginning
B. the same as the total amount at the beginning
C. equal to zero
D. always more than at the beginning

**5.** A dry cell supplies 60 J of energy to a torch bulb. The bulb gives out 18 J as light. The energy given out as heat is

A. 60 J
B. 78 J
C. 18 J
D. 42 J

**6.** Which of the following statements about energy changes is TRUE?

A. Energy is only changed from one useful form into other forms
B. Energy disappears when a machine stops working
C. New energy is made inside a dry cell
D. Energy can be weighed on a balance

**7.** A pupil said that the electricity used by a fan is 'lost' when the fan is switched off. The correct statement is that the energy has been

A. changed into kinetic energy, sound and heat
B. destroyed by the motor
C. stored inside the blades

**8.** A machine is said to waste energy when some of the energy supplied to it is

A. destroyed completely inside the machine
B. changed into forms that are not useful for the job
C. weighed and thrown away
D. returned to the source of the energy

**9.** The energy change that takes place in a dry-cell torch when it is switched on is

A. electrical to chemical to sound
B. light to electrical to chemical
C. chemical to electrical to light and heat
D. heat to chemical to light

**10.** A solar panel on the roof of a clinic changes

A. solar energy into electrical energy
B. sound energy into electrical energy
C. electrical energy into solar energy
D. heat energy into chemical energy

**11.** An electric pressing iron changes electrical energy mainly into

A. heat energy
B. chemical energy
C. sound energy
D. light energy

**12.** The main energy change in a loudspeaker of a radio set is

A. chemical energy to light energy
B. sound energy to electrical energy
C. heat energy to kinetic energy
D. electrical energy to sound energy

**13.** An electric fan changes electrical energy mainly into

A. kinetic energy
B. chemical energy
C. light energy
D. nuclear energy

**14.** A microphone used at a school gathering changes

A. heat energy into sound energy
B. sound energy into electrical energy
C. electrical energy into sound energy
D. light energy into sound energy

**15.** When a mobile phone is being charged, the energy change is

A. sound energy to heat energy
B. light energy to electrical energy
C. chemical energy to electrical energy
D. electrical energy to chemical energy

**16.** Green plants carry out an energy conversion in which

A. chemical energy is changed into light energy
B. heat energy is changed into sound energy

**17.** Which device changes kinetic energy into electrical energy?

A. A generator

C. A pressing iron
D. A dry cell

A. chemical to heat to electrical

**19.** A boy winds up a toy car and releases it. The energy change is

A. heat energy to potential energy
B. sound energy to kinetic energy
C. kinetic energy to chemical energy
D. elastic potential energy to kinetic energy

**20.** A candle burning in a dark room changes chemical energy into

A. electrical and nuclear energy
B. potential and elastic energy
C. light and heat energy
D. sound and kinetic energy

**21.** A motor is supplied with 100 J of electrical energy. It gives 70 J of kinetic energy. The energy that appears as heat and sound is

A. 100 J
B. 30 J
C. 70 J
D. 170 J

**22.** A lamp supplied with 50 J of electrical energy gives out 10 J of light. The fraction of the energy that is useful is

A. the whole
B. four-fifths
C. one-half
D. one-fifth

**23.** In every energy conversion, some of the energy is usually changed into

A. solar energy
B. nuclear energy
C. chemical energy
D. heat energy

**24.** A pupil lists the energy chain of a petrol lorry as: chemical to ..... to kinetic. The missing form is

A. light energy
B. nuclear energy
C. heat energy
D. sound energy

**25.** Which of the following energy chains is CORRECT for an electric kettle boiling water?

A. kinetic energy to light energy
B. heat energy to electrical energy
C. electrical energy to heat energy
D. chemical energy to sound energy

**26.** A filament bulb gives out far more heat than light. This means that most of the energy supplied to it is

A. destroyed
B. stored
C. returned to the mains
D. wasted

**27.** An LED lamp is preferred to a filament bulb for lighting a classroom because the LED lamp

A. gives out more heat
B. uses a larger current
C. changes a greater part of the electrical energy into light
D. needs no switch to control it

**28.** Oiling the moving parts of a machine saves energy because it reduces the energy wasted as

A. light given out by the metal
B. heat and sound caused by friction
C. electrical energy in the wires
D. chemical energy in the oil

**29.** Of the energy supplied to it, the useful energy given out by a machine is always

A. equal to the energy supplied
B. less than the energy supplied
C. equal to zero
D. more than the energy supplied

**30.** Heat lost through the walls of an electric oven is an example of

A. destroyed energy
B. created energy
C. wasted energy
D. stored energy

**31.** A pupil claimed to have built a machine that works for ever without any supply of energy. The claim must be false because

A. machines are always made of metal
B. no machine can give out heat
C. energy cannot be created; a machine must be supplied with energy
D. every machine must have an electric motor

**32.** Energy conservation means

A. using energy carefully so that less of it is wasted
B. making new energy in a laboratory
C. destroying energy that is not needed
D. using as much energy as possible

**33.** Which of the following is the BEST way of conserving electrical energy at home?

A. Using filament bulbs in every room
B. Switching off lights and fans in rooms that are not in use

D. Opening the fridge door often

**34.** Drying clothes in the open air instead of using a drying machine conserves energy because it

A. increases the cost of electricity

**35.** Ironing all the family's clothes at one time rather than one garment at a time conserves energy because

A. the iron gives out no heat
B. the clothes need less water
C. the iron is heated once instead of many times
D. the iron works at a lower voltage

**36.** A sign of energy being wasted in a school is

A. an LED lamp used in the library
B. a kettle switched off after the water has boiled

**37.** Which of the following sources of energy will NOT run out if it is used wisely?

A. Sunlight
B. Crude oil
C. Coal
D. Natural gas

**38.** A reason for conserving energy in Ghana is that it

A. increases the number of power cuts
B. raises the cost of electricity for everybody

**39.** Putting a lid on a cooking pot conserves energy because it

A. changes the heat into light
B. keeps the heat in the pot so that the food cooks faster
C. adds more heat to the food
D. makes the fire burn more fuel

**40.** A school wishes to teach the community about saving energy. The MOST suitable activity is to

A. make posters and leaflets on energy saving and display them in the town

C. fulcrum
D. pivot arm

**33.** A lever in which the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load is a

A. second-class lever
B. third-class lever
C. fourth-class lever
D. first-class lever

**34.** A wheelbarrow is an example of a

A. second-class lever
B. first-class lever
C. pulley
D. third-class lever

**35.** In a pair of sugar tongs, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. The tongs are therefore a

A. second-class lever
B. wheel and axle
C. third-class lever
D. first-class lever

**36.** The work done by the effort on a machine is called the

A. work input
B. work output

**37.** The efficiency of a machine is the ratio of

A. work input to work output, expressed as a percentage
B. load to effort, expressed in newtons
C. effort to distance, expressed in joules

A. 133%

A. increasing the mass of the machine

D. destroying the load

A. adding more load to the machine
B. removing the fulcrum

D. making the parts rougher

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the local name of a material provided the material meant is clear. (3) A chemical symbol must be written with a capital first letter and, where there is a second letter, a small letter; 'NA' for sodium earns no mark. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Diagrams and tables need not be works of art; marks are for correct entries and correct labels. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - **solid** (1 mark).
- Q - **liquid** (1 mark).
- R - **gas** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One mark for each correct state; no half marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P - **the particles are closely packed in a regular pattern and the material keeps its own shape** (1 mark).
- Q - **the particles are close together but irregular and there is a flat surface; the material takes the shape of the bottom of the jar** (1 mark).
- R - **the particles are far apart, moving, and spread through the whole jar** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must come from the figure; 'because it is a solid' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **It escapes and spreads out into the room** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The particles of a gas move freely in all directions, so a gas spreads to fill the space available** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It finishes' alone earns no mark in (i).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- P - any solid, e.g. **salt, sugar, charcoal, stone, cooking pot** (1 mark).
- Q - any liquid, e.g. **water, palm oil, kerosene, milk** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The example must be found in a home; 'iron ore' is not accepted.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- Solids - **chalk**, **river sand** (1 mark each).
- Liquids - **borehole water**, **groundnut oil** (1 mark each).
- Gases - **cooking gas**, **air in the balloon** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A material entered under the wrong heading earns no mark; the table must be copied.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Fixed shape and fixed volume** (1 mark).
- (ii) **No fixed shape, but fixed volume** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Neither fixed shape nor fixed volume** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both halves of the answer are needed for the mark in each case.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Push an inverted empty glass (or blow up a balloon) into a bucket of water** (1 mark).
- **Observation: the water does not fill the glass and the inside remains dry (the balloon swells)** (1 mark).
- **Conclusion: the air (gas) in the glass occupies the space** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An activity with no stated observation earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **drinking**; **cooking**; **bathing or washing the body**; **washing clothes and utensils**; **cleaning the house and compound**; **watering plants**; **giving to livestock** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that mean the same thing, such as 'washing' and 'washing clothes', score once.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **helps in digestion**; **carries digested food and oxygen round the body in the blood**; **removes waste as urine and sweat**; **controls body temperature** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Uses outside the body earn no mark here.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **water is scarce, especially in the dry season**; **it costs time, labour and money to fetch**; **it cannot be replaced at once when wasted**; **uncovered or wasted water breeds mosquitoes and causes disease**; **all life in the village depends on it** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Liquid: **palm oil, groundnut oil, kerosene, petrol or diesel** (1 mark).
- Use: **cooking** / **lighting a lamp or stove** / **fuel for vehicles and machines** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The use must match the liquid named.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Wood - **furniture, doors or roofing timber** (1 mark).
- Cement blocks - **building walls or foundations** (1 mark).
- Iron - **cutlasses, hoes, nails or burglar bars** (1 mark).
- Glass - **windows, louvre blades, bottles or mirrors** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The table must be copied; one correct use per material is enough.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Iron is hard and strong** (1 mark); **so it takes and keeps a sharp edge without breaking or bending** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Wood is light but strong** (1 mark); **and it is easily cut, shaped and smoothed with simple tools** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A property without the reason earns 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **measure carefully and avoid wastage**; **keep and use off-cuts**; **repair and re-use old articles**; **send scrap iron and glass for recycling**; **plant trees to replace the timber used** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A measure that does not preserve material, such as 'work faster', earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **magnesium** (1 mark).
- X - **sulphur** (1 mark).
- Y - **argon** (1 mark).
- Z - **potassium** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the correct chemical symbol written in place of the name.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Y** (1 mark).
- (ii) **X** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The letter alone is enough; no mark for naming a different element.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Beryllium (Be)** or **calcium (Ca)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **They have similar chemical properties** (accept: the same number of outermost electrons) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only one element need be named in (i).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Rule: **in order of increasing atomic number** (1 mark).
- Evidence: **the numbers in the boxes increase by one from each element to the next across a period and on to the next period** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'In order of their mass' earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Carbon - **C** (1 mark).
- Sodium - **Na** (1 mark).
- Aluminium - **Al** (1 mark).
- Helium - **He** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A symbol written wholly in capitals, such as NA or AL, earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Place the sample in a simple circuit with a cell and a bulb** (accept: hammer it gently, or rub it) (1 mark).
- **If the bulb lights, the sample conducts electricity and is a metal** (accept: it flattens into a sheet instead of breaking; it is shiny) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A test with no stated result earns 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO differences, each stated for both sides: **metals conduct heat and electricity, non-metals generally do not**; **metals are shiny, non-metals are dull**; **metals can be beaten into sheets and drawn into wires, non-metals are brittle**; **most metals are solids with high melting points, non-metals may be solids, liquids or gases** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A statement about metals only, with nothing said about non-metals, earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 1: Diversity of Matter | **Sub-strand:** 1: Materials | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.1.1.1** - Recognise materials as important resources for providing human needs. **B7/JHS1.1.1.2** - Understand the periodic table as different elements made up of metals and non-metals and noble gases arranged in an order.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 1: Diversity of Matter, Sub-Strand 1: Materials, Basic 7, pages 2 to 4 (pages 39 to 41 of the published PDF). Content standard B7/JHS1.1.1.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.1, classify materials into liquids, solids and gases, with the exemplars: create and complete a table to record the texture, appearance, colour and shape of a group of materials assembled from the environment; group materials into liquids, solids and gases; discuss the differences among liquids, solids and gases; and give examples of solids, liquids and gases that can be identified from your environment. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.2, discuss the importance of liquids in the life of humans, with the exemplars: present a report on the importance of liquids to human life; describe the need to preserve liquids for human use; and record liquids they see being used in their community. It further carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.1.3, discuss the importance of specific solids to life, with the exemplars: identify solids in the environment that support the survival of humans and other life forms; explain the need to preserve useful solid materials in the environment for life; and model objects from solid materials that can be useful to humans and other life forms. Content standard B7/JHS1.1.1.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.1.2.1, demonstrate the knowledge of the orderly arrangement of metals, non-metals and noble gases in the periodic table, with the exemplars: name and write the chemical symbol of the first 20 elements in the periodic table; identify metals, non-metals and noble gases in the periodic table; and deduce from the periodic table that the elements are arranged in order of their atomic number and that those in the same group have common properties.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.1.1.1.1) carries topics 1.1 and 1.2 and Questions 1 and 2; I2 (B7/JHS1.1.1.1.2) carries topic 1.3 and Question 3; I3 (B7/JHS1.1.1.1.3) carries topic 1.4 and Question 4; I4 (B7/JHS1.1.1.2.1) carries topics 1.5 and 1.6 and Questions 5 and 6. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.1.1.1 and B7.1.1.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This is the first sub-strand of Basic 7 and it sets the language of the whole course. Insist from the beginning on the words matter, material, state, solid, liquid, gas, element and symbol, used exactly.
- In Question 1(b) the marks are for evidence taken from the figure. Candidates who merely repeat the answer to (a) in other words earn nothing; teach them to point to the spacing, the pattern and the movement of the particles.
- Question 2(b) is the classic table of shape and volume. The liquid row, no fixed shape but a fixed volume, is the one most often lost, and it is worth demonstrating by pouring the same water through three differently shaped containers.
- Chemical symbols are a mark-earning skill with a strict rule: a capital first letter and a small second letter. NA, CL and AL are wrong and earn nothing. Give a two-minute symbol drill at the start of every lesson until the first twenty are secure.
- In Question 5 the letters W, X, Y and Z replace magnesium, sulphur, argon and potassium, and the atomic numbers of those four boxes have been removed on purpose, so candidates must read the position in the table rather than recall a number.
- The periodic table at this level is about pattern, not theory. Candidates should be able to say that the elements are arranged in order of atomic number, that a group is a vertical column whose members behave alike, and that a period is a horizontal row.
- Follow-up work: let each group assemble twelve materials from the school compound, record texture, appearance, colour and shape in a table, classify them, and then make one useful article from a solid material and report on it. The table and the article together cover the first three indicators of this sub-strand.
