## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a drawing, marks are for the correct shape and the correct labels, not for beauty; every label line must touch the part it names. (3) Accept the singular or the plural form of the name of an organelle, for example mitochondrion or mitochondria. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) 'Cell wall' and 'cell membrane' are different parts; one written for the other earns no mark. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- A - **cell membrane** (1 mark).
- B - **cytoplasm** (1 mark).
- C - **nucleus** (1 mark).
- D - **mitochondrion** (1 mark).
- E - **vacuole** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Cell wall' written for A earns no mark; an animal cell has no cell wall.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A - **controls what enters and leaves the cell** (accept: holds the cell together) (1 mark).
- C - **controls the activities of the cell** (1 mark).
- D - **releases energy from food (respiration)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It protects the cell' alone is not accepted for C.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **there is no cell wall and the shape is irregular**; **there are no chloroplasts**; **there is no large central vacuole**; **the nucleus is not pushed to one side** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The reason must be visible in the figure.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **The smallest unit of a living organism** (1 mark) **that can carry out the activities of life / from which all living things are built** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **both plants and animals are made of cells**; **the cell is the basic unit of all living things**; **cells are too small to be seen without a microscope** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'A small thing in the body' earns no mark in (i).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Cytoplasm - **where the organelles lie and most reactions of the cell take place** (1 mark).
- Nucleus - **controls the activities of the cell** (1 mark).
- Mitochondrion - **releases energy from food** (1 mark).
- Ribosome - **makes proteins** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The table must be copied; one correct function each is enough.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **A rounded cell with an irregular outline and no cell wall** (1 mark).
- **Four correct parts shown and named** - cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondrion (accept vacuole or ribosome) (2 marks; 1 mark if only two or three are correct).
- **Each label written outside the drawing with a straight line touching the part named** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A drawing that includes a cell wall or chloroplasts loses the first mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- P - **cell wall** (1 mark).
- Q - **cell membrane** (1 mark).
- R - **nucleus** (1 mark).
- S - **chloroplast** (1 mark).
- T - **vacuole (large central vacuole)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: P and Q must not be interchanged; the cell wall is the outer line.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P - **gives the cell a fixed shape and gives support and protection** (1 mark).
- S - **makes food for the plant by photosynthesis / holds the chlorophyll** (1 mark).
- T - **stores cell sap and keeps the cell firm** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It protects the cell' alone is not enough for P; the idea of shape or support is needed.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **The root is in the soil where there is no light, so no food can be made there** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Food made in the leaves is carried down to the root through the stem** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Because it is not green' is accepted for (i) only if the absence of light is also stated.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Cell wall - **present / absent** (1 mark).
- Chloroplast - **present / absent** (1 mark).
- Vacuole - **present in both, large and central in the plant cell but small in the animal cell** (1 mark).
- Nucleus - **present / present** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: For the vacuole row, both 'present' entries and the difference are needed for the mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The plant cell has a firm cell wall made of cellulose** (1 mark).
- **The wall is rigid and holds the cell in a fixed shape** (1 mark).
- **The animal cell has only a thin flexible membrane, so its shape is irregular** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'the plant cell has a cell wall' earns 1 mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The pupil is not correct; a nucleus and cytoplasm occur in both kinds of cell** (1 mark).
- Any TWO of: **a cell wall**; **chloroplasts**; **a large central vacuole**; **a regular box-like shape** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the features if the candidate says the pupil is correct.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Cell membrane - **rubber bag; thin and flexible and holds everything in** (1 mark).
- Cytoplasm - **starch paste; jelly-like and fills the cell** (1 mark).
- Nucleus - **one stone or large seed; rounded, firm and single** (1 mark).
- Mitochondrion - **maize grains; small, oval and several** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A material named without a reason earns no mark. Accept any sensible alternative use of the materials listed.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **The wooden box** (1 mark); **it is firm, straight-sided and keeps a fixed box-like shape** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **chloroplasts (green leaf pieces)**; **a large central vacuole**; **the nucleus pushed to one side** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Naming the same part twice in (ii) scores once.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the model is far larger than the real cell and gives a wrong idea of size**; **the materials are not alive and carry out none of the activities of a cell**; **some organelles are too small or too many to be shown**; **the model is fixed while the contents of a living cell move** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is not real' alone earns no mark; the limitation must be explained.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **The chloroplasts could make no food in the dark** (1 mark); **the chlorophyll broke down and was not replaced, so the green colour faded** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The vacuoles lost water (cell sap)** (1 mark); **so the cells were no longer firm against their cell walls and the plant drooped** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An answer in terms of the whole plant only, with no mention of cells, earns at most 1 mark in each part.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Water the plant (and return it to the light)** (1 mark).
- **The vacuoles fill with water again and the cells become firm** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark needs the vacuole or the cell, not just 'the plant drinks water'.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The animal cell has no cell wall to resist the water entering** (1 mark).
- **So it swells and may burst instead of becoming firm, while the plant cell is held by its wall** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the membrane is thin and flexible' for the first mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 1: Diversity of Matter | **Sub-strand:** 2: Living Cells | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.1.2.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the structure of organisms and functions of cells in living systems.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 1: Diversity of Matter, Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells, Basic 7, pages 5 and 6 (pages 42 and 43 of the published PDF). Content standard B7/JHS1.1.2.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.2.1.1, describe the structure and function of living cells of an animal, with the exemplars: identify and describe the structure of an animal cell seen in a video, a chart and a magnifier; state the function of each organelle in the animal cell; look at a sample of animal cell from different parts of an animal with a microscope, magnifier or watch a video or pictures of cells and draw the conclusion that animals are made up of cells; draw and label an animal cell; and develop a model to represent an animal cell. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.1.2.1.2, state the functions of each organelle in a plant cell, with the exemplars: identify and describe the structure of a plant cell as seen in a video, a chart, pictures and magnifiers; state the function of each organelle in the plant cell; look at a sample of a plant cell from different parts of a plant with a microscope, magnifier or watch a video or pictures and confirm that plants are made up of cells; draw and label a plant cell; and develop a model to represent a plant cell.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.1.2.1.1) carries topics 2.1 to 2.3 and Questions 1, 2 and 5(a); I2 (B7/JHS1.1.2.1.2) carries topics 2.4 to 2.6 and Questions 3, 4 and 6. The drawing, labelling and modelling exemplars are examined in Questions 2(c), 5 and 6, which is the part of that practical work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.1.2.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The commonest error in this sub-strand is writing 'cell wall' for the boundary of an animal cell. Teach the rule plainly: every cell has a cell membrane; only the plant cell adds a cell wall outside it.
- Marks in Question 1(a) and Question 3(a) are for naming the lettered parts exactly. The nucleus is a part; 'nucleolus' is not accepted for it, and 'chlorophyll' is not accepted for 'chloroplast' - chlorophyll is the green substance inside the chloroplast.
- In drawings (Question 2(c)) candidates lose marks for label lines that stop in the middle of nowhere. Insist on a straight ruled line from the written label to the part itself, and on labels written outside the drawing.
- Question 4(a) is a comparison table. Candidates who write only 'yes' and 'no' should be accepted, but those who leave the vacuole row without the difference in size lose that mark.
- Question 5 examines the modelling exemplar. The reasons matter more than the materials: a bag chosen because it is flexible shows real understanding, while a bag chosen 'because it is there' does not.
- Question 6 links the cell to the whole plant. Candidates who explain wilting without once mentioning the vacuole have not met the indicator; this is worth practising with a wilted and a watered plant side by side.
- Follow-up work: let each pupil look at onion epidermis, a leaf peel and a cheek smear under the school microscope or a hand lens, make one large labelled drawing of each, and then build one model cell from local materials and present it to the class.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a flow chart or diagram, marks are for the correct stages, the correct order and the arrows that join them, not for beauty. (3) The names of the stages must be used correctly: 'evaporation' written for 'transpiration', or 'condensation' for 'precipitation', earns no mark. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Accept 'water vapour' and 'vapour' as the same thing, but 'steam' is accepted only where boiling is involved. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- A - **evaporation** (1 mark).
- B - **transpiration** (1 mark).
- C - **condensation** (1 mark).
- D - **precipitation** (accept: rainfall) (1 mark).
- E - **run-off** (accept: surface run-off, collection of water in rivers returning to the sea) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Evaporation' written for B earns no mark; water lost from the leaves of a plant is transpiration.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The sun** (1 mark).
- (ii) **It is left behind in the sea; only pure water vapour rises** (1 mark).
- (iii) **The air is cooler high up, so the vapour condenses into tiny water drops** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is hot' is not accepted for (i); the sun must be named.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The water returns to the sea, the place where it started, so the same water is used again** (1 mark).
- **The same stages follow one another in the same order without ending** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'because it happens every year' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- All four stages written in the correct order (2 marks; 1 mark if one stage is out of place).
- Arrows drawn between the stages to show the direction of the change (1 mark).
- An arrow from **collection back to evaporation**, closing the cycle (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A chart that stops at precipitation loses the last mark, however neat it is.*

**(b)** [5 marks]

- Any FIVE of: **a source of energy - energy released during condensation warms the environment**; **a carrier of nutrients**; **it improves (raises) the water table**; **it regulates the weather pattern**; **it provides clean, fresh water**; **it supplies water for crops, animals and people** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It gives us water' may be credited once only, as the provision of clean water.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **rain falling on the town, the farms or the hills**; **the river or the wells being refilled (the water table rising)**; **people using the water for drinking, washing, farming or watering animals**; **water returning to the air by evaporation from the river and transpiration from trees** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for what the diagram would show, not for drawing it; a candidate who draws it correctly still earns the marks.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - **steam / water vapour rising from the water** (1 mark).
- Q - **drops of water (condensed water) on the underside of the plate** (1 mark).
- R - **the water collected in the cup** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Smoke' written for P earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P - **evaporation** (1 mark).
- Q - **condensation** (1 mark).
- R - **precipitation and collection** (accept either) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'rainfall' for R.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Burner - **the sun** (1 mark).
- Cold metal plate - **the cool air high up in the atmosphere (where clouds form)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The sky' alone is not accepted for the plate; the idea of cool air or cloud level is needed.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **in nature the sun heats the water slowly and the water does not boil**; **the model leaves out transpiration by plants**; **the model leaves out run-off and water soaking into the ground**; **in nature the wind carries the clouds far away before the rain falls**; **the model is very much smaller and lasts only a few minutes** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is not real water' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Trees release water vapour into the air by transpiration** (1 mark).
- **With fewer trees, less water vapour enters the air** (1 mark).
- **Less vapour means fewer clouds form by condensation, so less rain falls** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word 'transpiration' is not compulsory if the idea of water vapour from the leaves is clear.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The level below the ground at which the soil or rock is filled (saturated) with water** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Rain water soaks into the soil (infiltration)** (1 mark) **and collects below the surface, raising the stored water so that wells do not dry up** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Water under the ground' alone earns the mark in (i) only if the idea of a level is given.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any TWO actions (1 mark each) with a matching reason (1 mark each): **plant trees and grasses** - *roots slow the water and help it soak into the soil*; **leave open ground, dig trenches or infiltration pits** - *the water is held until it soaks in*; **harvest rain water from roofs into tanks** - *less water runs over the ground and water is stored for the dry season*; **clear and maintain the gutters** - *run-off is carried away without flooding the streets*.
  - *Marking note: An action without a reason earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Dish 1 - **48 cm3** (1 mark).
- Dish 2 - **22 cm3** (1 mark).
- Dish 3 - **6 cm3** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept answers without the unit, but a wrong unit (for example g) loses the mark for that dish.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The dish in the sun received more heat energy from the sun** (1 mark).
- **More heat makes water evaporate faster** (1 mark).
- **The cupboard was cool and the still, closed air soon held as much vapour as it could, so evaporation was slow** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'there was no wind in the cupboard to carry the vapour away' for the third mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the dishes were identical, so the exposed surface was the same**; **the same volume of water was used in each dish**; **all the dishes were left for the same time (six hours)** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'They used water' is not a fair-test measure and earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The pupil is not correct** (1 mark).
- **The water has changed into water vapour and entered the air; it is not destroyed and will return as rain** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the explanation if the candidate agrees with the pupil.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Evaporation leaves salts and dirt behind, so the rain that falls is fairly pure** (1 mark).
- **Falling rain picks up dust and smoke from the air** (1 mark).
- **The roof and gutters add dust, leaves, bird droppings and germs to the water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'the tank may be dirty' earns 1 mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **boil the water before drinking**; **filter it through a clean cloth or filter**; **treat it with an approved water-treatment agent (for example chlorine tablets)**; **keep the tank covered and clean**; **clean the roof and gutters and let the first dirty water run to waste** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Accept any safe, practical method used in Ghanaian homes.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the water in the tank is still part of the cycle; when it is used it evaporates or soaks into the ground**; **the total amount of water on the earth does not change, it is only used again and again**; **the tank holds only a very small part of the rain that falls**; **collecting roof water reduces run-off and flooding** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who merely writes 'the neighbour is wrong' without a reason earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 1: Earth Science | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.2.1.1** - Recognise that the water cycle is an example of repeated patterns of change in nature and understand how it occurs.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 1: Earth Science, Basic 7, pages 44 and 45 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.2.1.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.1.1.1, explain how the water cycle occurs as a repeated pattern of change in nature, with the exemplars: identify natural sources of water and list the stages of the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation and transpiration) from pictures and videos; draw a flow chart or diagram to show the order of the stages and how they are linked; and explain why the water cycle is a repeated pattern of change in nature using the internet, books, journals, television and radio. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.1.1.2, describe the importance of the water cycle, with the exemplars: describe the stages of the water cycle from a video or picture; describe the importance of the water cycle in terms of its being a source of energy (release of energy that warms the environment), a carrier of nutrients, a means of improving the water table, a regulator of weather pattern and a provider of clean water; and illustrate with a diagram the importance of the water cycle in a community.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.2.1.1.1) carries topics 3.1 to 3.5 and Questions 1, 3 and 5; I2 (B7/JHS1.2.1.1.2) carries topic 3.6 and Questions 2(b), 2(c), 4 and 6. The 'draw a flow chart of the stages' exemplar is examined in Question 2(a) and the 'illustrate the importance of the water cycle in a community' exemplar in Question 2(c), which is the part of that work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.2.1.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The commonest confusion in this sub-strand is between evaporation and transpiration. Fix the difference by the place it happens: evaporation from any free water surface, transpiration from the leaves of a plant. Both put water vapour into the air.
- Candidates often write that rain falls 'because the cloud is heavy'. The mark in Question 1 and in Section A item 22 is for the idea that the tiny drops join together until they are too heavy to be held up in the air.
- In Question 2(a) the last mark is for the arrow that returns collection to evaporation. Insist in class that a water-cycle chart is not finished until the loop is closed; that single arrow is what makes it a repeated pattern.
- Question 3 uses the boiling-water model. Teach pupils to say what each piece of apparatus stands for - burner for sun, cold plate for the cool upper air - and also where the model falls short, which is the thinking the 'challenging' marks reward.
- Question 5 is a fair-test question. Many candidates can calculate the water lost but cannot say what was kept the same. Practise naming the controlled variables in any simple experiment.
- The 'importance' indicator is examined in Questions 2(b), 4 and 6. The five headings in the curriculum - energy, carrier of nutrients, water table, weather pattern and clean water - are worth learning as a list, but candidates should be able to explain each one in a sentence of their own.
- Follow-up work: set up the Fig. 2 model in class, then send pupils out to map the natural sources of water in their own community and to draw one labelled diagram showing how the water cycle serves the town.

# PAPER 4 - LIFE CYCLE OF ORGANISMS: THE HOUSEFLY

**Strand 2: Cycles | Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms | B7/JHS1.2.2.1**

## ANSWER KEY

### Section A - Objective Test

| Question | Answer | Curriculum Area (Topic) | Cognitive Level |

| 1 (b) | The cycle begins with the eggs, so the order is C, A, D, B, and after B the adult lays eggs and the cycle begins again at C. | The Stages of the Life Cycle of the Housefly | Understand |
| 1 (c) | At stage A, the larva feeds greedily on the rotting matter in which it hatched and grows quickly, moulting as it grows. At stage D, the pupa rests inside a hard brown case, does not feed, and changes inside the case into the adult housefly. | Features of Each Stage of the Housefly | Understand |
| 1 (d) | The adult that comes out of the pupa lays eggs of its own, so the same four stages begin again in the same order. The series of changes has no end as long as houseflies continue to breed. | Life Cycles and Metamorphosis | Analyse |
| 2 (a) | J is a bowl of food left uncovered on a table, with houseflies on it; K is a heap of refuse with houseflies above it; L is a bowl of food protected by a net food cover, with no flies on it. | Feeding Habits and Breeding Places of the Housefly | Remember |
| 2 (b) | The refuse heap at K gives the flies food and a moist, warm place in which to lay their eggs, so they gather there. The open food at J is easy to reach and smells attractive, so flies move from the refuse straight onto it. The food at L is shut in by the net cover, so although the flies may smell it they cannot land on it or feed. | Feeding Habits and Breeding Places of the Housefly | Analyse |
| 2 (c) | The flies transfer germs from the refuse and from faeces to the food and cause diseases such as dysentery, diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid fever; the food they settle on becomes contaminated and may cause food poisoning; and the flies are a nuisance, disturbing people while they eat, rest or work and making the compound unpleasant. | The Housefly as a Menace to Humans | Understand |
| 2 (d) | They should keep all food covered, as at L, until it is eaten; clear the refuse heap and keep rubbish in a container with a tight lid, emptying it at the proper dumping site; sweep and keep the compound and the gutters clean and dry so that flies have no place to breed; and wash the plates and sweep up food remains immediately after eating. | Reducing the Housefly Menace in the Community | Create |
| 3 (a) | The eggs are laid in rotting rubbish, animal manure, faeces or decaying food. The larva lives and feeds in the same rotting material in which the eggs were laid. The pupa is found in the drier parts of the rubbish or in the soil just below it. The adult flies about the compound, settling on refuse, faeces, dead animals and uncovered food. | Features of Each Stage of the Housefly | Understand |
| 3 (b) | The rains leave rubbish heaps, gutters and compounds warm and damp, which are the conditions in which eggs hatch and larvae feed best; the whole life cycle is then completed in one to three weeks; and each female lays very many eggs, so a few flies quickly become a very large number. | Life Cycles and Metamorphosis | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | Eggs and larvae are all together in the rubbish and waste, so clearing those places destroys very many at once, while adults fly away and can enter from neighbouring compounds. Removing the breeding material stops new flies from being produced at all, so the problem does not return as soon as the spraying stops, and it costs nothing but labour, needs no chemicals and is safe for people and food. | Reducing the Housefly Menace in the Community | Apply |
| 4 (a) | The housefly cannot bite or chew. | 4 (b) | The fly feeds and walks in the gutter, where germs stick to its hairy legs, body and mouth parts; it then flies onto the kenkey and walks over it, leaving the germs on the food, and it may also vomit or pass out waste onto the food; the customer then eats the food together with the germs and falls ill. | The Housefly as a Menace to Humans | Analyse |
| 4 (c) | Dysentery, diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid fever and food poisoning are all spread in this way. | The Housefly as a Menace to Humans | Remember |
| 4 (d) | Spraying insecticide over food is dangerous, because the chemical settles on the kenkey and fish and can poison the customers; and it kills only the flies present at that moment, while the gutter goes on breeding fresh flies all day. | 5 (b) | (i) A clear plastic bottle, a small piece of rotting fruit or fish as bait, a little water with soap, a knife and tape. (ii) The top of the bottle is cut off and pushed back into the body of the bottle upside down to make a funnel. The bait is placed in the bottom. The smell attracts the flies, which crawl in through the narrow neck, and they cannot easily find their way out again, so they are trapped and die in the soapy water. | Reducing the Housefly Menace in the Community | Create |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of the stages must be used correctly: 'maggot' is accepted for larva, but 'caterpillar' and 'nymph' are not. (3) In a drawing or a flow chart, marks are for the correct stages, the correct order and the arrows that join them, not for beauty. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Malaria is not a housefly-borne disease and earns no mark anywhere in this paper. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **larva** (accept: maggot) (1 mark).
- B - **adult (adult housefly)** (1 mark).
- C - **egg (eggs)** (1 mark).
- D - **pupa** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Caterpillar' or 'nymph' written for A earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **C, A, D, B** (2 marks; 1 mark if only one letter is out of place).
  - *Marking note: Accept the same order written in a circle, for example A, D, B, C, provided the sequence is unbroken.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A - **the larva feeds on the rotting matter and grows quickly** (1 mark).
- D - **the insect rests inside a hard case, does not feed, and changes into the adult** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It sleeps' alone is not accepted for D; the change into the adult must be shown.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The adult lays eggs, which start the same stages again** (1 mark).
- **The same stages follow one another in the same order over and over again** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'because it is round' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- J - **food left uncovered (open) on a table, with flies on it** (1 mark).
- K - **a heap of refuse (rubbish) with flies around it** (1 mark).
- L - **food covered with a net cover, with no flies on it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of 'uncovered' at J and 'covered' at L must be clear.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **K provides food and a breeding place for the flies** (1 mark).
- **J is open and easy to reach, and the smell attracts the flies** (1 mark).
- **The net at L keeps the flies off the food although they can still smell it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the flies cannot pass through the holes of the net' for the third mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **they transfer disease germs to the food and cause diseases such as dysentery, diarrhoea, cholera or typhoid fever**; **they contaminate the food and cause food poisoning**; **they are a nuisance in the home and environment**; **they spoil the food so that it must be thrown away** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Malaria earns no mark; it is spread by the mosquito.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **keep all food covered until it is eaten**; **clear the refuse heap and use a bin with a tight lid**; **dispose of refuse at the proper dumping site regularly**; **sweep the compound and keep gutters clean and dry**; **clear away food remains and wash plates at once** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Kill all the flies' is not accepted as a lasting change.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Egg - **in rotting rubbish, manure, faeces or decaying food** (1 mark).
- Larva - **in the same rotting matter, where it feeds** (1 mark).
- Pupa - **in the drier part of the rubbish or in the soil beneath it** (1 mark).
- Adult - **flying about the compound, on refuse, faeces and uncovered food** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'In dirty places' may be credited once only.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The warm, damp conditions suit the eggs and larvae** (1 mark).
- **Rotting rubbish and waste, which are food and breeding places, are plentiful** (1 mark).
- **The life cycle is completed in only one to three weeks and many eggs are laid each time** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the flies breed faster because it is warm and wet' for 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the eggs and larvae cannot move away, so they are easy to destroy**; **killing adults does not stop the ones already breeding in the refuse from hatching**; **removing the breeding places prevents new flies altogether, so the control lasts**; **adults can fly in from other compounds**; **cleaning needs no chemicals, so it is cheap and safe** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who merely repeats 'it is better' without a reason earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **It settles on the food and pours out saliva onto it** (1 mark).
- **The saliva dissolves or softens the food** (1 mark).
- **The fly sucks up the liquid food through its sponge-like mouth parts** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It bites the food' earns no mark; the housefly has no biting mouth parts.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Germs from the gutter stick to the hairy legs, body and mouth parts of the fly** (1 mark).
- **The fly lands on the kenkey and leaves the germs on it (it may also vomit or pass waste on the food)** (1 mark).
- **The customer eats the contaminated food and takes in the germs** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The three steps must be in a sensible order for full marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **dysentery**; **diarrhoea**; **cholera**; **typhoid fever**; **food poisoning** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Malaria earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **insecticide on or near food can poison the customers**; **it kills only the flies present at the time**; **the gutter keeps breeding new flies, so they return at once** (1 mark each, maximum 1 mark if no alternative is given).
- **She should clear the gutter and keep the food in a covered glass case or under a net cover** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Full marks need both a reason and the better practice.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **a clean-up of refuse heaps and choked gutters**; **refuse containers with tight lids, emptied regularly**; **keeping the school toilets clean and covered**; **asking vendors to keep food covered**; **keeping the compound swept and dry** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A bare list is enough; a short description is not required for the mark but should be encouraged.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Any TWO materials, for example **a plastic bottle** and **bait such as rotting fruit, fish or sugar water** (1 mark for both).
- (ii) **The smell of the bait attracts the flies into the bottle through a narrow opening** (1 mark); **the flies cannot find their way out and are trapped** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any workable trap, for example a bowl of soapy water with bait covered by a perforated lid.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Count the flies (in a trap or at a fixed place) before the intervention and again some weeks after it** (1 mark).
- **Compare the two counts; fewer flies afterwards shows that the intervention worked** (accept: check whether fewer pupils report sick with diarrhoea) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'look at the place' earns no mark; some form of comparison is needed.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO short, correct messages about covering food, clearing refuse, keeping gutters clean, using and covering latrines or washing hands (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The message must be about reducing flies or protecting food; a general greeting earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Home W** (1 mark).
- (ii) **39** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 39 flies written with or without the word 'flies'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Homes with open refuse (W and Y) caught many more flies than homes with covered refuse (X and Z)** (1 mark).
- **Open refuse gives the flies food and a breeding place** (1 mark).
- **Emptying often also matters: X, emptied daily, caught fewer flies than Z, emptied weekly, because refuse left standing allows the eggs to hatch** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Candidates must quote at least one pair of figures from the table for the first mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Keep refuse in a covered bin and empty it daily** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **only four homes were tested**; **the count was made on one day only**; **other differences between the homes, such as cleanliness or a nearby dump, were not controlled**; **the traps may not catch the same share of the flies in every home** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'They did not count well' earns no mark without a reason.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 2: Life Cycle of Organisms | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.2.2.1** - Show skills in showing the stages of the life cycle of the housefly, the effects of its activities on humans and how to reduce them.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms, Basic 7, pages 46 and 47 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.2.2.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.2.1.1, describe the life cycle of the housefly, with the exemplars: identify and describe the stages in the life cycle of the housefly; put the stages in their correct order (eggs, larva, pupa, adult) using flashcards or cut-outs; draw each stage and link the drawings with arrows to complete the cycle; and write short notes on each stage. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.2.1.2, discuss the housefly as a menace to humans and how to reduce it, with the exemplars: discuss the feeding habits of the housefly (dead animals, rotten food, manure, solid and liquid waste) using drawings, pictures and cartoons; discuss the effects of the activities of the housefly on humans, namely the transfer of diseases such as dysentery, food poisoning and nuisance in the environment; and design an intervention to reduce the menace and educate the community on it.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.2.2.1.1) carries topics 4.1 to 4.3 and Questions 1 and 3; I2 (B7/JHS1.2.2.1.2) carries topics 4.4 to 4.6 and Questions 2, 4, 5 and 6. The 'draw each stage and link them with arrows' exemplar is examined in Question 1 and Question 3(a), and the 'design an intervention and educate the community' exemplar in Question 5, which is the part of that practical work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.2.2.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The letters in Fig. 1 are deliberately not in the order of the cycle. Candidates who answer 1(b) with 'A, B, C, D' have read the letters instead of the arrows; train pupils to follow the arrows in any cycle diagram.
- 'Maggot' is the common name for the larva and is fully accepted. 'Caterpillar' is the larva of a butterfly or moth and must not be credited, nor 'nymph', which belongs to insects with incomplete metamorphosis.
- Question 3(c) rewards the key public-health idea of this sub-strand: control the breeding places, not the adult flies. Many candidates will write 'spray insecticide' for everything; the marks go to those who reason about where the eggs and larvae are.
- In Question 4(b) the three steps must form a chain - germs onto the fly, fly onto the food, food into the person. Answers that merely say 'the fly is dirty' earn one mark at most.
- Malaria appears as a distractor in Section A and is explicitly refused in the marking scheme. The housefly does not spread malaria; the mosquito does. This single correction is worth making in every lesson on this sub-strand.
- Question 6 brings numbers into the sub-strand. Candidates should be taught to quote figures from a table when they are asked to use results, and to see that a small sample taken on one day proves very little.
- Follow-up work: let pupils build the simple bottle trap of Question 5(b), set it in two different places in the school for the same length of time, count what is caught and present the comparison to the class.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Trade names of fertilizers are accepted provided the type is clear, for example 'NPK 15-15-15' for a compound inorganic fertilizer. (3) 'Manure' written alone is accepted for an organic source only where the question does not ask for a named example. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a table of differences, each row must compare the SAME property in both columns before the mark is awarded. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **organic** (1 mark).
- X - **inorganic** (1 mark).
- Y - **organic** (1 mark).
- Z - **inorganic** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Natural' and 'artificial' are accepted for organic and inorganic respectively.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- W - any TWO of: **dark brown or black**; **crumbly or loose**; **bulky and heavy**; **moist**; **earthy-smelling** (1 mark each).
- X - any TWO of: **small hard granules (or crystals)**; **dry**; **light in colour (white, grey or pinkish)**; **sold in a sealed sack**; **concentrated, so little is needed** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A characteristic that is not physical, such as 'it is cheap', earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **W (the compost)** (1 mark); accept Y (poultry manure) with the same reason.
- **Because organic manures are bulky and contain only a small proportion of nutrients, while inorganic fertilizers are concentrated** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must mention the low concentration or the bulkiness of the organic material.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Any TWO organic: **compost**; **farmyard (cattle, sheep or goat) manure**; **poultry droppings**; **green manure**; **household or market waste** (1 mark each).
- Any TWO inorganic: **NPK**; **sulphate of ammonia**; **urea**; **superphosphate**; **muriate of potash**; **liquid (foliar) fertilizer** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Fertilizer' written alone earns no mark; a named type is required.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Source - **remains of plants and animals / manufactured from minerals in a factory** (1 mark).
- Quantity - **bulky, large quantities needed / concentrated, small quantities needed** (1 mark).
- Speed of action - **slow release over a long time / quick action** (1 mark).
- Effect on the soil - **adds humus and improves soil structure / adds no humus and may spoil the soil if used alone** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both halves of a row must be filled in correctly before the mark for that row is given.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **No, it would not feed the plot as well** (1 mark).
- **The manure is bulky and contains a much smaller proportion of nutrients, so a far larger quantity is needed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the reason if the candidate answers 'yes'.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Organic - any ONE of: **cheap or free**; **made from waste on the compound**; **adds humus and improves the soil**; **releases nutrients slowly** (1 mark).
- Inorganic - any ONE of: **concentrated and easy to carry**; **acts quickly**; **supplies known amounts of named nutrients** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An advantage written twice in different words earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - **broadcasting** (1 mark).
- Q - **ring application** (accept: circle or spot application) (1 mark).
- R - **applying liquid fertilizer by watering at the base of the plant** (accept: liquid or soil drench application) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Foliar spraying' is not accepted for R; the liquid is poured at the base, not sprayed on the leaves.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **P (broadcasting)** (1 mark).
- **The plants are many and close together, so the whole bed must be covered evenly; ringing each plant would be slow and would disturb them** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the reason if Q is chosen.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Fertilizer against the stem would scorch (burn) the stem and roots** (1 mark).
- **At a short distance it lies over the feeding roots, which can still take up the nutrients** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It will spoil the plant' alone earns 1 mark.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **use only the measured quantity**; **apply when the soil is moist, not in a dry, hot afternoon**; **do not broadcast on a windy day**; **keep the fertilizer off the leaves and stems**; **use gloves or a scoop and wash the hands afterwards**; **keep fertilizer away from food and drinking water** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Be careful' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Clear a shaded space or dig a shallow pit** (1 mark).
- **Heap the materials in layers, mixing dry and fresh material, with a little soil between the layers** (1 mark).
- **Water the heap to keep it damp and cover it** (1 mark).
- **Turn the heap regularly (every one to two weeks) until it is well rotted** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The steps must be in a workable order; a bare list of materials earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **dark brown or black in colour**; **crumbly, with the original materials no longer recognisable**; **earthy smell, not a foul smell**; **the heap has cooled down and shrunk in size** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It looks like soil' is accepted once, for the colour or the crumbly texture, but not for both.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **it costs nothing and uses waste from the compound**; **it adds humus and improves the soil**; **it releases nutrients slowly and is not easily washed away**; **there is no risk of scorching the crop**; **it keeps the compound clean** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Candidates who argue that NPK should also be used in small amounts should not be penalised, provided three reasons for compost are given.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Bed 3** (1 mark).
- (ii) **7 kg** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Bed 1** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 7 without the unit in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Too much fertilizer was applied** (1 mark).
- **The excess made the soil solution too strong and scorched (burnt) the roots and leaves** (1 mark).
- **The damaged plants grew poorly, so the yield fell** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the plants were burnt by the fertilizer' for 2 marks if the idea of excess is also stated.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the same size and type of bed and soil**; **the same crop**; **the same number of plants**; **the same watering and weeding**; **the same length of time** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The treatment itself is the variable being tested and must not be given as an answer.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Use poultry manure worked into the soil together with the correct measured amount of NPK** (accept: use the measured amount of NPK only) (1 mark).
- **Reason drawn from the table: Bed 3 (correct amount) gave the best yield and Bed 4 shows that extra fertilizer lowers the yield; the manure also improves the soil** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must refer to the results in the table.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE, each with its reason: **store in a dry place** - *it absorbs moisture and cakes*; **keep the bag sealed and off the floor** - *to keep out moisture*; **store away from food, water and children** - *the chemicals are poisonous*; **keep it out of the sun and away from fire** - *heat spoils it and some fertilizers are a fire risk* (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A rule given without its reason earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **In dry soil the fertilizer cannot dissolve, so the plant cannot take it up** (1 mark).
- **The plants may be scorched, and some of the nutrient is lost in the heat** (1 mark).
- **Apply when the soil is moist - after a light rain or watering, in the cool of the morning or evening** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The better time must be stated for the third mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **read the label and dilute it with the stated volume of water**; **apply in the cool of the morning or evening**; **spread it evenly and avoid spraying into the wind**; **wash the sprayer and his hands after use**; **do not apply just before harvesting** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Pour it on the plants' earns no mark; the idea of diluting or of measuring must appear in at least one answer.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 3: Crop Production | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.2.3.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the different plant nutrients (organic and inorganic fertilizers) and their application in school farming or gardening.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production, Basic 7, page 48 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.2.3.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.3.1.1, observe and list all the sources of plant nutrients in the community and categorise them as organic or inorganic, with the exemplars: create a table showing the differences between the sources of plant nutrients; and compare the volumes of organic and inorganic sources of plant nutrients required by different plants. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.3.1.2, describe the physical characteristics of the different plant nutrients and how each of them is applied in the field, with the exemplars: identify the different sources of plant nutrients and explain how the physical structure or appearance of each affects the way it is applied; describe in groups how each source is applied, for example in the school garden; and demonstrate the practical application of the different sources of plant nutrients.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.2.3.1.1) carries topics 5.1 to 5.4 and Questions 1(a), 2 and 4(c); I2 (B7/JHS1.2.3.1.2) carries topics 5.5 and 5.6 and Questions 1(b), 1(c), 3, 4(a), 4(b), 5 and 6. The 'table of differences' exemplar is examined in Question 2(b) and the 'compare the volumes required' exemplar in Question 2(c); the practical application exemplar is examined in Questions 3, 4 and 6, which is the part of that work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.2.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The division organic/inorganic is the backbone of this sub-strand. A quick class test is to ask, 'Did it once live, or was it made in a factory?' Wood ash and green manure are the two that candidates most often place wrongly.
- Question 2(b) is the curriculum's own 'table of differences' exemplar. Insist that both columns of a row compare the same property; many candidates write 'organic is from plants' against 'inorganic is quick', which compares nothing.
- The volume comparison in Questions 1(c) and 2(c) is poorly done in most classes. Weigh a wheelbarrow of manure against a 1 kg scoop of NPK in front of the pupils; the idea of concentration is then never forgotten.
- In Question 3, 'foliar spray' is refused for R because the liquid is poured at the base. Teach the three common methods by what the farmer actually does: scatter over the whole bed, place in a ring round each plant, or wet the soil or the leaves with a solution.
- Question 5 carries the most important practical lesson of the sub-strand: more fertilizer is not better. Bed 4 in the table is the one to discuss at length after the paper has been marked.
- Safety and storage (Question 6) are frequently skipped in teaching. A bag of fertilizer beside a basket of tomatoes in a kitchen is a real and common danger; make the rule concrete - fertilizer never shares a room with food.
- Follow-up work: let each group prepare one bed of the school garden, measure out the correct quantity of manure or fertilizer, apply it by the right method and keep a simple record of the growth of the crop for the rest of the term.

Correct-answer distribution: A = 10, B = 10, C = 10, D = 10 (40 items).

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| 1 (b) | A, the goat, is a ruminant; C, the pig, is a monogastric animal; D, the fowl, is poultry, which is also a monogastric bird. | Comparing Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry | Understand |
| 1 (c) | (i) B is a large four-legged animal with a hairy body, hooves, horns and a long tail, while D is a two-legged bird with feathers, wings, a beak and a comb. (ii) A and B are both ruminants with four-chambered stomachs that chew the cud; both are four-legged mammals covered with hair; both have horns and hooves; both feed on grass and both give birth to live young and suckle them with milk. | Comparing Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry | Analyse |
| 2 (a) | P, the eggs, come from a fowl, a duck, a guinea fowl or a turkey; Q, the milk, comes from a cow, a goat or a sheep; R, the skin of the drum head, comes from a goat, a sheep or a cow; S, the dung, comes from any of the animals kept in the pen, such as cattle, goats, sheep, pigs or poultry. | Commercial Uses and By-Products | Understand |
| 2 (b) | (i) A by-product is a useful material obtained from an animal other than the main product for which it is kept, such as the hide, skin, horns, bones or dung. (ii) R and S are by-products: the skin used for the drum is obtained after the animal has been slaughtered for its meat, and the dung is the waste of the animal, not the food it was kept to produce. | Commercial Uses and By-Products | Understand |
| 2 (c) | The dung should be heaped, kept moist and allowed to rot down (composted) for several weeks, turning it from time to time, before it is spread. Fresh dung is too strong and would scorch the roots of the crop; rotting kills many weed seeds and disease germs in the dung and removes the foul smell and the flies; and the rotted manure releases its nutrients in a form the plant can use. | Domestic Uses of Animals | Apply |
| 2 (d) | Hide and skin for leather bags, sandals and belts; horns and hooves for combs, buttons and ornaments; bones for bone meal fed to animals or for glue; feathers for stuffing pillows and for decoration; and blood and offal, which are processed into animal feed. | Commercial Uses and By-Products | Remember |
| 3 (a) | Body covering: the cattle have hair on the skin while the fowl has feathers. Legs: four for the cattle, two for the fowl. Stomach: the cattle have a stomach of four chambers (a rumen and three others) while the fowl has a simple stomach with a crop and a gizzard. Feed: grass and crop residues for the cattle, prepared mash with grit for the fowl. | Comparing Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry | Understand |
| 3 (b) | A fowl has no teeth and swallows its food whole. The food passes to the gizzard, a strong muscular organ, and the small stones of grit held there grind the grain into small pieces so that it can be digested. Cattle chew their food with their teeth and chew the cud again later, so no grinding stones are needed. | Monogastric Animals and Poultry | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | The pigs will be the most difficult. A pig is monogastric and cannot digest much fibre, so it must be given bran, kitchen waste and other concentrates, which are exactly the feeds that have become expensive. The cattle can still manage on crop residues, straw and browse because the micro-organisms in their rumen break down fibre, and the fowls eat only a small quantity each, so the cost of feeding them is lower. | Ruminants | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | (i) Ama spent 900 + 400 = GH₵1,300; Kojo spent 600 + 2,100 = GH₵2,700. (ii) Ama's profit = 2,100 - 1,300 = GH₵800; Kojo's profit = 3,400 - 2,700 = GH₵700. | Domestic Uses of Animals | Apply |
| 4 (b) | Goats are ruminants and can live on grass, browse and crop residues, which Ama can cut free around the farm, and they can be allowed to graze; broiler fowls are monogastric and must be fed on bought, prepared feed every day, and a large number of birds eats a great deal in a year. Kojo received more because broilers grow to market weight in only a few weeks, so he was able to sell several batches of many birds within the year. | Ruminants | Analyse |
| 4 (c) | Either answer can earn full marks if it is argued from the table. Goats: the profit was higher (GH₵800 against GH₵700) and the money spent during the year was much lower, so less cash is tied up and the risk of loss if prices fall is smaller. Broilers: the money returns quickly, several times a year, and the sales were larger, so the enterprise can be expanded faster, provided the farmer can find the GH₵2,100 for feed. | Domestic Uses of Animals | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | Divide the class into groups and share the community among them, choosing the homes and farms each group will visit; prepare a simple record sheet and ask permission from the head teacher and from each household before entering; visit the pens and compounds, observe and count the animals seen and ask the keeper what each animal is used for; record the answers on the sheet at the time; then bring the sheets together in class, add up the numbers, and present the findings in a table or chart. | Domestic Animals and their Breeds | Create |
| 5 (b) | Suitable headings are: name of the animal; group (ruminant, monogastric or poultry); number seen; name or number of the home or farm; uses given by the keeper; and by-products obtained. | Domestic Animals and their Breeds | Create |
| 5 (c) | Greet the household and ask permission before entering, and thank them afterwards; do not enter a pen or touch, chase or frighten the animals, and keep away from a bull, a boar or a nursing mother; wash the hands with soap after the visit, since animals and their droppings carry germs; wear shoes and avoid stepping in dung; and move in groups with the teacher's knowledge of where each group has gone. | Commercial Uses and By-Products | Apply |
| 6 (a) | The space available and the kind of housing she can build; the feed she can obtain cheaply and regularly, such as her kitchen waste; the money she has for stock, feed and drugs; the market, that is, whether people nearby will buy the meat, eggs or milk; the time and labour she can give to the animals each day; and the rules of the town about keeping animals, including the nuisance of smell and noise to neighbours. | Domestic Uses of Animals | Apply |
| 6 (b) | Clean, dry housing protects the animals from rain, sun, thieves and stray dogs and keeps them from wandering into the neighbours' property; it prevents diseases and parasites that spread quickly in wet, dirty pens, so the animals grow well and fewer die; it keeps flies, smells and germs away from the people in the house; and the droppings can be collected in one place and used as manure. | Domestic Uses of Animals | Understand |
| 6 (c) | Animals supply meat, eggs and milk, which improve the diet and health of the people and reduce the money spent on importing food; they provide work and income for farmers, traders, butchers and feed sellers; their hides, skins and horns supply raw materials for leather and craft industries, some of which are exported; and their dung provides manure that improves the soil on farms. | Commercial Uses and By-Products | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Local names of animals and breeds are accepted where the animal is clear, for example 'West African Dwarf goat'. (3) 'Fowl' and 'chicken' are accepted for the same bird. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a comparison table, each row must compare the SAME feature across the animals before the mark is awarded. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **goat** (1 mark).
- B - **cow / cattle** (1 mark).
- C - **pig** (1 mark).
- D - **fowl (chicken)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'she-goat', 'nanny goat' for A and 'hen' for D.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A - **ruminant** (1 mark).
- C - **monogastric animal** (1 mark).
- D - **poultry** (accept: poultry, a monogastric bird) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Monogastric' written for D is accepted, but 'ruminant' is not.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Any ONE of: **B has four legs and D has two**; **B is covered with hair while D has feathers**; **D has a beak, comb and wings**; **B has horns and hooves** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **both are ruminants (chew the cud)**; **both are four-legged mammals covered with hair**; **both have hooves and horns**; **both feed mainly on grass**; **both give birth to live young and suckle them** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) a difference written in place of a similarity earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **fowl** (accept: duck, guinea fowl, turkey) (1 mark).
- Q - **cow** (accept: goat, sheep) (1 mark).
- R - **goat** (accept: sheep, cow) (1 mark).
- S - **cattle** (accept: goats, sheep, pigs, poultry) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A wild animal named anywhere in this part earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A useful material obtained from an animal apart from the main product (meat, milk or eggs), such as hide, skin, horn, bone or dung** (1 mark).
- (ii) **R and S** (1 mark) **because the skin is obtained after the animal is slaughtered for meat and the dung is the animal's waste, neither being the main product** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only one mark for naming R and S without a reason.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Heap it and allow it to rot (compost it), turning it from time to time, before spreading** (1 mark).
- Any TWO reasons: **fresh dung scorches the roots of the crop**; **rotting destroys weed seeds and disease germs**; **it removes the smell and the flies**; **the nutrients are then in a form the plant can take up** (1 mark each, maximum 2 marks).
  - *Marking note: 'Dry it in the sun' alone is not accepted as the treatment.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO, each with a use: **hide or skin** - *leather for bags, sandals and belts*; **horns or hooves** - *combs, buttons, ornaments*; **bones** - *bone meal or glue*; **feathers** - *stuffing pillows, decoration* (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A by-product named without a use earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Body covering - **hair / feathers** (1 mark).
- Number of legs - **four / two** (1 mark).
- Type of stomach - **four-chambered (ruminant) stomach / simple stomach with a gizzard** (1 mark).
- Main feed - **grass and crop residues / prepared mash (with grit)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both halves of a row must be correct before the mark for that row is given.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The fowl has no teeth and swallows its food whole** (1 mark).
- **The grit in the gizzard grinds the food into small pieces** (1 mark).
- **Cattle chew with their teeth and chew the cud, so they do not need grit** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the gizzard uses the stones like teeth' for the second mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The pigs** (1 mark).
- **A pig has a simple stomach and cannot digest fibre, so it needs bran and other concentrates, which are costly** (1 mark).
- **Cattle can still use crop residues and browse because the rumen breaks down fibre (or: fowls eat only small quantities each)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who names the cattle may earn at most 1 mark, for a reasoned point about the scarcity of grass.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) Ama - **GH₵1,300** (1 mark); Kojo - **GH₵2,700** (1 mark).
- (ii) Ama - **GH₵800** (1 mark); Kojo - **GH₵700** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Follow through: a correct subtraction from a wrong total in (i) earns the mark in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any TWO of: **goats are ruminants and feed on grass, browse and crop residues, which cost nothing**; **goats can be grazed or tethered on free pasture**; **broilers are monogastric and need bought, prepared feed daily** (1 mark each).
- **Broilers grow quickly, so Kojo sold several batches of many birds within the year** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Goats eat less' alone, without the reason, earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- A clear recommendation (1 mark).
- Any TWO supporting reasons drawn from the table, for example: **the goats gave the higher profit (GH₵800 against GH₵700)**; **the goats needed far less cash for feed (GH₵400 against GH₵2,100)**; **the broilers returned money several times within the year**; **the broilers had larger total sales** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Either enterprise is acceptable; the marks are for the reasons, which must use the figures.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Divide into groups and share out the area to be visited** (1 mark).
- **Prepare a record sheet and obtain permission before visiting** (1 mark).
- **Observe and count the animals and ask the keepers about their uses, recording at once** (1 mark).
- **Bring the records together, add up the numbers and present them in a table or chart** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Steps given in a workable order; a single step split into two earns one mark only.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **name of animal**; **group (ruminant, monogastric, poultry)**; **number counted**; **home or farm visited**; **uses of the animal**; **by-products obtained** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Information' or 'remarks' is too vague and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **ask permission and greet the household politely**; **do not enter pens or chase, touch or frighten the animals**; **keep away from dangerous animals such as a bull or a nursing mother**; **wash hands with soap after the visit**; **wear shoes and avoid dung**; **stay in groups and report to the teacher** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Be careful' or 'behave well' earns no mark without the action.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the space and housing available**; **the feed she can get cheaply**; **the money she has**; **the market for the product**; **the time and labour needed**; **the neighbours and the rules of the town** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A reason that is not a real consideration, such as 'the colour of the animal', earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **it protects the animals from rain, sun, thieves and stray animals**; **it prevents diseases and parasites, so the animals grow well**; **it keeps flies, smells and germs away from the household and the neighbours**; **the droppings can be collected and used as manure**; **the animals do not stray and destroy the neighbours' property** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Each reason must be different; 'it keeps them safe' twice earns 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **they supply protein food (meat, eggs, milk) and improve nutrition**; **they create employment and income**; **their hides, skins and horns supply raw materials for industry and export**; **their dung provides manure for crops**; **they reduce the money spent on imported meat** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A domestic benefit to one family only, such as 'Afia will eat the eggs', does not answer this part.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 4: Animal Production | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.2.4.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the differences among domestic animals (ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, which are monogastric herbivores). **B7/JHS1.2.4.2** - Demonstrate understanding of the usefulness of the different types of animals for domestic and commercial purposes.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production, Basic 7, pages 49 to 52 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.2.4.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.1.1, examine and list the domestic animals found in the community, with the exemplars: identify the types of domestic animals; match the animals with their breeds; and list and discuss the characteristics (shape, colour, size, food and feeding) used to classify them. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.1.2, show the differences and similarities among ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, with the exemplars: classify domestic animals into ruminants, monogastrics and poultry and give examples of each; write the differences among them; and write the similarities in their nature and characteristics in Ghana and in other countries. Content standard B7/JHS1.2.4.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.2.1, discuss and write the domestic and commercial uses of the different types of animals, with the exemplars: explain the concepts of domestic use and commercial use; and make a poster of any two useful domestic animals and describe the domestic uses of ruminants, monogastrics and poultry. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.2.4.2.2, observe and compare the uses of the different types of animals, with the exemplars: research the animals in the community by observing them and discuss their uses; and list and match domestic animals to their commercial uses, including by-products such as animal waste.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.2.4.1.1) carries topic 6.1 and Questions 1(a) and 5; I2 (B7/JHS1.2.4.1.2) carries topics 6.2 to 6.4 and Questions 1(b), 1(c) and 3; I3 (B7/JHS1.2.4.2.1) carries topic 6.5 and Questions 2(c), 4 and 6; I4 (B7/JHS1.2.4.2.2) carries topic 6.6 and Questions 2(a), 2(b), 2(d) and 5(c). The observation and poster exemplars are examined in Questions 5 and 6, which is the part of that practical work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.2.4.1 and B7.2.4.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand carries TWO content standards, B7/JHS1.2.4.1 and B7/JHS1.2.4.2, and the paper is balanced between them. Teachers who stop at classification leave half of the sub-strand untaught.
- Poultry are monogastric birds. Candidates should be taught the three working groups - ruminants, other monogastric animals and poultry - and should not be penalised for writing 'monogastric' for a fowl, provided they do not call it a ruminant.
- The surest classroom test of a ruminant is behaviour, not anatomy: watch a resting goat or cow bring food back to the mouth and chew it again. Section A item 25 and Question 1(c) both reward that observation.
- Question 3(b) on grit and the gizzard is often answered with 'the fowl likes stones'. Open a gizzard in class if the school kills a fowl; the small stones inside make the point in a way no diagram can.
- Question 4 brings money into the sub-strand. Candidates must subtract total cost from total sales; many subtract only the feed cost. Either enterprise may be recommended in 4(c), but the reasons must come from the figures.
- In Question 2, keep the distinction between a main product and a by-product clear. Milk and eggs are main products; hide, skin, horn, bone and dung are by-products obtained in addition to them.
- Follow-up work: let the class carry out the survey of Question 5 for real, draw a bar chart of the animals counted in the community, and invite a local keeper of animals to answer the pupils' questions about feeding and uses.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of the parts of the alimentary canal must be used correctly: 'oesophagus' or 'gullet' is accepted, but 'windpipe' or 'trachea' is not. (3) 'Sugar' is accepted for glucose and 'fatty acids and glycerol' for the end products of oils. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a flow chart, both the starting food and the end product must be shown before the mark is awarded. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [6 marks]

- A - **mouth** (1 mark).
- B - **oesophagus** (accept: gullet) (1 mark).
- C - **stomach** (1 mark).
- D - **small intestine** (1 mark).
- E - **large intestine** (accept: colon) (1 mark).
- F - **anus** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Windpipe' or 'trachea' written for B earns no mark; that tube carries air, not food.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- D - **completes digestion and absorbs the digested food into the blood** (1 mark).
- E - **absorbs water from the undigested material (and stores faeces)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It digests food' alone is too vague for E.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **A, B, C, D, E, F** (2 marks; 1 mark if one letter is out of place or missing).
  - *Marking note: No mark if the list begins anywhere other than A.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **A substance taken into the body** (1 mark) **which provides energy, builds and repairs the body or protects it from disease** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any FOUR of: **carbohydrates**; **proteins**; **fats and oils**; **vitamins**; **mineral salts**; **water** (half a mark each, 2 marks for four correct).
  - *Marking note: 'Something we eat' alone earns 1 mark in (i).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **to supply energy**; **for growth**; **to repair worn-out or damaged parts**; **to protect the body from disease (keep healthy)**; **to keep the body warm**; **to supply water and roughage for the proper working of the body** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'To become fat' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any THREE differences: **thin, with ribs showing / normal weight**; **dull hair, dry skin, sunken eyes / bright eyes and healthy skin**; **weak and tired / active and playful**; **often ill and heals slowly / resists disease** (1 mark each).
- **The child should be given regular balanced meals and taken to a health centre** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are given for the comparison; 'he is sick' without a visible feature earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Mouth - **chewing by the teeth, moistening with saliva and the start of starch digestion** (1 mark).
- Stomach - **churning with acid and enzymes; protein digestion begins** (1 mark).
- Small intestine - **digestion is completed and the digested food is absorbed into the blood** (1 mark).
- Large intestine - **water is absorbed and the waste is stored as faeces** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A row that merely says 'food passes through' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Physical digestion: food is broken into smaller pieces without a change in the substance** (1 mark).
- **Chemical digestion: the food substances are changed into simpler ones by enzymes** (1 mark).
- **One correct example of each from the breakfast** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both examples are needed for the third mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **She cannot chew, so large pieces of food are swallowed** (1 mark).
- **Large pieces give the enzymes a small surface to act on, so digestion is slow and incomplete** (1 mark).
- **Advice: eat soft, mashed or well cooked food, eat slowly, or see a dentist** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of surface area or of slower enzyme action is needed for the second mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A continuous tube from mouth to anus, drawn large and in pencil (1 mark).
- Any THREE further parts correctly placed and clearly named, with label lines touching the parts (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for correct position and labelling, not for beauty; a label line that does not touch its part earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The statement is not correct** (1 mark).
- **Food is pushed along by waves of muscular squeezing in the wall of the canal** (1 mark).
- **This works in any position, so a person lying down can still swallow (and food travels upwards in part of the large intestine)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the explanation if the candidate agrees with the pupil.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **It is made up of several different organs joined together** (1 mark).
- **Each organ does a special piece of work** (1 mark).
- **The organs work together in order for one purpose, the digestion and absorption of food** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'other organs such as the liver help it' for the third mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **starch to glucose (simple sugar)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **protein to amino acids** (1 mark).
- (iii) **oils and fats to fatty acids and glycerol** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The arrow or the word 'gives' must be shown; a bare list of products earns 1 mark in total.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The passing of digested food through the wall of the alimentary canal into the blood** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The small intestine** (1 mark).
- (iii) **By the blood, through the blood vessels** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Digestion' written for (i) earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **They increase the surface area of the inner wall** (1 mark).
- **So more digested food is absorbed, and absorbed more quickly** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'They catch the food' earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) **To release energy in the cells during respiration** (1 mark).
- (ii) **To build new tissue for growth and for the repair of worn-out parts** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'For strength' is accepted for (i) only if energy is mentioned.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **starch** (1 mark).
- Q - **glucose (a simple or reducing sugar)** (1 mark).
- R - **protein** (1 mark).
- S - **oil or fat** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Carbohydrate' is accepted for P and Q only if the candidate also writes starch or sugar.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- P - any ONE of: **boiled yam**; **cassava**; **plantain**; **cocoyam**; **rice**; **kenkey or banku**; **bread** (1 mark).
- R - any ONE of: **egg white**; **meat**; **fish**; **beans**; **groundnut**; **milk** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A food named for the wrong test earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The enzyme in saliva changed some of the starch into sugar** (1 mark).
- **Some starch was left, so the iodine test was still positive but weaker** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The bread was wet' earns no mark; the action of saliva must be given.*
