## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 1: The Human Body System | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.3.1.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the concept of food, the process of digestion and its importance in humans.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System, Basic 7, pages 53 to 55 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.3.1.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.1, explain the concept of food and the need to eat, with the exemplars: explain what food is and the nutrients in it and deduce a definition of food; compare the appearance of starved people with that of people who eat well and look healthy; and deduce the importance of feeding. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.2, examine what happens to food at the various stages of digestion, with the exemplars: identify the parts of the alimentary canal on a drawing; research and describe what happens to food such as boiled yam, cassava, plantain, cocoyam or bread, egg, meat, orange and palm oil in the mouth, the stomach and the small and large intestines; and draw and label the human digestive system. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.3, identify the end products of digestion of starchy, protein and oily foods and explain how they are absorbed, with the exemplars: describe absorption using an animation; draw a flow chart showing starch changing to sugar, protein to amino acids and oils to fatty acids; and perform practical food tests on starch, glucose, protein, fats and oils.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.3.1.1.1) carries topic 7.1 and Question 2(a) and 2(b); I2 (B7/JHS1.3.1.1.2) carries topics 7.2 and 7.3 and Questions 1, 3 and 4; I3 (B7/JHS1.3.1.1.3) carries topics 7.4 to 7.6 and Questions 5 and 6. The 'draw and label the human digestive system' exemplar is examined in Question 1, the flow-chart exemplar in Question 5(a) and the practical food-test exemplar in Question 6, which is the part of that practical work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.3.1.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The oesophagus and the trachea are confused by many candidates. Fix the difference once: the oesophagus carries food to the stomach, the trachea carries air to the lungs; a paper that sends food down the windpipe earns no mark.
- In Question 1(a) the small and large intestines must be told apart by their appearance: the small intestine is the long, narrow, coiled tube, while the large intestine is the shorter, wider tube that frames it.
- The three end products - glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids and glycerol - are the heart of indicator B7/JHS1.3.1.1.3. Drill them as a flow chart, not as a list, so that candidates write 'starch gives glucose' rather than three unconnected words.
- Question 3(b) separates physical from chemical digestion. Candidates who give no example from the meal should not be given the third mark, however good the definitions are.
- Question 4(b) attacks the common idea that food falls down the canal by gravity. The muscular squeezing of the canal wall is the correct answer; a class demonstration with a soft ball pushed along a rubber tube makes it plain.
- The food tests in Question 6 should be done, not only read about. Iodine on yam, Benedict's solution on a glucose drink, and the grease spot from palm oil on paper can all be managed in any Ghanaian school laboratory.
- Follow-up work: let pupils chew a piece of bread for two minutes and then test it with iodine and with Benedict's solution, as in Question 6(c). The result teaches the action of saliva better than any amount of dictation.

| 3 (d) | The Sun pulls the planet towards itself with the force of gravity, so the planet cannot fly off into space. It is also the source of the energy used in solar panels. | The Solar System and the Sun | Understand |
| 6 (c) | Darken the room and shine a torch on a globe or a large ball, with a mark on it to show Ghana. The torch stands for the Sun. Keep the torch still and slowly turn the globe on its axis. The class will see that only the half facing the torch is lit, and that the mark for Ghana moves into the light and then into the darkness as the globe turns, showing day and night. | The Solar System and the Sun | Apply |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of planets must be spelt well enough to be recognised and must begin with a capital letter; 'Earth' and 'the earth' are both accepted. (3) 'Oval' is accepted for elliptical. (4) 'Spinning' or 'turning on its axis' is accepted for rotation, and 'going round the Sun' for revolution; the two must not be interchanged. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **Mercury** (1 mark).
- X - **Venus** (1 mark).
- Y - **Earth** (1 mark).
- Z - **Mars** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The four names must be in the correct order from the Sun; a correct name in the wrong position earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **The inner planets** (accept: the rocky or terrestrial planets) (1 mark).
- Any ONE of: **they have solid rocky surfaces**; **they are small**; **they are close to the Sun**; **they have few or no moons** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'They are hot' alone is too vague.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Y, the Earth** (1 mark).
- Any ONE of: **it is neither too hot nor too cold**; **it has liquid water**; **it has air (oxygen) to breathe** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Because people live there' is a restatement and earns no mark for the reason.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Z is farther from the Sun, so its path (orbit) is much longer** (1 mark).
- **It also travels more slowly than W, so it takes much more time to complete one round** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of a longer path is essential for the first mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A very large group (collection) of stars, dust and gas** (1 mark) **held together by gravity** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The Milky Way** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Many stars' alone earns 1 mark in (i).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The light of the Milky Way is faint** (1 mark).
- **The bright lights of the town brighten the sky and hide it, while the village is dark** (1 mark).
- **Suggestion: travel to a dark place outside the town, or switch off the compound lights and observe on a moonless night** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Too many buildings in Accra' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Planet, solar system, galaxy** (1 mark).
- **Reason: the planet is one member of the solar system, and the solar system is one small part of the galaxy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the reason if the order is wrong.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **a star gives out its own light and heat, a planet reflects light**; **a star is far larger and hotter**; **stars twinkle, planets shine steadily**; **a planet moves round a star** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Stars are far away and planets are near' is too weak on its own.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **the axis (of the planet)** (1 mark).
- Q - **rotation** (accept: the planet turning or spinning on its own axis) (1 mark).
- R - **revolution** (accept: the planet moving round the Sun) (1 mark).
- S - **the orbit** (accept: the elliptical path of the planet) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Rotation written for R, or revolution for Q, earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Q - **day and night** (1 mark).
- R - **the year** (accept: the seasons) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Day and night written for R earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Elliptical (an ellipse)** (1 mark).
- **The distance between the planet and the Sun changes as the planet moves; it is nearer at some times and farther at others** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The planet is always the same distance from the Sun' is wrong and earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The gravitational pull of the Sun holds the planet and stops it flying away** (1 mark).
- **The planet is also moving forward fast along its path, so it keeps going round instead of falling in** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Gravity alone earns 1 mark; the forward motion is needed for the second.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Mercury - **first (nearest) planet from the Sun** (1 mark).
- Venus - **second planet from the Sun** (1 mark).
- Mercury - any ONE of: **the smallest inner planet**; **has almost no atmosphere**; **very hot by day and very cold by night**; **has the shortest year** (1 mark).
- Venus - any ONE of: **the hottest planet**; **has a very thick atmosphere**; **nearly the same size as the Earth**; **seen as the morning or evening star** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A property given for the wrong planet earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Venus has a very thick atmosphere** (1 mark).
- **The atmosphere traps the heat so that it cannot escape, and the heat builds up** (1 mark).
- **Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat escapes quickly into space** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The trapping of heat must be stated; 'Venus is bigger' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **365 / 88** (1 mark) **= 4.1, which is about 4 times** (1 mark).
- (ii) **A year on Mercury is much shorter than an Earth year (about a quarter as long)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the second mark for 4 even if the division is not shown, but the working mark is then lost.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **It is seen shining brightly just before sunrise or just after sunset** (1 mark).
- **It is not a star but a planet, which shines by reflecting the light of the Sun** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark requires the idea of reflected light or of Venus being a planet.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE materials, each with a correct use, for example: **a large ball of clay for the Sun**; **smaller balls, beads or seeds for the planets**; **loops of wire or lines on cardboard for the paths**; **thread or sticks to hold the planets** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A material named with no use, or a use with no material, earns no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR steps in a workable order: **fix the largest ball at the centre as the Sun**; **make four planets of different sizes**; **make four oval paths of increasing size round the Sun**; **place each planet on its own path in the correct order**; **label the bodies and state that the model is not to scale** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Steps given out of a workable order lose 1 mark overall.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the order of the planets from the Sun**; **that each planet has its own path**; **the oval shape of the paths**; **that the Sun is at the centre** (1 mark each).
- Any ONE of: **the true sizes of the bodies**; **the true distances between them**; **the real speeds of the planets**; **that the paths are not solid rings** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is not real' is too vague for the third mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The pupil is not correct** (1 mark).
- **The Earth rotates on its own axis once in about 24 hours** (1 mark).
- **The half facing the Sun has day and the half turned away has night, so the Sun only appears to move** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who agrees with the pupil can earn no mark in this part.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **it supplies light for seeing and for photosynthesis**; **it supplies heat and keeps the Earth warm**; **it drives the water cycle and the winds**; **its gravity holds the planets in their paths**; **it supplies energy for solar panels** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It makes the day bright' and 'it gives light' count as one answer only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Shine a torch (the Sun) on a globe or ball marked to show Ghana, in a darkened room** (1 mark).
- **Keep the torch still and turn the globe slowly; the lit half has day, the dark half night, and the mark passes from one to the other** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for an activity in which the torch is moved round the globe.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 2: The Solar System | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.3.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of the inner planets of the solar system and understand their movement in the system.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System, Basic 7, pages 56 and 57 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.3.2.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.2.1.1, identify the inner planets of the solar system and describe their properties, with the exemplars: identify and describe what constitutes the inner planets of the solar system using pictures, videos and the like; describe the galaxy, the Milky Way and the elliptical shape of the paths of movement of the inner planets; and design and construct a model of the solar system. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.2.1.2, discuss the properties and the relative motions of the planets Mercury and Venus, with the exemplars: outline properties peculiar to each of the planets Mercury and Venus; and describe the movement of the planets Mercury and Venus around the Sun.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.3.2.1.1) carries topics 8.1 to 8.4 and 8.6 and Questions 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6; I2 (B7/JHS1.3.2.1.2) carries topic 8.5 and Question 4. The 'design and construct a model' exemplar is examined as a written design task in Question 5, which is the part of that practical work a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.3.2.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The order of the inner planets - Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars - must be known cold. A short mnemonic made by the class in Twi, Ga or Dagbani is usually remembered better than one copied from a textbook.
- Rotation and revolution are interchanged by many candidates every year. Teach them together with their effects: rotation gives day and night, revolution gives the year, and insist on that pairing in every answer.
- Candidates often assume that the planet nearest the Sun must be the hottest. Question 4(b) is built on that misconception; the atmosphere of Venus, and not its distance, is the key, which matches core competency CP 5.8 in the curriculum.
- Note that the planets' paths are elliptical, not circular. Pupils should draw them with a loop of thread round two pins, which shows at once why the distance from the Sun changes.
- In Question 5 the marks are for design thinking, not for art. A candidate who states clearly what each material stands for and places the planets in the right order scores well even if the model is described in plain language.
- Insist on the words 'not drawn to scale' whenever pupils draw the solar system. The distances are so great that no true-scale drawing can be made on a sheet of paper, and saying so is part of honest scientific work.
- Follow-up work: on a clear night, ask pupils to find the bright object near the western sky just after sunset and to note how it does not twinkle. Comparing it with a twinkling star makes the star-planet difference in Question 2(d) real.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) 'Living' is accepted for biotic and 'non-living' for abiotic, but the terms must not be interchanged. (3) A named Ghanaian example is accepted wherever an example is asked for, provided it fits the category. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a food chain the arrows must point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- A - **the Sun (sunlight)** (1 mark).
- B - **a water plant** (accept: reed, water weed) (1 mark).
- C - **a fish** (1 mark).
- D - **the mud and stones at the bottom of the pond** (accept: soil, the pond bed) (1 mark).
- E - **a bird** (accept: a wading bird such as a heron or an egret) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A general answer such as 'plant' for B and 'animal' for C or E is accepted at this level.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any TWO of **B**, **C** and **E** as biotic (1 mark each).
- Either **A** or **D** as abiotic (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Letters alone are enough; names need not be repeated.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Water plant to fish to bird** (1 mark).
- **Arrows drawn in the correct direction, from the eaten to the eater** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A chain written the wrong way round earns the first mark only if the three organisms are correct.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - **terrestrial** (accept: land ecosystem) (1 mark).
- Q - **aquatic** (accept: water ecosystem) (1 mark).
- R - **arboreal** (accept: tree ecosystem) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Forest' written for R earns no mark; the category wanted is arboreal.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Terrestrial - any ONE named Ghanaian land area, for example **the northern savanna grassland** (1 mark).
- Aquatic - any ONE named Ghanaian water body, for example **the Volta Lake** (1 mark).
- Arboreal - **the life on the branches of a named tall tree, such as a silk-cotton tree** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example placed under the wrong category earns no mark.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Q - a named water organism, for example **tilapia** (1 mark), with **gills for breathing in water, fins for swimming or a streamlined body** (1 mark).
- R - a named tree-living organism, for example **a monkey, a squirrel or a bird** (1 mark), with **limbs or a tail for gripping branches, claws for climbing or wings for flying** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The feature must match the organism named; a feature with no organism earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The fish breathes through gills, which work only in water** (1 mark).
- **On land the gills dry up, so the fish cannot take in oxygen and it suffocates** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'There is no water' alone earns 1 mark; the gills must be mentioned for the second.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **A living part of the ecosystem** (1 mark) **plus a correct example** (1 mark).
- (ii) **A non-living part of the ecosystem** (1 mark) **plus a correct example** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example that does not match the definition earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Grass - **producer, makes its own food using sunlight** (1 mark).
- Grasshopper - **consumer, feeds on plants** (1 mark).
- Fungus - **decomposer, breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The name of the role alone is enough for the mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The grass makes its own food from sunlight, so food is produced inside the ecosystem** (1 mark).
- **The grasshopper and other consumers feed on the grass** (1 mark).
- **The fungus breaks down the dead material and returns the nutrients to the soil for the grass to use again** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The return of nutrients is essential for the third mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The waste killed the water plants** (1 mark).
- **The fish lost their food (and the polluted water also harmed them), so their numbers fell** (1 mark).
- **The birds, which feed on the fish, had no food and left** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The chain must run plants to fish to birds; a single sentence naming pollution earns 1 mark only.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **The components are linked and depend on one another (interdependence)** (1 mark).
- **A change in one part affects the other parts, including people** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Pollution is bad' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **stop the untreated waste or require the factory to treat it**; **enforce by-laws and punish offenders**; **stop the dumping of refuse at the lagoon**; **replant the plants around the lagoon**; **close the lagoon to fishing for a season**; **educate the community** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Pray for the lagoon' and other non-scientific measures earn no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any ONE of: **competition**; **pollination**; **shelter or nesting**; **seed dispersal** (1 mark).
- **A correct example of the interaction named** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Predation is a feeding relationship and earns no mark here.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR, each with a correct reason: **water - the medium in which the organisms live**; **sand or gravel - holds the roots of the plants**; **water plants - make food and give out oxygen**; **small fish or snails - the consumers**; **light - needed by the plants to make food**; **stones - shelter for the animals** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: An item named with no reason earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Biotic items correctly grouped** (1 mark).
- **Abiotic items correctly grouped** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One item in the wrong group loses the mark for that group only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **remove dead material and uneaten food**; **top up or partly change the water**; **feed the fish lightly**; **keep the tank in the light but out of the hot midday Sun**; **check the plants** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Clean it' alone is too vague.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- A clear position, for example **I agree, the tank is a model rather than a true ecosystem** (1 mark).
- **Reason: a true ecosystem is self-sustaining, while the tank is too small and needs food to be added and waste removed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Either position may be taken; the mark is for the reason, which must mention self-sustaining or outside help.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **animals lose shelter and food and move away or die**; **the soil is eroded and loses fertility**; **the area becomes hotter and drier**; **streams dry up**; **shade-loving plants die** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'The forest is finished' is a restatement and earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **timber, firewood, fruits, bush meat or herbs**; **clean air and oxygen**; **protection of the soil from erosion**; **water and rainfall**; **shade and a cooler climate**; **a place for study and tourism** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers about wood and firewood count as one.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **A workable activity, for example raising and planting seedlings of local trees at the start of the rains** (1 mark).
- **A way of judging success, for example counting the surviving seedlings or noting the return of grasses, insects and birds** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An activity with no way of judging success earns 1 mark only.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 3: Ecosystem | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.3.3.1** - Recognise the components of and interdependences in an ecosystem, and appreciate their interactions.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem, Basic 7, pages 58 and 59 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.3.3.1 carries the single indicator B7/JHS1.3.3.1.1, analyse the components of ecosystems and identify the interactions within, with the exemplars: describe an ecosystem as a self-sustaining unit in which components interact, for example a pond, a forest and many others; group ecosystems into terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal categories; identify and list the components, such as biotic and abiotic, of each category of ecosystem; differentiate among organisms in the different ecosystems mentioned; and explain how the components of the different ecosystems affect one another.

> Note: This sub-strand has only ONE indicator, B7/JHS1.3.3.1.1, so every item in this paper is traced to it. The six topics follow the five exemplars: topic 9.1 the self-sustaining unit; topic 9.2 the three categories; topics 9.3 and 9.4 the biotic and abiotic components; topic 9.5 the differences among the organisms of the categories; and topic 9.6 how the components affect one another. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.3.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Biotic and abiotic are the two words on which this whole sub-strand turns. Drill them with a five-minute walk round the school compound in which pupils list what they see in two columns; the exercise is worth more than any definition copied from the board.
- Arboreal is the category pupils forget, because most textbooks name only land and water. Fix it with a real tree on the school compound: the ants, lizards, birds, mosses and climbing plants on it make an arboreal ecosystem that can be seen in five minutes.
- Insist on the direction of the arrows in a food chain. The arrow means 'is eaten by', so it points from the plant to the animal, never the other way round.
- Question 4 is built on interdependence, the heart of the content standard. Candidates who merely write 'pollution killed everything' cannot score full marks; the chain from plants to fish to birds must be shown.
- The tank in Question 5 should actually be set up if the school has a suitable container. Pupils who have watched a model ecosystem for a term answer questions of this kind from experience rather than from memory.
- Question 5(d) rewards honest reasoning rather than a fixed answer. Accept either position, provided the candidate argues from the idea of a self-sustaining unit.
- Follow-up work: ask pupils to choose any one local ecosystem - a pond, a lagoon, a wood lot, a school garden - and to keep a term-long notebook of the living and non-living things in it and the changes they observe. This covers core competencies CP 5.1 and DL 5.6 at the same time.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | A is mixed cropping, B is mixed farming and C is land rotation, which is also called shifting cultivation. | Mixed Cropping | Understand |
| 1 (b) | Advantages: he earns money from both crops and animals, so a poor harvest does not ruin him; the droppings of the animals manure his crops; the crop residues feed his animals; and his land and labour are used all year round. Difficulties: he needs more capital for housing, feed and veterinary care; he needs more labour and more skill; the animals may stray and destroy the crops; and diseases of the animals must be controlled. | Mixed Farming | Understand |
| 1 (c) | The plots have been cropped for some years and their fertility has fallen. By leaving them to bush, the natural vegetation grows again, its leaves and roots decay and the nutrients are returned to the soil, so the fertility is restored without buying fertilizer. The system is becoming difficult because the growing population has reduced the amount of land available, so the fallow periods are now too short for the land to recover. | Land Rotation | Analyse |
| 2 (a) | (i) Crop rotation. (ii) Different crops are grown one after another, in a planned order, on the same piece of land, and the plan is repeated after the fourth year. | Crop Rotation | Understand |
| 2 (b) | Groundnut is a legume. Bacteria living in nodules on its roots take nitrogen from the air and change it into a form the soil can hold. When the crop residues are left on the field, this nitrogen enriches the soil, so the crop that follows grows better without the farmer buying so much fertilizer. The groundnut also gives the family food and some income, and its spreading leaves cover the soil. | Crop Rotation | Understand |
| 2 (c) | The fertility of the soil is maintained, because the different crops take different nutrients and the legume adds nitrogen; pests and diseases of maize are controlled, because they do not find their food plant every season; weeds are kept down, because the different crops smother them differently; the soil structure is improved, because deep and shallow roots follow one another; the resting year allows the land to recover; and the family has a variety of food and more than one source of income. | Crop Rotation | Analyse |
| 2 (d) | A suitable plan is: Year 1 maize, Year 2 cowpea, Year 3 cassava, Year 4 rest. The heavy feeder, maize, comes first on the freshly rested land; the legume, cowpea, follows and restores nitrogen; cassava, which can still do well on poorer soil and roots deeply, comes next; and the land then rests before the plan begins again. | Crop Rotation | Create |
| 3 (a) | Opoku practises land rotation or shifting cultivation, Mariama practises crop rotation and Yaw practises mixed cropping. | Meaning and Types of Farming Systems | Apply |
| 3 (b) | In Opoku's system the piece of land changes while the crop may stay the same; in Mariama's system the land stays the same while the crop changes. Opoku needs a large area, because several plots must lie fallow at the same time; Mariama needs only a small area, because the one field is used every year. | Meaning and Types of Farming Systems | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | Supporting reasons: he harvests several different foods from one small piece of land; if one crop fails he still has the others; the crops cover the soil and reduce erosion and weeds; and the cowpea adds nitrogen to the soil. Difficulty: the crops compete for light, water and nutrients; the work cannot easily be done by machine; harvesting at different times is laborious; and a pest may spread easily from one crop to another. | Mixed Cropping | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | Mixed farming, because she keeps animals and grows crops on the same holding at the same time, and the two enterprises serve each other. | Mixed Farming | Apply |
| 4 (b) | The fowls help the crops by supplying droppings, which are a rich manure that adds nutrients and improves the soil, and by eating insect pests and weed seeds when they scratch about on the harvested beds. The crops help the fowls by supplying maize grain and bran as feed, and by supplying green leaves and crop residues, which reduce the cost of bought feed; the maize stalks can also be used in the poultry house. | Mixed Farming | Analyse |
| 4 (c) | The droppings should be composted or left to rot well before use, because fresh droppings are too strong and can scorch the plants and may carry disease organisms; they should be dug into the soil and not left on the leaves; they should not be applied just before harvesting leafy vegetables; and she should wash her hands and the vegetables well afterwards. | Mixed Farming | Evaluate |
| 4 (d) | She must stop using artificial fertilizers and chemical pesticides and weedicides on the beds, relying on compost, manure and natural pest control such as neem extract; she must be sure that the feed given to the fowls does not contain banned additives and that no chemical drains onto the beds from elsewhere; and she should keep records and seek certification from the proper body before labelling the produce organic. | Organic Farming and the Choice of a System | Apply |
| 5 (a) | Organic farming is a system of farming in which crops are grown and animals are kept without the use of artificial fertilizers, chemical pesticides and weedicides. The farmer feeds the soil with compost, animal manure and green manure, and controls pests and weeds by natural methods. | Organic Farming and the Choice of a System | Remember |
| 5 (b) | Applying compost, farmyard manure or green manure; practising crop rotation, including legumes; mulching the beds to hold moisture and suppress weeds; using neem extract, wood ash or soapy water against pests; hand weeding and hand picking of pests; encouraging natural enemies such as ladybirds and birds; and using clean, untreated seed of resistant varieties. | Organic Farming and the Choice of a System | Understand |
| 5 (c) | Merits: the food is free from chemical residues and is safer to eat; the soil organisms and the structure of the soil are protected and improved; water bodies are not polluted by fertilizer and pesticide run-off; the farmer spends less on bought chemicals; and organic produce can fetch a higher price. Demerits: yields are often lower, at least at first; much more labour is needed, especially for weeding and for making compost; pests and diseases are harder to control quickly; and certification, where it is required, costs money and takes time. | Organic Farming and the Choice of a System | Evaluate |
| 6 (a) | Mixed cropping, supported by crop rotation, suits him best. The two acres are small, so land rotation is out of the question; mixed cropping gives several foods from the same small plot and spreads the harvest through the year; if one crop fails he still has the others; including a legume keeps the soil fertile without costly fertilizer; the crops cover the soil and reduce erosion and weeding; and the work can all be done by hand, since he has no machinery. If he can afford a few animals, mixed farming would add manure and a second source of income. | Organic Farming and the Choice of a System | Evaluate |
| 6 (b) | Land rotation needs a large area, because while one plot is cropped several others must lie fallow for years. With only two acres he would have to shorten the fallow so much that the soil would never recover, and the land left resting would produce nothing for his family in the meantime. | Land Rotation | Evaluate |
| 6 (c) | Set up a demonstration plot in the school garden with sections showing mixed cropping, crop rotation and organic practices, and invite the farmers to see it; hold an open day or durbar at which pupils present posters on each system; prepare simple leaflets or posters in the local language for the market and the information centre; or arrange a radio talk on the local station. | Meaning and Types of Farming Systems | Create |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of the five systems must be used exactly: land rotation (accept shifting cultivation), crop rotation, mixed cropping, mixed farming and organic farming. Mixed cropping and mixed farming must not be interchanged. (3) A named Ghanaian crop, animal or district is accepted wherever an example is asked for. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a table, a correct entry earns its mark even if the handwriting is untidy. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A - **mixed cropping** (1 mark).
- B - **mixed farming** (1 mark).
- C - **land rotation** (accept: shifting cultivation) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Mixed farming written for A, or mixed cropping for B, earns no mark; the two must be told apart.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any TWO advantages: **income from two sources**; **manure for the crops**; **crop residues as feed**; **land and labour used all year** (1 mark each).
- Any TWO difficulties: **more capital needed**; **more labour and skill needed**; **animals may stray into the crops**; **animal diseases must be controlled** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A general answer such as 'it is good' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The plots have lost their fertility after cropping** (1 mark).
- **The bush that grows and decays on them returns nutrients and restores the fertility** (1 mark).
- **Reason: population growth has reduced the land available, so fallow periods are too short** (accept: land is now scarce or expensive) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'He is lazy' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Crop rotation** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Different crops follow one another in a planned order on the same land, and the plan is repeated** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Land rotation' earns no mark; the land does not change.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Groundnut is a legume** (1 mark).
- **Bacteria in the nodules on its roots fix nitrogen from the air** (1 mark).
- **The soil is therefore enriched for the crop that follows (and the farmer saves on fertilizer)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is a good food' alone earns no mark in this part.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **soil fertility is maintained**; **pests and diseases are controlled**; **weeds are kept down**; **the soil structure is improved by different rooting depths**; **the resting year lets the land recover**; **a variety of food and income** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that both say 'the soil becomes rich' count as one.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **A plan naming all four in a sensible order over four years** (2 marks; 1 mark if one item is missing or out of place).
- **A sound reason, for example the legume follows the heavy feeder to restore nitrogen, or the resting year comes last before the plan is repeated** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any order is accepted provided the reason given supports it.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Opoku - **land rotation** (accept: shifting cultivation) (1 mark).
- Mariama - **crop rotation** (1 mark).
- Yaw - **mixed cropping** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The names must match the descriptions exactly.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Opoku - **the piece of land changes (the crop may stay the same)** (1 mark).
- Mariama - **the crop changes, the land stays the same** (1 mark).
- Opoku - **a large area of land is needed** (1 mark).
- Mariama - **only a small area is needed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A row left blank earns no mark; both columns must be completed.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any TWO of: **several foods from one small plot**; **insurance if one crop fails**; **the soil is covered, so less erosion and fewer weeds**; **the legume adds nitrogen** (1 mark each).
- Any ONE of: **the crops compete for light, water and nutrients**; **machines cannot easily be used**; **the crops ripen at different times, so more labour is needed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A difficulty written as an advantage earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Mixed farming** (1 mark).
- **Reason: she keeps animals and grows crops on the same holding at the same time** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Mixed cropping' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Fowls to crops - any TWO of: **droppings used as manure**; **they eat insect pests**; **they scratch out weed seeds** (1 mark each).
- Crops to fowls - any TWO of: **maize grain and bran as feed**; **green leaves and crop residues as feed**; **stalks used as litter or for the house** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The same point written twice in different words counts once.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **compost or allow the droppings to rot before use**; **dig them into the soil and keep them off the leaves**; **do not apply shortly before harvesting leafy vegetables**; **wash hands and wash the vegetables well** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Use gloves' is accepted as one answer.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **stop using artificial fertilizer**; **stop using chemical pesticides or weedicides and use natural methods**; **check that the poultry feed and any water running onto the plot are free of chemicals**; **keep records and obtain proper certification** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Grow more vegetables' earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Farming without artificial fertilizers and chemical pesticides or weedicides** (1 mark).
- **Using compost, manure and natural methods of pest and weed control instead** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Farming without chemicals' alone earns 1 mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **apply compost or manure**; **practise crop rotation with legumes**; **mulch the beds**; **use neem extract, ash or other natural pest control**; **hand weed and hand pick pests**; **encourage natural enemies**; **use resistant varieties** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Do not use chemicals' is a definition, not a practice, and earns no mark here.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any TWO merits: **food free from chemical residues**; **soil life and structure protected**; **no pollution of water bodies**; **less money spent on chemicals**; **higher price for the produce** (1 mark each).
- Any TWO demerits: **lower yields**; **much more labour**; **pests and diseases harder to control quickly**; **certification costs money and takes time** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A merit written in the demerit column earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **A named system, for example mixed cropping (accept mixed farming or crop rotation, if well defended)** (1 mark).
- Any THREE reasons that fit the farmer's situation: **the land is small, so no land can be left fallow for long**; **several foods from one plot and food spread through the year**; **insurance if one crop fails**; **a legume keeps the soil fertile without costly fertilizer**; **the work can be done by hand** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The reasons must refer to this farmer's land, money or family; general praise of the system earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Land rotation needs a large area, with several plots lying fallow at a time** (1 mark).
- **On two acres the fallow would be too short to restore fertility, and the resting land would feed nobody** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is an old system' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **a demonstration plot in the school garden shown to the farmers**; **an open day, durbar or exhibition with posters**; **simple leaflets or posters in the local language**; **a talk on local radio** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Tell them' is too vague for a mark.*

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.3.4.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the differences among the various farming systems: Land Rotation, Crop Rotation, Mixed Cropping, Mixed Farming, and Organic Farming.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems, Basic 7, pages 60 to 62 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.3.4.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.1, examine and discuss the differences among the various farming systems, with the exemplars: identify and define types of farming systems in Ghana and elsewhere; discuss the characteristics of the different farming systems in Ghana; and compare and contrast the characteristics of the different farming systems. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.2, categorise different farming systems, with the exemplars: classify different descriptions of farming systems under Land Rotation, Crop Rotation, Mixed Cropping, Mixed Farming and Organic Farming; and group the farming systems prevailing in their community under the same five headings. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.3, discuss the usefulness of different farming systems, with the exemplars: discuss and tabulate the reasons behind the use of the various farming systems; and debate the merits and demerits of the different farming systems.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.3.4.1.1) carries topics 10.1 to 10.3 and Questions 2 and 3; I2 (B7/JHS1.3.4.1.2) carries topics 10.4 and 10.5 and Questions 1 and 4; I3 (B7/JHS1.3.4.1.3) carries topic 10.6 and Questions 5 and 6. The debate exemplar is examined in Question 6(b) as a written argument, which is the part of that activity a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.3.4.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Mixed cropping and mixed farming are confused by candidates every year. Fix the difference in one line: mixed CROPping is crops only, grown together; mixed FARMing is crops plus animals on the same farm.
- Land rotation and crop rotation are the second common confusion. In land rotation the LAND moves and the crop may stay; in crop rotation the CROP moves and the land stays. Question 3(b) is built on exactly that distinction.
- Candidates should be able to say why a legume is in every good rotation. The nodules on the roots of groundnut or cowpea can be dug up and shown in a single lesson; pupils who have seen them never forget the point.
- The marks in Question 6 are for advice fitted to the farmer's own situation - two acres, little money, no machinery. A well-learnt list of advantages that ignores his circumstances cannot score full marks.
- Organic farming must be presented honestly. It protects the soil and gives food free of chemical residues, but it is laborious and its yields are often lower at first; pupils who can state both sides are the ones who will argue well in the curriculum's debate exemplar.
- Use the community itself as the teaching aid. Ask pupils to name the systems used on their own family farms and to group them under the five headings; this covers indicator B7/JHS1.3.4.1.2 and competency CG 5.4 at the same time.
- Follow-up work: lay out a small demonstration plot in the school garden, half under mixed cropping and half under a single crop, and let the class record and compare the two harvests over the term.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In every calculation, award the method marks for a correct formula and correct substitution even when the final answer is wrong. (3) The unit must be shown with a final answer; a correct number without a unit loses the final mark only. (4) 'Joule' or 'J' is accepted for energy. (5) The three methods of heat transfer must be named correctly: conduction, convection and radiation. (6) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (7) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A - **potential energy** (1 mark).
- C - **kinetic energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Gravitational potential energy' is accepted for A.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The potential energy decreases as the height falls** (1 mark).
- **The kinetic energy increases as the speed rises (at B the ball has both)** (1 mark).
- **The potential energy lost is changed into kinetic energy, so the total mechanical energy stays the same** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The ball moves faster' alone earns 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) **PE = mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 3.2** (1 mark) **= 16 J** (1 mark).
- (ii) **KE = 16 J, so 1/2 x 0.5 x v2 = 16, v2 = 64** (1 mark) **v = 8 m/s** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the method marks for a correct formula and correct substitution even if the arithmetic is wrong.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **There is friction between the ball and the slope, and air resistance** (1 mark).
- **Some of the energy is used to do work against friction, so less becomes kinetic energy** (1 mark).
- **The missing energy becomes heat (and a little sound); it is not destroyed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The energy is lost' without naming heat or sound earns no mark for the third point.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **The ability (capacity) to do work** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The joule (J)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Power' or 'watt' earns no mark in (ii).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR forms, each with a correct source, for example **heat - a cooking fire**; **light - a lamp**; **sound - a drum**; **solar - the Sun**; **electrical - a dry cell**; **chemical - food or charcoal**; **nuclear - a nuclear reactor** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A form named without a source earns no mark.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Electric bulb - **electrical to light (and heat)** (1 mark).
- Dry cell - **chemical to electrical** (1 mark).
- Electric fan - **electrical to kinetic (mechanical)** (1 mark).
- Solar panel - **solar to electrical** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The change must be written as one form to another; a single word earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **The sum of the potential energy and the kinetic energy of a body** (1 mark).
- (ii) **PE = mgh, with m = mass, g = acceleration due to gravity and h = height** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The expression must be accompanied by the meanings of the letters.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **KE = 1/2 x 2 000 x 10 squared** (1 mark) **= 100 000 J** (1 mark).
- (ii) **KE = 1/2 x 2 000 x 20 squared** (1 mark) **= 400 000 J** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 100 kJ and 400 kJ. A missing unit loses the final mark of the part only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large, since KE depends on the square of the speed** (1 mark).
- **The lorry then needs a much longer distance to stop and does far more damage in a crash** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Speeding is bad' without reference to the energy earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The mass of the body** (1 mark).
- **The height above the ground** (accept: the acceleration due to gravity) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Speed' is a factor for kinetic energy and earns no mark here.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Pin P** (1 mark).
- **Metal is a good conductor, so heat travels quickly along the rod to the far end** (1 mark).
- **The wax at that end melts first and releases the pin (the other two rods are poor conductors)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No reason marks if the wrong pin is named.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Conduction** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Convection** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Radiation written for (i) earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the same length and thickness of rod**; **the same depth in the same hot water (same temperature)**; **the same amount of wax**; **pins of the same size, started at the same time** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'The material' must NOT be given; that is what is being changed.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Radiation** (1 mark).
- **It needs no material medium; it can travel through empty space (a vacuum)** (1 mark).
- **Example: heat from the Sun reaching the Earth, or warmth felt in front of a coal pot** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It does not need water' is not enough for the second mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Stand the three cards one behind the other and line up the holes, using the thread** (1 mark).
- **Place the lighted candle in line at one end and look through the nearest hole** (1 mark).
- **Observation: the flame is seen when the holes are in a straight line** (1 mark).
- **Observation: the flame cannot be seen when one card is moved out of line** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both observations are needed; the second is the one that proves the point.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- **Reflection: light bounces back when it falls on a surface** (1 mark), **example: an image in a mirror or in still water** (1 mark).
- **Refraction: light bends as it passes from one transparent medium into another** (1 mark), **example: a pencil looking bent in a glass of water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example that belongs to the other effect earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Dispersion** (1 mark).
- (ii) **A glass prism** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'A mirror' earns no mark in (ii).*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Solar energy to electrical energy** (1 mark).
- Any TWO of: **Ghana has strong sunshine for most of the year**; **sunlight is free, so running costs are low**; **the panels work when the mains supply fails**; **they are clean, quiet and give off no smoke** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is modern' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **switch off lights and fans in empty rooms**; **use energy-saving (LED) bulbs**; **use daylight instead of lights**; **service the appliances**; **appoint class energy monitors**; **cook with a lid on the pot on an efficient stove** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers about switching things off count as one.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The water at the bottom is heated, expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler water sinks to take its place** (1 mark).
- **These convection currents carry the heat through the whole pot of water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word convection alone, with no mention of the rising and sinking water, earns 1 mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 1: Energy | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.4.1.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of forms of energy and their daily applications. **B7/JHS1.4.1.2** - Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of heat transfer and its applications in life. **B7/JHS1.4.1.3** - Demonstrate understanding of characteristics of light, such as travelling in a straight line, reflection, refraction and dispersion.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 1: Energy, Basic 7, pages 63 to 66 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.1.1, identify the various forms of energy and show how they are related, with the exemplars: list forms of energy in terms of potential, kinetic, heat, sound, solar, electrical, nuclear, chemical and light; and demonstrate and show by diagrams how potential energy is related to kinetic energy, mechanical energy being the sum of the two. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.1.2, explain daily applications of forms of energy, with the exemplars: discuss how forms of energy are used in daily life; match forms of energy to appliances used daily at school, in the home and in the community; explain factors that affect potential and kinetic energy in their application in daily life; and use the mathematical expressions PE = mgh and KE = half mv squared to solve problems involving mechanical energy. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.2.1, explain and demonstrate how heat is transferred in various media, with the exemplars: explain how heat is transferred through different media (gas, plastic, metal, liquid); and carry out an activity to show how heat is transferred through different media. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.1.3 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.1.3.1, demonstrate how light travels in a straight line, with the exemplars: perform experiments to show that light travels in a straight line and can be reflected and refracted, and produce reports, posters or diagrams; and perform an experiment to show dispersion of light into colours.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.4.1.1.1) carries topics 11.1 and 11.2 and Questions 1 and 2; I2 (B7/JHS1.4.1.1.2) carries topics 11.3 and 11.4 and Questions 3 and 6; I3 (B7/JHS1.4.1.2.1) carries topic 11.5 and Question 4; I4 (B7/JHS1.4.1.3.1) carries topic 11.6 and Question 5. The acceleration due to gravity is taken as 10 m/s squared throughout, and this is stated on the paper. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.4.1.1, B7.4.1.2 and B7.4.1.3.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Potential and kinetic energy are best taught with the body, not the board. A stone held up, dropped, and caught again makes the exchange obvious, and Fig. 1 then reads as a record of something the class has already seen.
- In every calculation insist on three lines: the formula, the substitution and the answer with its unit. Candidates who write only a number lose marks they could have had, since the method marks are given for the first two lines.
- Question 3(c) is the road-safety application of KE = half mv squared. The square is the whole point: doubling the speed multiplies the energy by four. Pupils who grasp that remember it long after the examination.
- The rod experiment in Question 4 needs no laboratory. A knitting needle, a plastic pen barrel and a stick of the same length, a tin of hot water and three blobs of candle wax are enough, and the result is seen in minutes.
- Keep conduction, convection and radiation tied to media: conduction mainly in solids, convection in liquids and gases, radiation through empty space. Candidates who learn the three words without the media interchange them under pressure.
- The three-card experiment in Question 5(a) is the standard demonstration of rectilinear propagation. The telling observation is the NEGATIVE one - the flame disappears when a card is moved out of line - and candidates should be trained to report it.
- Follow-up work: on a sunny morning, let pupils hold a glass prism or a basin of water with a mirror in it and throw a spectrum onto a white wall. Seeing the colours themselves settles the meaning of dispersion for good.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of the components must be used correctly: cell or battery, switch, resistor, diode, LED, capacitor and inductor. 'Bulb' written for LED earns no mark. (3) In a circuit diagram, the recognised symbols must be used and the circuit must be complete; a broken circuit loses the completeness mark. (4) 'Thermal' is accepted for a station that burns fuel and 'nuclear' for one that splits atoms; the two must not be interchanged. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **battery (two dry cells in series)** (1 mark).
- X - **switch** (1 mark).
- Y - **resistor** (1 mark).
- Z - **LED (light-emitting diode)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Bulb' or 'lamp' written for Z earns no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- W - **supplies the electrical energy (drives the current)** (1 mark).
- X - **completes or breaks the circuit, switching the current on and off** (1 mark).
- Y - **limits the current and so protects the LED** (1 mark).
- Z - **gives out light when current passes through it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It carries current' is true of every part and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **No, the LED is not lit** (1 mark).
- **The switch is open, so the circuit is incomplete and no current flows** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the reason if the candidate says the LED is lit.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Each dry cell supplies 1.5 V** (1 mark).
- **Two cells joined in series add up: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word 'series' or a correct description of it is needed for the second mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **furnace or boiler** (1 mark).
- B - **turbine** (1 mark).
- C - **generator** (1 mark).
- D - **transmission pylon (power lines)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Chimney' written for A earns no mark; the chimney only carries away the waste gases.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **A: chemical energy of the fuel to heat energy** (1 mark).
- **B: heat energy of the steam to kinetic energy of the turbine** (1 mark).
- **C: kinetic energy to electrical energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The three changes must be in the right order.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the heat comes from splitting uranium nuclei in a reactor, not from burning fuel**; **no smoke or carbon dioxide is given off**; **a very small mass of fuel gives a great deal of energy**; **it produces radioactive waste**; **it is far more costly to build** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A point that is true of BOTH stations, such as 'it uses a turbine', earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **carbon dioxide adds to global warming**; **smoke and soot cause breathing diseases**; **sulphur dioxide causes acid rain**; **hot water kills fish in the river**; **oil spills pollute land and water**; **noise pollution**; **a non-renewable fuel is used up** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that both say 'air pollution' count as one.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **fit filters or scrubbers to the chimneys**; **use cleaner fuel such as natural gas**; **use more solar, wind and hydro power**; **cool the water before returning it**; **site stations away from homes and plant trees**; **save electricity so that less is generated** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Stop making electricity' is not a practical measure and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Agree that it gives off no smoke and no carbon dioxide** (1 mark).
- **But it produces radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a very long time** (1 mark).
- **And an accident or leak would release harmful radiation (accept: warm water still harms aquatic life)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A reply that merely says 'he is wrong' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Correct symbol for the two cells in series** (1 mark).
- **Correct symbols for the switch and the resistor** (1 mark).
- **Correct symbol for the LED (triangle and bar)** (1 mark).
- **A complete single loop with all four components in series and labelled** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A circuit with a gap anywhere, other than at the switch, loses the completeness mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The longer leg (positive leg or anode) is joined towards the positive terminal of the battery** (1 mark).
- **Connected this way the LED is forward biased and lights** (1 mark).
- **Turned round it is reverse biased, no current flows and it does not light** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It will burn out' is wrong for a reversed LED at this voltage and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The circuit is complete, current flows and the LED lights** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The path is broken, the current stops and the LED goes out** (1 mark).
- **The resistor limits the current and protects the LED** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The electricity rests' earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Resistor - **limits or controls the current** (1 mark).
- Capacitor - **stores charge and releases it later** (1 mark).
- Diode - **allows current in one direction only** (1 mark).
- Inductor - **opposes a change in the current (stores energy in a magnetic field)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A function written against the wrong component earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A component made by joining a P region and an N region of semiconductor, which passes current one way only** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The P region and the N region** (1 mark); **the P region is joined to the positive terminal** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'positive region' for P and 'negative region' for N.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **unplug the gadget and remove the cells first**; **never open a gadget connected to the mains; leave mains parts to the teacher**; **work under supervision with the proper tools**; **keep the parts safely and sketch the arrangement before removing anything**; **handle sharp edges with care and wash hands afterwards** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Be careful' alone is too vague for a mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The LED becomes dimmer** (1 mark).
- **The total resistance of the circuit increases** (1 mark).
- **So the current falls, and the brightness depends on the current** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No reason marks if the candidate says the LED becomes brighter.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The LED did not light** (1 mark).
- **The diode was reverse biased and a diode conducts in one direction only** (1 mark).
- **So no current flowed round the circuit** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The diode was spoilt' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The components depend on one another; a change in one affects the working of the others** (1 mark).
- **Example: the resistor fixes the current, and the current decides the brightness of the LED (or protects it from damage)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A definition with no example earns 1 mark only.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 2: Electricity and Electronics | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.4.2.1** - Demonstrate understanding of forms of electricity, its generation and effects on the environment. **B7/JHS1.4.2.2** - Demonstrate knowledge of how to assemble and explain the functions of basic electronic components and their interdependence in an electronic circuit.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics, Basic 7, pages 67 to 69 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.2.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.1.1, describe the various forms of electricity generation, with the exemplar: search for and discuss information about the nature and generation of thermal and nuclear electricity and produce reports, posters, diagrams and charts about the findings. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.1.2, explain the impact of electricity generation on the environment, with the exemplar: debate the negative effects of both thermal and nuclear electricity generation on the environment and how to reduce the effects, and create posters and leaflets of the outcome of the debate. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.2.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.1, demonstrate how to assemble basic electronic components in an electronic circuit, with the exemplar: examine electronic components such as types of LEDs, P-N junction diodes, colour code resistors and capacitors, and arrange them in an electronic circuit. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.2, discuss the function of each electronic component and their interdependence with each other, with the exemplars: dismantle and assemble spoilt electronic gadgets such as a radio, a television, mobile phones and electronic watches and name the parts; identify the positive (P) region and the negative (N) region of the P-N junction diode and construct a simple electronic circuit comprising a 3 V battery made of two dry cells in series with a switch and an LED; and explain what happens when the switch in an electronic circuit is closed and when it is opened. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.2.2.3, discuss the function of each electronic component such as resistor, diode and inductor and their interdependence for the functioning of an electronic gadget, with the exemplars: discuss the roles and significance of the LED, the resistor, the diode and the inductor in a circuit and how they affect each other; and explain changes in the brightness of an LED in relation to the addition of resistors, diodes and inductors in an electronic circuit.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.4.2.1.1) carries topic 12.1 and Question 2; I2 (B7/JHS1.4.2.1.2) carries topic 12.2 and Question 3; I3 (B7/JHS1.4.2.2.1) carries topic 12.5 and Question 4; I4 (B7/JHS1.4.2.2.2) carries topics 12.3 and 12.4 and Questions 1 and 5; I5 (B7/JHS1.4.2.2.3) carries topic 12.6 and Question 6. The 'dismantle a spoilt gadget' exemplar is examined in Question 5(c) as a written account, which is the part of that activity a written paper can fairly test, and the debate exemplar in Question 3(c). Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.4.2.1 and B7.4.2.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Thermal and nuclear stations differ only in HOW the heat is obtained. Teach the common chain once - heat, steam, turbine, generator - and then show that one burns fuel while the other splits uranium nuclei. Question 2(c) rewards exactly that distinction, and points true of both stations earn nothing.
- The chimney is not the boiler. Candidates who label A in Fig. 2 'chimney' have seen a picture but have not followed the process.
- A real LED, two dry cells in a holder and a 220-ohm resistor cost very little and turn this whole sub-strand into a practical lesson. Once pupils have reversed an LED themselves and seen it refuse to light, Questions 4(b) and 6(b) answer themselves.
- Insist on correct circuit symbols and on a CLOSED loop. The commonest loss of marks in Question 4(a) is a diagram that leaves a gap or that shows the components side by side instead of one after another.
- Brightness follows current. Candidates should reason in three steps - more resistance, less current, dimmer LED - rather than asserting the answer.
- On safety: no class should open any gadget that can be plugged into the mains, and large capacitors can hold a charge long after a set is switched off. Make the safety rules of Question 5(c) part of the lesson, not an afterthought.
- Follow-up work: let groups prepare the posters and leaflets named in the curriculum, one group arguing for thermal and another for nuclear generation, and display them for the whole school during Science Week.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The names of the forms of energy must be correct and complete: chemical, electrical, heat (thermal), light, sound, kinetic, potential and nuclear. 'Power' or 'force' written for a form of energy earns no mark. (3) In an energy chain the forms must appear in the right order; one mark is lost for each form placed out of order. (4) In a calculation, award the working mark and the answer mark separately; the unit J must appear for the final mark. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **chemical energy** (1 mark).
- Q - **electrical energy** (1 mark).
- R - **light energy** (1 mark).
- S - **heat (thermal) energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Battery energy' or 'current' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Energy supplied = 60 J** (1 mark).
- **Energy given out = 15 J + 45 J = 60 J** (1 mark).
- **The two totals are equal, so the energy has only been changed in form and none has been destroyed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The sum must be shown; a bare statement of the law earns the third mark only.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **R, the light energy** (1 mark); **because the torch is used in order to give light** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The torch feels warm (the cells or the bulb heat up)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Reason mark only if R is chosen.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **In a closed system no energy enters or leaves without being counted** (1 mark).
- **So all the energy given out can be added up and shown to equal the energy supplied** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is covered' or 'it is in a box' alone earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **solar (light) energy to electrical energy** (1 mark).
- B - **electrical energy to heat energy** (1 mark).
- C - **electrical energy to kinetic energy** (1 mark).
- D - **chemical energy to electrical energy to sound energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'electrical to sound' for D.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Useful: kinetic energy of the blades** (1 mark).
- **Wasted: sound energy and heat energy** (1 mark).
- **The wasted energy spreads into the air and surroundings and cannot be used again** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is destroyed' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **sunlight is free and renewable, so no fuel is bought**; **no smoke or carbon dioxide is given off**; **it makes no noise**; **it needs little maintenance** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is modern' is not a scientific reason.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Energy can neither be created nor destroyed** (1 mark).
- **It can only be changed from one form to another (the total remains the same)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both halves are needed for the full 2 marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Potential energy of the stored water shown first** (1 mark).
- **Kinetic energy of the falling water and of the turbine shown next** (1 mark).
- **Electrical energy shown last, with the boxes joined by arrows in the correct order** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A written chain with arrows is accepted in place of boxes.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **1,000 J - 850 J** (1 mark) **= 150 J** (1 mark, unit required).
- (ii) **Heat energy (accept sound energy)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A correct answer with no unit scores 1 of the 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The 150 J is not destroyed; it is changed into heat and sound** (1 mark).
- **Counting every form, the total is still 1,000 J** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The generator is weak' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Microphone - **sound to electrical** (1 mark).
- Phone being charged - **electrical to chemical** (1 mark).
- Candle burning - **chemical to heat and light** (1 mark).
- Green plant - **light (solar) to chemical** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A change written the wrong way round earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plants change light energy into chemical energy stored in food (photosynthesis)** (1 mark).
- **People and animals eat the food and obtain this energy** (1 mark).
- **The energy is released in respiration for growth, movement and warmth (accept: wood and charcoal fuels come from plants)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Plants give us oxygen' is true but does not answer the question on energy.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Materials named: a small motor, dry cells, wires, switch and a paper blade or disc** (1 mark).
- **Method: join them in a complete circuit and close the switch** (1 mark).
- **Observation: the blade spins, showing electrical energy changed into kinetic energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any other workable activity, such as a battery-driven toy car, earns full marks.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Using energy carefully and avoiding waste** (1 mark).
- **So that the supply lasts longer and is available in the future** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not confuse this with the LAW of conservation of energy; a statement of the law earns no mark here.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **switch off lights, fans and the television in empty rooms**; **use LED lamps in place of filament bulbs**; **dry clothes in the sun**; **iron all the clothes at one time**; **cover cooking pots and open the fridge less often**; **unplug chargers that are not in use** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that are really the same point count once.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) **A smaller electricity bill; appliances and cells last longer** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Less electricity has to be generated, so less fuel is burnt and there are fewer power cuts** (1 mark); **the money saved can be used for other national needs** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Less smoke and carbon dioxide, so cleaner air, less global warming and fewer habitats destroyed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the marks under the correct headings.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Renewable: replaced naturally and does not run out** (1 mark); **non-renewable: exists in a fixed amount and is used up for ever** (1 mark).
- (ii) **One correct example of each, for example sunlight and crude oil** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both examples are needed for the single mark in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Agree that energy is never destroyed** (1 mark).
- **But it is changed into heat and sound that spread out and can no longer be used** (1 mark).
- **The fuels used to supply useable energy are limited and burning them harms the environment, so saving is still necessary** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A reply that only says 'he is wrong' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Two slogans, each naming a clear energy-saving action or giving a sound reason** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A slogan with no action and no reason, such as 'Save energy', earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.4.3.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the principle of conservation and conversion of energy and their application in real life situations.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy, Basic 7, pages 70 and 71 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.3.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.1, explain the principle underlying conservation and conversion of energy, with the exemplars: explain the law of conservation of energy by using a diagram to show that in a closed system the value of chemical energy, for example in a dry cell, which changes into electrical, heat and light energy will remain the same; and use that exemplar to explain energy conversion and its application to life. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.2, demonstrate the conversion of energy into useable forms, with the exemplar: illustrate the everyday use of conversion of energy and show diagrammatically the conversion of energy to other forms. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.3.1.3, know how energy could be conserved for future use in life, with the exemplar: describe how energy is conserved and explain how it can be done for the benefit of humans and other life forms.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.4.3.1.1) carries topics 13.1 and 13.4 and Questions 1 and 3; I2 (B7/JHS1.4.3.1.2) carries topics 13.2 and 13.3 and Questions 2 and 4; I3 (B7/JHS1.4.3.1.3) carries topic 13.5 and Questions 5 and 6. The dry-cell exemplar named in the curriculum is examined directly in Question 1, which uses the torch of Fig. 1 as the closed system. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.4.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The commonest error in this sub-strand is to say that energy is 'lost' or 'used up'. Insist on the wording of the law: energy is changed in form, never destroyed. Question 3(d) and Question 6(b) both turn on that distinction.
- Keep the two meanings of 'conservation' apart. The LAW of conservation of energy is a statement about nature; energy conservation in the home is a habit of avoiding waste. Question 3(a) asks for the first and Question 5(a) for the second, and candidates who confuse them lose marks in both.
- Teach the energy chain with arrows from the first lesson. Pupils who write 'chemical to electrical to light and heat' confidently will handle Fig. 1, the table in Question 4(a) and the diagram in Question 3(b) without difficulty.
- A torch, a solar garden lamp and a small motor from a spoilt toy are enough apparatus for the whole sub-strand. Let pupils feel the warm torch after five minutes; that single observation explains the 45 J in Fig. 1 better than any amount of talk.
- In calculations, insist on the unit. Question 1(b) and Question 3(c) each carry a mark that is lost by an answer written as '150' instead of '150 J'.
- Follow-up work: let the class carry out an energy audit of the school for one week - lights left on, fans in empty rooms, filament bulbs still in use - and present the findings with the posters and leaflets named in the curriculum.
