### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | (i) A force is a push or a pull acting on a body, which can change the body's state of rest or of motion, or its shape. (ii) Force is measured in newtons (N). | Forces, Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Inertia | Remember |
| 1 (b) | (i) Resultant force = 500 N - 420 N = 80 N. (ii) The rope moves towards the Blue House team, that is, in the direction of the larger force. | Forces, Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Inertia | Apply |
| 1 (c) | Balanced forces are equal in size and act in opposite directions on a body, so that their resultant is zero; unbalanced forces do not cancel out and leave a resultant force acting in one direction. A body at rest under balanced forces stays at rest, while unbalanced forces set it moving in the direction of the resultant force. | Forces, Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Inertia | Understand |
| 1 (d) | Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. The inertia of a body is measured by its mass: the greater the mass, the greater the inertia. | Forces, Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Inertia | Understand |
| 2 (a) | A body continues in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a straight line, unless an unbalanced (external) force acts on it. | Newton's First Law of Motion | Remember |
| 2 (b) | (i) The ball was at rest and would have stayed at rest; it started to move because the push of the pupil was an unbalanced force acting on it. (ii) Once moving, the ball would have continued in a straight line; it stopped because the block exerted an unbalanced force on it in the opposite direction (helped by friction between the ball and the table). | Newton's First Law of Motion | Analyse |
| 2 (c) | The statement is not correct. By Newton's first law a body already moving will keep moving in a straight line at the same speed if no unbalanced force acts on it. On the Earth a force is needed only because friction and air resistance act against the motion; remove those opposing forces, as in space, and no driving force is needed at all. | Newton's First Law of Motion | Evaluate |
| 3 (a) | The passengers and the vehicle were moving forward together at the same speed. When the brakes were applied, an unbalanced force acted on the vehicle and brought it to rest. No such force acted at once on the passengers, so their bodies tended to continue moving forward because of their inertia, and they were thrown forward in their seats. | Applications of Newton's First Law in Everyday Life | Analyse |
| 3 (b) | The seat belt supplies the backward force that the passenger's body needs in order to stop with the vehicle, holding the passenger in the seat so that the body does not continue forward into the seat in front or through the windscreen; it also spreads the force over the strong parts of the body and slows the stop, so reducing injury. | Applications of Newton's First Law in Everyday Life | Understand |
| 3 (c) | Passengers are thrown backwards when a vehicle starts off suddenly; the blade of a hoe or cutlass is tightened by knocking the end of the handle on the ground; dust is beaten out of a mat; a tablecloth can be pulled quickly from under a glass without upsetting it; a book on a car seat slides forward when the car brakes; and water drops fly off an umbrella when it is shaken. | Applications of Newton's First Law in Everyday Life | Apply |
| 3 (d) | It explains why safety measures such as seat belts, head rests and careful loading of vehicles are necessary, so it helps to prevent injury; it guides drivers to keep a safe distance and to avoid sudden braking; and it is used in designing vehicles, machines and tools, and in simple tasks such as tightening a tool on its handle. | Applications of Newton's First Law in Everyday Life | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | (i) P and Q are both north poles. The far ends of both magnets are marked S, so the facing ends must be north poles; and the magnets moved apart, which shows that they repelled each other, and only like poles repel. (ii) X is the north pole, because the freely hanging magnet comes to rest with its north pole pointing towards the north. | Magnets: Their Behaviour and Uses | Analyse |
| 4 (b) | Like poles of magnets repel each other; unlike poles attract each other, and a magnet attracts iron and other magnetic materials; and a magnet suspended so that it can swing freely always comes to rest pointing in the north-south direction. | Magnets: Their Behaviour and Uses | Understand |
| 4 (c) | Bring one end of each bar in turn near one end of a known suspended magnet. Attraction is not a sure test, because a magnet attracts an unmagnetised steel bar as well. The bar that REPELS the pole of the known magnet is itself the magnet, because only a magnet can repel another magnet. | Magnets: Their Behaviour and Uses | Evaluate |
| 4 (d) | Magnets are used in the compass, for finding direction; in loudspeakers, earphones, radios and mobile phones; in electric motors and generators; on refrigerator and cupboard doors to keep them closed; in cranes at scrap yards for lifting iron and steel; for separating iron from other waste; and in the magnetic strips of bank cards and in door catches. | Magnets: Their Behaviour and Uses | Apply |
| 5 (a) | (i) A simple machine is a device that makes work easier to do, for example by allowing a small effort to move a large load or by changing the direction of a force. (ii) Other simple machines include the inclined plane, the pulley, the wheel and axle, the screw and the wedge. | Simple Machines and the Classes of Levers | Remember |
| 5 (b) | A is a first-class lever, because the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load. B is a second-class lever, because the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort. C is a third-class lever, because the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. | Simple Machines and the Classes of Levers | Understand |
| 5 (c) | In the wheelbarrow the fulcrum is at the axle of the wheel, at the front; the load is in the tray, between the wheel and the handles; and the effort is applied by the hands lifting at the ends of the handles. | Simple Machines and the Classes of Levers | Analyse |
| 5 (d) | In a third-class lever the effort is nearer the fulcrum than the load, so the effort must be larger than the load. The gain is in speed, distance and control: a small movement of the hand moves the load through a much greater distance and more quickly, and the grip is delicate and easy to control, which is what is wanted when picking up a lump of sugar. Other third-class levers are a pair of kitchen tongs, a broom swept with one hand fixed at the top, a fishing rod, a spade in use and the human forearm. | Simple Machines and the Classes of Levers | Evaluate |
| 6 (a) | The work input is the work done by the effort on the machine, that is, the energy supplied to it. The work output is the useful work done by the machine on the load. | Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency | Remember |
| 6 (b) | Efficiency = (work output / work input) x 100% = (1,800 / 2,400) x 100% = 0.75 x 100% = 75%. | Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency | Apply |
| 6 (c) | (i) 2,400 J - 1,800 J = 600 J was used in overcoming friction in the pulley wheel and the rope, and in raising the moving parts of the machine itself; it appears as heat and a little sound, so it is not destroyed, only wasted. (ii) Oil the axle of the pulley to reduce friction (accept: use lighter, smoother parts, or keep the rope in good condition). | Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency | Understand |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The terms force, inertia, friction, effort, load and fulcrum must be used correctly; 'power' written for force earns no mark. (3) In statements of Newton's first law, both the state of rest and the state of uniform motion in a straight line must appear for full marks. (4) In a calculation, award the working mark and the answer mark separately; efficiency must carry the percentage sign and work must carry the unit J. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **A push or a pull acting on a body** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The newton (N)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Energy used' earns no mark for (i).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **500 N - 420 N** (1 mark) **= 80 N** (1 mark, unit required).
- (ii) **Towards the Blue House team (the direction of the larger force)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An answer of 920 N shows that the directions have been ignored; no marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Balanced: equal forces in opposite directions, resultant zero** (1 mark).
- **Unbalanced: the forces do not cancel; a resultant force remains** (1 mark).
- **A body at rest stays at rest under balanced forces but starts to move under unbalanced forces** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Credit a clear labelled sketch that makes the same points.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or of motion** (1 mark).
- **It is measured by the mass of the body** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Weight' is not accepted for the second mark.*

### Question 2 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **A body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line** (1 mark).
- **unless an unbalanced (external) force acts on it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only one mark if the state of uniform motion is left out.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The ball was at rest and the push was an unbalanced force that set it moving** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The moving ball would have continued in a straight line** (1 mark); **the block (and friction) exerted an unbalanced force that stopped it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It became tired' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The statement is not correct** (1 mark).
- **A body keeps moving at constant velocity when no unbalanced force acts on it** (1 mark).
- **A force is needed on Earth only to overcome friction and air resistance** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No explanation marks if the candidate agrees with the statement.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **The passengers were moving forward with the vehicle** (1 mark).
- **The braking force stopped the vehicle** (1 mark).
- **The passengers' bodies continued moving forward because of inertia** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word inertia, or a correct description of it, is needed for the third mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **It provides the backward force that stops the passenger with the vehicle** (1 mark).
- **So the passenger is held in the seat and is not thrown forward and injured** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It makes the person comfortable' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **passengers thrown backwards when a vehicle starts off**; **tightening a hoe or cutlass blade by knocking the handle**; **beating dust out of a mat**; **pulling a cloth from under a glass**; **shaking water off an umbrella** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Three versions of the same braking example count once.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **it explains the need for seat belts and other safety measures, so preventing injury**; **it guides safe driving, such as keeping a safe distance**; **it is used in designing vehicles, machines and tools** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is in the syllabus' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **P is a north pole** (1 mark); **Q is a north pole** (1 mark); **because the magnets repelled each other and like poles repel (accept: the other ends are marked S)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **North pole** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'north-seeking pole'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Like poles repel each other** (1 mark).
- **Unlike poles attract each other (a magnet attracts iron)** (1 mark).
- **A freely suspended magnet comes to rest in the north-south direction** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is strong' is not a characteristic.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Bring each bar near a known suspended magnet (or hang each bar freely)** (1 mark).
- **The bar that repels is the magnet, since repulsion is the sure test (accept: the bar that comes to rest north-south is the magnet)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An answer based on attraction alone earns no second mark.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **in a compass for finding direction**; **in loudspeakers, earphones and phones**; **in electric motors and generators**; **in fridge and cupboard door catches**; **in cranes for lifting scrap iron**; **for separating iron from other waste** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers naming devices that work in the same way, such as a radio and an earphone, count once.*

### Question 5 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A device that makes work easier to do** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **inclined plane, pulley, wheel and axle, screw, wedge** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A lever named in (ii) earns no mark, as it is excluded by the question.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A - **first-class lever** (1 mark).
- B - **second-class lever** (1 mark).
- C - **third-class lever** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'first order', 'second order' and 'third order'.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Fulcrum: at the wheel (the axle at the front)** (1 mark).
- **Load: in the tray, between the wheel and the handles** (1 mark).
- **Effort: at the handles, where the hands lift** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the positions, not merely for the words.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **The load moves a greater distance (and faster) than the effort** (1 mark).
- **The tool gives a delicate, well-controlled grip or movement** (1 mark).
- **One other example: a broom, a fishing rod, a spade or the human forearm** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A wheelbarrow or a see-saw named as the example earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Work input: the work done by the effort on the machine (the energy supplied to it)** (1 mark).
- **Work output: the useful work done by the machine on the load** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word 'useful' is expected in the second answer.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Efficiency = (work output / work input) x 100%** (1 mark).
- **= (1,800 / 2,400) x 100%** (1 mark).
- **= 75%** (1 mark, percentage sign required).
  - *Marking note: A correct answer with no working earns 2 of the 3 marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **600 J was used in overcoming friction and in lifting the moving parts of the machine** (1 mark); **it appears as heat (and sound), so it is wasted but not destroyed** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Oil the moving parts to reduce friction (accept: use lighter or smoother parts)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The machine is old' earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 4: Force and Motion | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.4.4.1** - Examine the concept of motion, Newton's first law of motion, magnetic force in relation to motion and understand their applications to life. **B7/JHS1.4.4.2** - Recognise some simple machines, and show understanding of their efficiency in doing work.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion, Basic 7, pages 72 to 77 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.4.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.1, understand that unbalanced forces acting on an object cause it to move, with the exemplars: explain inertia as a tendency of a body to resist motion; and demonstrate how unbalanced forces cause motion. It carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.2, state and explain Newton's First Law of motion, with the exemplar: research to find what Newton's first law is and discuss it. It carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.3, examine the application of Newton's First Law of motion in life, with the exemplars: discuss some applications of Newton's First Law of Motion, for example when a metallic ball is put on a smooth surface and given a push it will be in motion until it gets to a blockade and it stops, and the use of seat belts in a vehicle; and explain the importance of Newton's First Law of Motion. It carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.1.4, demonstrate the behaviour of magnet and its use to life, with the exemplars: discuss what magnets are and describe the types of magnets that exist; demonstrate the characteristics (repulsive, attractive, and orientation in the north-south direction) of a magnet; and discuss the uses of magnet in everyday life. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.4.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.2.1, identify simple machines, with the exemplar: list examples of simple machines. It carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.2.2, describe the types and functions of levers, with the exemplars: name the types of levers and explain their general functions; and classify levers into first, second and third classes and demonstrate how the principles involved in each class make work easier in everyday life. It carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.4.2.3, know work input, and output and efficiency as they apply to machines, with the exemplars: explain the terms work input, work output and efficiency; explain efficiency of a machine as the ratio of work output to work input expressed as a percentage; explain the concept of efficiency of a machine; and describe how efficiency of simple machines can be improved, for example by oiling its parts to reduce friction.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.4.4.1.1) carries topic 14.1 and Question 1; I2 (B7/JHS1.4.4.1.2) carries topic 14.2 and Question 2; I3 (B7/JHS1.4.4.1.3) carries topic 14.3 and Question 3; I4 (B7/JHS1.4.4.1.4) carries topic 14.4 and Question 4; I5 (B7/JHS1.4.4.2.1) and I6 (B7/JHS1.4.4.2.2) carry topic 14.5 and Question 5, the lists of simple machines in Question 5(a) being the part set on I5; I7 (B7/JHS1.4.4.2.3) carries topic 14.6 and Question 6. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.4.4.1 and B7.4.4.2.

The 'S' markings on the far ends of the magnets, the direction of north and the words 'load', 'push', 'lift' and 'press' are given information needed for the reasoning, not the answers asked for |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Inertia is the heart of this sub-strand. Pupils who can say 'the body tends to continue doing what it was already doing' will answer Questions 2 and 3 easily; those who have learnt the law only as a sentence to recite will not.
- Insist on BOTH halves of Newton's first law. Half the candidates stop at 'a body at rest remains at rest' and lose a mark in Question 2(a).
- Repulsion, not attraction, is the sure test for a magnet. This is the single most frequently missed point in the magnetism indicator, and Question 4(c) is set on it. A pair of bar magnets and a length of thread are all the apparatus the lesson needs.
- When classifying levers, teach pupils to find the fulcrum first, then ask which of the load and the effort lies between the fulcrum and the other. That single rule settles all three classes without memorising lists of tools.
- Third-class levers often puzzle pupils because the effort is larger than the load. Point out the gain in speed, distance and control, as Question 5(d) requires; the human forearm is the example every pupil carries about.
- In efficiency calculations, insist on the formula line, the substitution line and the percentage sign. Remind pupils that an efficiency above 100% is impossible and is a sign that the fraction has been inverted.
- Follow-up work: let groups measure the effort needed to raise a load with a single pulley and with an inclined plane, calculate the efficiency of each, then oil the pulley and repeat the measurement.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Tools must be named correctly; local names are accepted only where the standard English name is also clear from the answer. (3) A rule of handling must say what the user should DO; a bare instruction such as 'be careful' earns no mark. (4) A maintenance practice must be matched to the correct tool; a right practice written against the wrong tool earns no mark. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **cutlass (machete)** (1 mark).
- B - **hoe** (1 mark).
- C - **rake** (1 mark).
- D - **watering can** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'matchet' for A.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- A - **clearing weeds and bushes (accept harvesting)** (1 mark).
- B - **weeding, making ridges or mounds** (1 mark).
- C - **gathering leaves and trash, levelling a seedbed** (1 mark).
- D - **watering seedlings and nursery beds** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Farming' is too general and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **feeding or drinking trough**; **broom, brush or scraper for cleaning pens**; **shovel or spade**; **bucket**; **wheelbarrow**; **rope or halter** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A tool already shown in Fig. 1 earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **They are operated by hand and need no engine or fuel** (1 mark).
- **They are cheap, easy to use and easy to repair and maintain** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'They are small' alone earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - **the blade is rusty (not cleaned and oiled)** (1 mark).
- Q - **the handle is split or cracked** (1 mark).
- R - **the blade is left lying in water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The cutlass is old' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P - **wash off the soil, dry the blade and oil it after use** (1 mark).
- Q - **keep the handle dry and oiled; refit or replace it when it splits** (1 mark).
- R - **store the tool in a dry store, hung on a rack, not on wet ground** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The practice must match the fault it is written against.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the tools are hung on racks or nails off the floor**; **the tools are clean and free of rust**; **oil is kept ready for oiling the tools**; **the store is dry and under cover** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'The store is nice' earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the tool is spoilt early and money must be spent replacing it**; **work on the farm becomes slow and tiring with a blunt, rusty tool**; **it is dangerous and can cause injury** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that both say 'it will spoil' count once.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **The way a tool is held, carried and used during work** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The care given to a tool to keep it in good working condition** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Examples alone, with no explanation, earn no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **check the tool and the handle before use**; **carry a cutlass with the blade down and away from the body**; **give a cutlass to another person handle first**; **work a safe distance apart**; **use a tool only for its proper work**; **wear boots and hand gloves**; **keep idle tools together with the edges down or covered** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Be careful with the cutlass' is too vague for a mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the edge is chipped, bent or blunted**; **the blade may break**; **the blade may fly off the handle and injure someone** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The rule broken is that a tool must be used only for its proper work.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **they prevent injury to the user and to others**; **they protect the tools from damage**; **work is in fact finished faster and better with safe, sound tools** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Because the teacher said so' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Cutlass - **sharpen with a file or whetstone; clean and oil the blade** (1 mark).
- Hoe - **clean, dry and oil the blade; keep the wooden handle dry and oiled** (1 mark).
- Knapsack sprayer - **wash out the tank and nozzle after use and oil the moving parts** (1 mark).
- Wheelbarrow - **oil the wheel and axle and tighten the bolts** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A practice written against the wrong tool earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Scrape and wash off the soil, then dry the blade** (1 mark).
- **Rub the blade with oil and check or wipe the handle** (1 mark).
- **Hang it in a dry store, off the floor** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The three steps must be in a sensible order.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Rust eats away the metal, so the tool becomes blunt, weak and finally breaks** (1 mark).
- **Condition 1: moisture, from water, rain, dew or damp soil** (1 mark).
- **Condition 2: air (oxygen) in contact with the bare metal, especially under soil left on it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Dirty tools' alone is not a condition; the moisture must be named.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the tools used and the work each does**; **how the farmer holds, carries and uses them, and the protective clothing worn**; **what is done to the tools after work (cleaning, sharpening, oiling, repair)**; **where and how the tools are stored**; **the condition of the tools** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Everything about the farm' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **greet the farmer and ask permission**; **stay together and follow instructions**; **do not touch tools or animals without being told**; **ask questions politely and do not criticise the farmer**; **do not trample the crops or frighten the birds**; **thank the farmer before leaving** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Accept any clear rule of courtesy or safety.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) Any TWO of: **oil the wheelbarrow wheel and tighten the bolts**; **refit or replace the loose hoe handles**; **wash out the sprayer after every use** (1 mark each).
- (ii) **A correct reason beside each of the two recommendations given** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The reason must match the recommendation it is written against.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Four clear rules, each stating an action** (1 mark each), for example: **sign for and return each tool to its rack**; **clean and dry tools before returning them**; **oil the metal parts**; **report damaged tools at once**; **use each tool only for its proper work**; **keep the store dry and locked**.
  - *Marking note: A rule with no action, such as 'tools are important', earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Two tools named with a correct use for each** (1 mark each), for example **hoe - to dig and loosen the soil**; **rake - to level the bed**.
  - *Marking note: A tool named without its use earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Well-kept tools last longer, so money is not spent replacing them each season** (1 mark).
- **Work is done faster and with fewer accidents, so less is spent on hired labour and on treatment** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A general statement about saving money, with no link to the tools, earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 5: Agricultural Tools | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.4.5.1** - Demonstrate knowledge and skills in handling and maintenance of basic and simple agricultural tools.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools, Basic 7, pages 78 to 80 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.4.5.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.5.1.1, explain the basic rules in handling and maintaining simple agricultural tools, with the exemplars: list some simple or basic farm tools in agriculture, giving examples found in animal and crop farms; discuss the meaning and importance of handling and maintenance of agricultural tools; list and match the basic rules in handling and maintenance of tools with specific simple tools used in agriculture; and describe how handling and maintenance of simple and basic agricultural tools are done. It also carries indicator B7/JHS1.4.5.1.2, apply the handling and maintenance of basic and simple agricultural tools in their community, with the exemplars: observe and discuss the handling and maintenance of basic and simple agricultural tools used in farms visited in the community and write a report; assemble agricultural tools from the community and practise handling the tools to perform simple agricultural operations, and write down the operational rules of handling agricultural tools; and assemble agricultural tools from the community and practise the basic rules in tools maintenance and list the rules used.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.4.5.1.1) carries topics 15.1 to 15.4 and Questions 1, 2, 3 and 4; I2 (B7/JHS1.4.5.1.2) carries topic 15.5 and Questions 5 and 6. The farm-visit and report exemplar is examined in Question 5, and the 'write down the operational rules' exemplar in Question 6, both of which are the parts of those practical activities that a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B7.4.5.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand is best taught with the tools in the pupils' hands. A lesson in the tool store - naming the tools, checking the handles, filing an edge and oiling a blade - will teach more than any number of notes, and it is exactly what the exemplars ask for.
- Candidates lose marks by writing vague rules. 'Be careful' and 'handle with care' earn nothing; 'carry the cutlass with the blade pointing downwards and away from the body' earns the mark. Train pupils to write an action.
- Insist that a maintenance practice be matched to the right tool. Question 4(a) is marked tool by tool, and 'sharpen it' written against the wheelbarrow earns no mark.
- Rust is the thread running through the whole sub-strand: soil plus moisture plus bare metal. Once pupils can explain that, Questions 2(a), 2(b) and 4(c) follow naturally.
- A community farm visit is the heart of indicator B7/JHS1.4.5.1.2. Prepare the pupils with a simple observation sheet before they go - tools used, how handled, how maintained, where stored - and the report in Question 5 will be within every candidate's reach.
- Safety first: pupils must never be allowed to sharpen or swing a cutlass without close supervision, and boots and gloves should be worn for every practical lesson on the school farm.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | A is organic waste, that is, food or kitchen waste; B is plastic waste; C is a mixture of glass and metal waste; D is paper waste. | Types and Sources of Waste | Understand |
| 1 (b) | A is biodegradable; B is non-biodegradable; C is non-biodegradable; D is biodegradable. | Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Waste | Analyse |
| 1 (c) | Biodegradable waste can be broken down (decomposed) into simple harmless substances by micro-organisms such as bacteria and fungi within a short time. Non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down by these organisms, so it remains in the environment for a very long time. | Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Waste | Understand |
| 1 (d) | The broken glass and tins should be wrapped or placed carefully in a separate container for hard waste and sent for recycling, or buried in a properly prepared pit. They must not be burnt or thrown into gutters, because glass and metal do not rot, the broken glass can cut people and the tins collect water in which mosquitoes breed. | Good Waste Management Practices | Apply |
| 2 (a) | Houseflies breeding on the heap settle on food and spread typhoid fever, cholera, dysentery and diarrhoea; mosquitoes breeding in the water in the tins spread malaria; rats and cockroaches attracted to the heap spread other diseases; the bad smell and the dust and smoke irritate the nose and chest; and the broken glass and sharp metal can injure pupils. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Analyse |
| 2 (b) | The organic waste in the heap is being broken down by bacteria and fungi in the absence of enough air, and this decay releases gases such as ammonia and hydrogen sulphide, which smell bad. The still water in the tins is dangerous because female mosquitoes lay their eggs in it, and the larvae develop there into adult mosquitoes, which spread malaria. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Understand |
| 2 (c) | Open burning of refuse releases thick smoke and poisonous gases from the plastics and rubber, which pollute the air and harm the lungs of everybody nearby, including the pupils in the classrooms. The fire can also spread out of control and burn buildings or crops, and it destroys material such as peels and paper which could have been composted or recycled, as well as leaving ash and half-burnt waste behind. | Good Waste Management Practices | Evaluate |
| 3 (a) | Reduce means to produce less waste in the first place, for example by buying only what is needed and avoiding unnecessary packaging. Reuse means to use an article again, in the same form, for the same or another purpose, instead of throwing it away. Recycle means to collect used material and process it in a factory into new articles. | Good Waste Management Practices | Understand |
| 3 (b) | Reduce: use both sides of exercise-book paper, carry a refillable water bottle instead of buying sachet water daily. Reuse: use empty tins as containers for seedlings in the school garden, use old newspapers to wrap books. Recycle: collect plastic bottles and sachets and send them to a recycling centre, or send paper for pulping. | Good Waste Management Practices | Apply |
| 3 (c) | Waste segregation means separating waste into different containers according to its kind - organic waste, plastics, paper, glass and metal - at the point where it is produced. It is important because each kind can then be dealt with in the proper way: the organic waste can be composted and the plastics, paper and metal can be reused or recycled, so that far less waste has to be dumped. | Good Waste Management Practices | Understand |
| 3 (d) | For example: a bin labelled ORGANIC WASTE, for fruit peels and food remains; a bin labelled PLASTICS, for water sachets and bottles; and a bin labelled PAPER, for used exercise-book sheets and cartons. | Good Waste Management Practices | Create |
| 4 (a) | P, the bottom layer, should be coarse material such as dry maize stalks, twigs or sticks, which allows air to enter and water to drain. Q should be green plant material and kitchen waste such as grass cuttings, weeds and peels. R should be a thin layer of topsoil or animal droppings, which supplies the micro-organisms. S is the covering layer, of palm fronds, dry grass or an old sack, which keeps in the moisture and warmth. | Composting and the Science Behind It | Understand |
| 4 (b) | (i) Water is added to keep the heap moist, because the bacteria and fungi that break down the waste need moisture in order to live and work; a dry heap stops decaying. (ii) The warmth is given off because these micro-organisms are respiring as they feed on the waste, and respiration releases heat energy. | Composting and the Science Behind It | Understand |
| 4 (c) | Turning the heap lets fresh air, and so oxygen, into the inner parts. The bacteria and fungi that break down waste quickly are aerobic: they need oxygen for respiration. Turning also mixes the layers so that all the material decays evenly. If the heap were never turned, the inside would run out of oxygen and anaerobic decay would take over: decomposition would be slow, the heap would give off foul-smelling gases, and the compost would take much longer to form. | Composting and the Science Behind It | Analyse |
| 4 (d) | Composting turns the waste into manure, which supplies nutrients to the school garden and improves the soil, so the waste becomes a useful resource and money is saved on fertiliser. It also keeps the waste out of the refuse heaps and gutters, so there are fewer flies, less smell and less burden on the town's dump. | Composting and the Science Behind It | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | Research good waste management practices from books, the internet and the environmental health office; obtain permission from the head teacher, the market queen or the assembly and inform the traders; fix the date, divide the members into groups and agree on what each group will do; arrange for the tools and materials needed - brooms, rakes, shovels, sacks, gloves and nose masks; and arrange with the waste company or the assembly for a vehicle to carry away the waste collected. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Apply |
| 5 (b) | Hand gloves, to protect the hands from cuts by broken glass and metal and from germs in the waste; nose masks, to keep out dust and the bad smell and to reduce the breathing in of germs; and boots or closed shoes, to protect the feet from sharp objects and dirty water. Overalls or old clothing keep the body and uniform clean. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Apply |
| 5 (c) | They should sort the waste as they collect it, into separate sacks or bins. The organic waste - peels, food remains and leaves - should be taken to a compost pit to be made into manure. The plastic sachets and bottles should be collected separately and sent to a recycling centre or buyer. Paper and cartons should be kept dry and sent for recycling or reused. Only the little that is left - broken glass, dirty rags and other unusable material - should be wrapped safely and handed over to the waste company for proper disposal, not burnt in the open. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Create |
| 6 (a) | Title and date, with the place of the exercise; aim or purpose, saying what the project set out to do; materials and methods, listing the tools used and describing how the work was done; findings or observations, giving the kinds and quantity of waste found and the condition of the place; conclusion, saying what was achieved; and recommendations, suggesting what the traders and the assembly should do next. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Create |
| 6 (b) | Provide enough covered, labelled bins at several points in the market and empty them regularly; arrange a fixed day each week for a general clean-up of the square; employ or assign someone to sweep the market daily; educate the traders through announcements and posters; and set a by-law with penalties for dumping waste in the gutters. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Evaluate |
| 6 (c) | It passes on what the club learnt to the whole school, so that many more pupils know how waste should be managed and may change their own habits and those of their homes. It also makes the club's findings and recommendations public, so that the school authorities can act on them, and it encourages other pupils to take part in the next project. | Effects of Poor Waste Management and Community Action | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The terms biodegradable, non-biodegradable, segregation, composting, recycling and reuse must be used correctly; 'reuse' written for 'recycle' earns no mark. (3) Where a practice is asked for, the answer must state an action; 'keep the place clean' alone is too vague. (4) In classification tasks, mark each entry separately and do not carry an error forward. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **organic (food or kitchen) waste** (1 mark).
- B - **plastic waste** (1 mark).
- C - **glass and metal waste** (1 mark).
- D - **paper waste** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'biodegradable waste' for A and D only if the material is also named.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- A - **biodegradable** (1 mark).
- B - **non-biodegradable** (1 mark).
- C - **non-biodegradable** (1 mark).
- D - **biodegradable** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Mark each entry separately.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Biodegradable waste is broken down by micro-organisms into simple substances** (1 mark).
- **Non-biodegradable waste is not broken down and stays in the environment for a very long time** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'One rots and the other does not' is accepted for the first mark only if decay is clearly meant.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Sort it into a separate container and send it for recycling (accept: bury it safely in a pit)** (1 mark).
- **Because glass and metal do not decay; broken glass causes injury and tins collect water in which mosquitoes breed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Burn it' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **flies spread typhoid, cholera or diarrhoea**; **mosquitoes breeding in the tins spread malaria**; **rats and cockroaches spread disease**; **the smell and smoke affect breathing**; **sharp objects cause injury** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A disease named without its link to the heap still earns the mark if the link is obvious.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **The organic waste is decaying, being broken down by bacteria and fungi** (1 mark).
- **Gases such as ammonia and hydrogen sulphide are released, and these smell bad** (1 mark).
- **Mosquitoes lay eggs in the still water and breed there, spreading malaria** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'rotting' for decay.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **burning plastics and rubber releases poisonous smoke and gases that pollute the air and harm the lungs**; **the fire may spread and destroy property**; **useful material that could be composted or recycled is destroyed** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is against the law' earns no mark without a scientific reason.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Reduce: produce less waste by using less and avoiding unnecessary items** (1 mark).
- **Reuse: use an article again as it is, instead of throwing it away** (1 mark).
- **Recycle: process used material into new articles** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example alone, with no explanation, earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Reduce: one sound example, such as a refillable bottle instead of daily sachets** (1 mark).
- **Reuse: one sound example, such as tins used for seedlings** (1 mark).
- **Recycle: one sound example, such as collecting plastic bottles for a recycling centre** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example placed under the wrong term earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Separating waste into different containers according to its kind** (1 mark).
- **So that each kind can be composted, reused or recycled instead of being dumped** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'sorting' for segregation.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Three sensible labels, such as organic waste, plastics and paper** (1 mark).
- **A correct item named for each bin** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Labels such as 'rubbish 1, rubbish 2' earn no mark.*

### Question 4 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **coarse dry material: maize stalks, twigs or sticks** (1 mark).
- Q - **green plant material and kitchen waste: grass, weeds, peels** (1 mark).
- R - **topsoil or animal droppings (manure)** (1 mark).
- S - **a cover of palm fronds, dry grass or an old sack** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Plastics or tins named in any layer earn no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Water keeps the heap moist** (1 mark); **the micro-organisms need moisture to live and act on the waste** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The micro-organisms respire as they feed, and respiration gives out heat** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The Sun heats it' earns no mark for (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Turning lets air (oxygen) into the heap** (1 mark).
- **The decomposing micro-organisms are aerobic and need oxygen; turning also mixes the layers for even decay** (1 mark).
- **Without turning, decay becomes slow and anaerobic and the heap smells foul** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the heap would rot slowly and smell' for the third mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the waste is turned into manure that feeds the garden and improves the soil**; **money is saved on fertiliser**; **less waste goes to the dump, so fewer flies, less smell and less pollution** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is cheaper' alone, with no explanation, earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **research good waste management practices**; **obtain permission from the authorities and inform the traders**; **fix a date and share the members into groups with clear duties**; **collect the tools and protective items needed**; **arrange for the waste collected to be carted away** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Tell everybody' is too vague for a mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Hand gloves - to protect the hands from cuts and germs** (1 mark).
- **Nose mask - to keep out dust, smell and germs** (1 mark).
- **Boots or closed shoes - to protect the feet from sharp objects and dirty water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for an item named without a reason.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **Sort (segregate) the waste as it is collected** (1 mark).
- **Compost the organic waste** (1 mark).
- **Send the plastics, paper and metal for recycling or reuse** (1 mark).
- **Hand over only the remaining unusable waste for proper disposal, with no open burning** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A plan that ends with everything being dumped or burnt scores no more than 1 mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **title, date and place**; **aim of the project**; **materials and method used**; **findings or observations**; **conclusion**; **recommendations** (1 mark each, the heading with a correct phrase of content).
  - *Marking note: A heading with nothing said about its content earns half of nothing - award the mark only when both are given.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **provide enough covered, labelled bins and empty them regularly**; **fix a weekly clean-up day**; **assign someone to sweep daily**; **educate the traders with posters and announcements**; **enforce a by-law against dumping in gutters** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'They should keep it clean' is too vague for a mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **It spreads the knowledge to the whole school, so that others change their habits** (1 mark).
- **It makes the findings and recommendations known so that they can be acted upon (accept: it encourages others to take part)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Because the teacher asked for it' earns no mark.*

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand has only one indicator, but it is a wide one. Do not let the teaching stop at lists of types of waste: the curriculum asks pupils to 'explain the science underlying' waste management, which means decomposition, micro-organisms, respiration and pollution.
- Biodegradable does not mean 'soft'. Pupils often classify paper as non-biodegradable because it is manufactured, and classify a tin as biodegradable because it rusts. Rusting is not decomposition by micro-organisms; make the distinction explicitly.
- Reduce, reuse and recycle are frequently confused in scripts. Fix each with one memorable school example - a refillable bottle, a tin used for seedlings, sachets sent to a recycling buyer - and insist that candidates match the example to the right term.
- A compost heap is the cheapest laboratory in the school. Build one, take its temperature with a thermometer after a week, and the warmth in Fig. 2 stops being a fact to memorise and becomes evidence of respiration.
- Open burning must be treated as a wrong answer throughout. Pupils meet it every day, so they need the reason - the poisonous gases from plastics and rubber - not merely the prohibition.
- Follow-up work: carry out the clean-up project the indicator describes, weigh or count the sacks of each kind of waste collected, and let the club present the figures at assembly. The report in Question 6 then writes itself.

| 2 (a) | The first child has kwashiorkor; the second has rickets; the third has anaemia. | Deficiency Diseases and the Nutrients Concerned | Analyse |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Diseases and nutrients must be named correctly and spelt recognisably; 'kwashiorkor' written for 'marasmus' or the reverse earns no mark. (3) A symptom must be something that can be seen or felt in the patient; naming the cause instead of a symptom earns no mark. (4) A method of prevention must state an action. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A - **protein** (1 mark).
- B - **vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** (1 mark).
- C - **vitamin A (accept: fats and oils)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Vitamins' alone for B or C earns no mark; the particular vitamin is required.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Protein - growth and repair of worn-out tissues** (1 mark).
- **Vitamin C - keeps the gums, skin and blood vessels healthy; helps wounds to heal** (1 mark).
- **Vitamin A - needed for vision, especially in dim light, and for healthy skin** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It makes the body strong' is too vague for a mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- A - **kwashiorkor** (1 mark).
- B - **scurvy** (1 mark).
- C - **night blindness** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'protein-energy malnutrition' for A.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Carbohydrates - one local example such as yam or kenkey** (1 mark).
- **Fats and oils - one local example such as palm oil or groundnut** (1 mark).
- **Vitamins and mineral salts - one local example such as kontomire or oranges (accept water and roughage)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A class named without an example earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- First child - **kwashiorkor** (1 mark).
- Second child - **rickets** (1 mark).
- Third child - **anaemia** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Mark each diagnosis separately.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- First child - **protein** (1 mark).
- Second child - **vitamin D (and calcium)** (1 mark).
- Third child - **iron** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The nutrient must match the disease named in (a).*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **Two protein-rich foods, such as fish, beans, eggs, groundnuts or milk** (1 mark each).
- **Two further effects, such as stunted growth, weakness, low resistance to infection, poor mental development or even death** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A food that is chiefly a carbohydrate, such as kenkey, earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Scurvy - **symptom: bleeding, swollen gums (accept slow healing of wounds)** (1 mark); **prevention: eat fresh fruits and vegetables rich in vitamin C** (1 mark).
- Goitre - **symptom: swelling in front of the neck** (1 mark); **prevention: use iodated salt; eat sea fish** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A cause written in the symptom column earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Sunlight on the skin helps the body to make vitamin D** (1 mark).
- **Vitamin D helps the body to absorb calcium, which hardens the bones** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The sun is good for the body' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the foods grown are mostly starchy staples, so meals are not balanced**; **the protein foods and vegetables are sold instead of eaten**; **ignorance of what each food supplies**; **poor cooking habits destroy the vitamins**; **customs that deny children certain foods** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'They are poor' alone earns no mark without an explanation.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A very small agent that can multiply only inside the living cells of a host** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **they spread easily, often before symptoms appear**; **antibiotics do not cure them**; **the viruses change into new forms**; **there is often no specific medicine** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is a germ' alone is too vague for (i).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **In droplets from coughing, sneezing or talking, breathed in or picked up from surfaces on the hands** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Infected people travel to markets, funerals and other gatherings in nearby communities** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Travellers carry it by air, road or sea, often before showing symptoms** (1 mark).
- **One correct symptom named, such as fever, dry cough or loss of taste and smell** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'By air' alone for (iii) is not enough; the travel of infected people must be clear.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **It spread to very many countries and continents at the same time** (1 mark); **and affected a very large number of people, beyond local control** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Ebola spreads by direct contact with body fluids, not chiefly by droplets in the air** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Many people died' alone does not define a pandemic.*

### Question 5 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **washing the hands with soap under running water** (1 mark).
- B - **wearing a nose mask** (1 mark).
- C - **keeping a social (physical) distance** (1 mark).
- D - **vaccination or immunisation** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Injection' is accepted for D only if vaccination is clearly meant.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- A - **removes and destroys virus particles on the hands** (1 mark).
- B - **traps the droplets breathed out and keeps out those from others** (1 mark).
- C - **droplets fall to the ground before reaching another person** (1 mark).
- D - **the body makes antibodies in advance, so the person is protected** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A repeat of the name of the measure, with no explanation, earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **cover the nose and mouth when coughing or sneezing**; **avoid crowded places**; **use hand sanitiser**; **isolate or quarantine infected persons**; **avoid handshaking and touching the face**; **keep rooms well ventilated** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A measure already shown in Fig. 2 earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **schools close and learning is lost**; **businesses close, people lose their incomes and the economy suffers**; **hospitals are overwhelmed so other patients suffer**; **travel, trade and social gatherings are restricted** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that both say 'people suffer' count once.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Observe the safety measures and report symptoms early** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Educate and support one another, avoid stigma and help the health workers** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Provide testing, treatment, vaccines and accurate information, and enforce regulations** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A role placed at the wrong level earns no mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **People hide their illness instead of reporting it, so cases are found late and spread unchecked** (1 mark).
- **The family is left without food and support and must move about to find help, spreading the disease** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is unkind' alone earns no mark; the effect on the spread of disease is required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **a clear heading naming the disease**; **the main symptoms**; **how the disease is spread**; **the preventive measures, with simple pictures**; **what to do and where to report, with a contact number**; **large, simple lettering in a language the people read** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Make it beautiful' earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 2: Human Health | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.5.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of common deficiency diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention. **B7/JHS1.5.2.2** - Demonstrate knowledge of the nature of selected viral diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and management.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 2: Human Health, Basic 7, pages 82 and 83 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.5.2.1 carries indicator B7/JHS1.5.2.1.1, explain the relationship between food nutrients and common deficiency diseases and how they affect humans, with the exemplars: name and analyse food nutrients such as carbohydrates, proteins, fatty acids, and their uses in the human body; discuss and make presentations on deficiency diseases associated with lack of food nutrients such as carbohydrates, proteins, fatty acids, vitamins and others in the human body; relate the nutrients they gain or lack to the foods they normally eat, for example lack of protein leads to kwashiorkor and lack of iron leads to anaemia; and describe symptoms, effects and prevention of common deficiency diseases such as night blindness, rickets, scurvy, kwashiorkor and others. Content standard B7/JHS1.5.2.2 carries indicator B7/JHS1.5.2.2.1, explain the nature of viral diseases with special emphasis on corona virus (COVID-19), Ebola and H1N1 disease, its causes, symptoms, effects on humans and its prevention, with the exemplars: discuss the nature of viral diseases; search for information and make presentations on COVID-19, Ebola and H1N1 diseases and their mode of transmission from person to person, community to community and from country to country; describe the symptoms, effects and prevention of COVID-19, Ebola and H1N1 diseases and why they are declared pandemic; describe the role of individuals, community members and government in managing COVID-19, Ebola and H1N1 diseases; and design and produce a poster to educate their community members on the incidence and control of the named viral diseases.

> Note: I1 (B7/JHS1.5.2.1.1) carries topics 17.1 to 17.3 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B7/JHS1.5.2.2.1) carries topics 17.4 to 17.6 and Questions 4, 5 and 6. The 'design and produce a poster' exemplar is examined in Question 6(c) as a written plan of the poster, which is the part of that activity a written paper can fairly test. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these content standards written as B7.5.2.1 and B7.5.2.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Pupils must be able to go in both directions: from the nutrient to the disease and from the symptom to the nutrient. Question 1 goes one way and Question 2 the other, and candidates who have learnt only a list of diseases are caught by the second.
- Insist on local foods in the answers. A pupil who writes 'eat protein' has not answered a question that asks what the mother should buy; 'fish, beans and eggs' has.
- A symptom is what is seen or felt in the patient. Many candidates write 'lack of vitamin C' in a symptom column; that is the cause. Train pupils to separate cause, symptom, effect and prevention - the four words the indicator itself uses.
- Antibiotics do not cure viral diseases. This single fact, taught early, prevents a great deal of harm in the community as well as earning marks.
- For the viral diseases, teach the three levels of spread named in the exemplar - person to person, community to community, country to country - and the difference between droplet spread (COVID-19, H1N1) and body-fluid contact (Ebola). Question 4 is built on exactly that distinction.
- Stigma is a scientific problem, not merely a social one: it drives cases underground. Question 6(b) rewards pupils who can explain that.
- Follow-up work: let groups actually design and display the poster named in the curriculum, and judge them on content - symptoms, spread, prevention, where to report - rather than on decoration.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) The name of a career must be the name of the worker or of the field, for example 'pharmacist' or 'pharmacy'; 'he works in a hospital' is not the name of a career. (3) Where a scientist is named, the field of work and the contribution must agree; a correct name with the wrong work earns no mark. (4) Titles such as Professor and Doctor need not be written, and spelling of the names is marked generously provided the person is clearly recognisable. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **laboratory scientist or technician (accept biologist, chemist)** (1 mark).
- B - **doctor or nurse (accept any named health worker)** (1 mark).
- C - **agricultural scientist (accept agronomist, soil scientist)** (1 mark).
- D - **civil engineer (accept architect, surveyor)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'He works in a laboratory' is not the name of a career.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- A - **tests samples so that disease is detected and food and water are safe** (1 mark).
- B - **treats the sick and immunises people, saving lives** (1 mark).
- C - **improves crops and methods, so more food is produced** (1 mark).
- D - **designs safe roads, bridges, dams and buildings** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'He earns money' is not a benefit to the people.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Integrated science and mathematics (accept English for one)** (1 mark).
- **Reason: science supplies the knowledge and mathematics the measurement and calculation that all these careers require** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Subjects named with no reason earn 1 mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **A scientist carries out research and makes discoveries in a field of science** (1 mark).
- **A science educator studies and improves the teaching and learning of science (trains teachers, writes books, develops the curriculum)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'One is cleverer than the other' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Alexander Fleming** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Penicillin** (1 mark).
- (iii) **A substance from the mould had killed or stopped the growth of the bacteria** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Antibiotic' alone is accepted for (ii) only if penicillin is named.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Q - **the substance is tested and studied in the laboratory and the results recorded** (1 mark).
- R - **the medicine is manufactured in a factory and packed** (1 mark).
- S - **the patient is treated and recovers** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Credit any clear wording of each stage.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Science makes the discovery and tests it** (1 mark).
- **Industry manufactures it in large quantities so that it reaches the people** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A general statement with no reference to the stages earns 1 mark at most.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **keen observation**; **curiosity and an open mind**; **patience and careful follow-up work**; **careful recording and reporting of findings** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'He was clever' is too vague for a mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Allotey - **mathematics and physics** (1 mark).
- Oduro - **food science (food and crop processing)** (1 mark).
- Addy - **biochemistry and the biological sciences** (1 mark).
- Anamuah-Mensah - **science education** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A field written against the wrong person earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Prof. Theophilus Ossei-Anto** (1 mark); **Prof. Christian Anthony-Krueger** (1 mark).
- **They improve the teaching and learning of science, so that more pupils understand it and take up science careers** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any other correctly named Ghanaian science educator is accepted.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **it shows that Ghanaians can succeed in science**; **it gives models the pupils can relate to**; **it shows science applied to Ghana's own problems**; **it builds national pride and encourages pupils to serve their country** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two answers that both say 'to encourage us' count once.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **One sound home example, such as a refrigerator or a mobile phone** (1 mark).
- (ii) **One sound school example, such as computers or laboratory apparatus** (1 mark).
- (iii) **One sound community example, such as treated water, electricity or mobile money** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The same example may not be used twice.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **people communicate quickly over long distances**; **farmers and traders check market prices before travelling**; **money is sent and received by mobile money**; **emergencies can be reported at once**; **information for learning becomes available** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'It is nice to have' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **air and water pollution from factories and vehicles**; **plastic and electronic waste**; **loss of jobs to machines**; **too much screen time harming study and health**; **destruction of land and rivers by mining machinery** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A harmful effect must be stated, not merely a device named.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Putting a new or improved idea into practical use to solve a problem** (1 mark).
- **One sound Ghanaian example, such as mobile money, delivery drones or solar lamps** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A copy of an existing article is not an innovation.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **First career named** (1 mark) **with a sound reason** (1 mark).
- **Second career named** (1 mark) **with a sound reason** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A career named with no reason earns 1 mark only.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **study science and mathematics seriously and ask questions**; **take part in practical work and the science club**; **read about science and about scientists**; **keep a portfolio of findings**; **visit places of work and talk to scientists** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Pray to become a scientist' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The belief is wrong; science needs observation and hard work, which do not depend on sex** (1 mark).
- **Evidence: named Ghanaian women scientists, such as Prof. Ibok Oduro or Prof. Ewurama Addy (accept women doctors, engineers and so on)** (1 mark).
- **Excluding girls wastes half the nation's talent, so girls should be encouraged equally** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A reply that agrees with the belief earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **An organised collection of one's own work and evidence on a topic** (1 mark).
- **One reason: it keeps the evidence in one place for presentation and shows how the work has developed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'A bag for books' earns no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **notes from books and the internet**; **photographs or drawings of technology in use**; **records of interviews with people at work**; **newspaper cuttings and leaflets**; **tables or charts of data the class collected**; **a written report with conclusions** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Everything about science' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **speak clearly and in an orderly sequence, keeping to time**; **show charts, pictures and specimens as evidence**; **share the work among the members**; **practise beforehand and be ready for questions** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: 'Wear fine clothes' earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 3: Science and Industry | **Class:** Basic 7 (JHS 1)

**Content Standard:** **B7/JHS1.5.3.1** - Realise how careers in science can improve human life, and research about Ghanaian and internationally recognised scientists and science educators and model after them.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry, Basic 7, page 84 of the published PDF. Content standard B7/JHS1.5.3.1 carries the single indicator B7/JHS1.5.3.1.1, printed in the curriculum as 'B.7. 5.3.1.1', discover and explain how careers in science can improve human conditions and relate these careers to the work of great national and international scientists and science educators, with the exemplars: describe various careers in science and relate them to the work of national scientists, for example Prof. Ibok Oduro, Prof. Francis Allotey, Prof. Ewurama Addy, and science educationists such as Prof. Anamuah-Mensah, Prof. Theophilus Ossei-Anto and Prof. Christian Anthony-Krueger; describe various careers in science and relate them to the work of international scientists such as Albert Einstein, Alexander Fleming, Charles Darwin and Stephen Hawking through presentations; research and build a portfolio on the impact of science, technology and innovation in homes, schools, communities and the universe and make a presentation; and identify the science and technology careers that Ghana must focus on and give reasons.

> Note: This sub-strand has a single content standard with a single indicator, so every item in the paper is set on I1. The paper is spread over the indicator's four exemplars: careers in science (topic 18.1, Question 1); the national scientists and science educators named in the curriculum (topic 18.2, Question 3); the international scientists named in the curriculum (topic 18.3, Question 2); the portfolio on the impact of science, technology and innovation (topic 18.4, Question 4 and Question 6); and the careers Ghana must focus on, with reasons (topic 18.5, Question 5). The curriculum prints this indicator's code as 'B.7. 5.3.1.1'; it is reproduced here in the regular form B7/JHS1.5.3.1.1. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find the content standard written as B7.5.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Keep the factual load fair. The curriculum names the scientists pupils should know, and nothing beyond the field of work and the main contribution should be demanded. Dates of birth and personal details are not science.
- Pair every name with a piece of work. 'Allotey - mathematics and physics' and 'Fleming - penicillin' are what earn marks; a list of names learnt by heart, with no work attached, earns nothing in Question 2 or Question 3.
- Careers should be taught through the workplace, as in Fig. 1. Ask pupils what they have seen a laboratory technician, a nurse, an extension officer or a mason actually doing, and the answers to Question 1 come from their own experience.
- Fleming's dish is the best lesson in this sub-strand: an accident that was noticed. Use it to teach observation, curiosity and follow-up rather than as a story to be recited.
- Insist on reasons in Question 5. 'Ghana should focus on engineering' is half an answer; 'because our roads, bridges and water systems must be designed and maintained by our own people' completes it.
- Girls must be addressed directly. The curriculum names two Ghanaian women scientists; put their pictures on the classroom wall beside Einstein's and the message of Question 5(c) is made without a word.
- Follow-up work: invite a local scientist, nurse, engineer or extension officer to the class, let the pupils interview the visitor and file the record in the portfolio of Question 6.
